Publisher’s Preface

Anyone with a serious interest in Arab cultural life knows the historic intellectual importance of Husayn Muruwwa’s Materialist Tendencies in Arab-Islamic Philosophy. They also know the gap this book filled in the Arabic library, especially for democratic and progressive readers. Muruwwa intended it to be an encyclopedic work, useful to intellectuals in general and progressive intellectuals in particular, as well as university students and anyone interested in cultural questions more broadly.

But this enormous book was originally published by Dar al-Farabi in only two volumes. The first ran to more than a thousand pages, while the second reached around eight hundred. Edition followed edition, and the book gradually became an essential reference for intellectuals, researchers, and students at Arab universities.

Today, some readers may be interested only in the pre-Islamic period, for example. Others may care mainly about Muruwwa’s method, or about his materialist analysis of Ibn Sīnā’s philosophy, without needing the other sections. Buying only the part a reader needs also costs less than buying the entire work.

We have therefore decided to publish a new edition in four volumes:

Volume I: The methodological introduction, followed by studies of the pre-Islamic period and of the rise and early period of Islam.

Volume II: Kalām—the Muʿtazila and Ashʿarism—followed by Aristotelian formal logic, which the Muʿtazila were the first to use.

Volume III: Sufism, examined through two examples only: Ibn ʿArabī and al-Suhrawardī; the Epistles of the Brethren of Purity; and a brief account of the development of the sciences among the Arabs.

Volume IV: The mature stage of philosophy: al-Kindī, al-Fārābī, and Ibn Sīnā.

The Shiʿa and the Kharijites

A — The Umayyad State

1 — Between Two Caliphs

Historians usually date the beginning of the Umayyad period to 661 CE. But this date reflects an Islamic judgment more than a purely historical one.

Muʿāwiya ibn Abī Sufyān had already proclaimed himself caliph in 660 and received the oath of allegiance from the people of Syria. Yet ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib was still alive, and a large part of the Muslim population—in Iraq, the Hijaz, and other regions—continued to recognize ʿAlī as the fourth caliph.

In effect, historians have removed one year from the history of the Umayyad caliphate because most Muslims considered ʿAlī to be the legitimate caliph during that year. Muʿāwiya’s rule was accepted as an established reality only after the period of the four Rightly Guided Caliphs ended with ʿAlī’s death.

For one year of Islamic history, then, religious and political authority was divided between two caliphs at the same time: ʿAlī and Muʿāwiya. It was also divided between two capitals: Kufa, ʿAlī’s capital, and Damascus, Muʿāwiya’s.

One sign of Muʿāwiya’s political skill was his decision to proclaim himself caliph in Jerusalem. There stood Bayt al-Maqdis, or the al-Aqsa Mosque, which Muslims regarded as comparable to Mecca in sanctity. In the earliest period of Islam, Muslims had been instructed to face al-Aqsa during prayer. This was later changed, and they were instructed instead to face the Kaʿba in Mecca. For this reason, al-Aqsa is known among Muslims as “the first of the two prayer directions.”

Muʿāwiya wanted to give his caliphate a religious character. Since he could not use the Kaʿba for this purpose, he chose the place that held a corresponding sacred status in Muslim eyes. His immediate aim, at least, was to influence the Muslims of Syria, secure the Umayyad throne in its first stronghold, and then prepare the way for extending that authority throughout the other Muslim regions.

2 — The Revival of Tribal Loyalties

The Umayyad state became known for moving away from the Islamic principle of equality among peoples. The Qurʾān had declared, “The most honored of you in the sight of God is the most righteous of you” (Qurʾān 49:13), while the Prophet had said, “An Arab has no superiority over a non-Arab except through piety.”

In fact, the strong Arab partisanship that marked Umayyad policy through much of its history had already begun under Muʿāwiya ibn Abī Sufyān himself.

Given the circumstances in which Muʿāwiya established his state in the name of the “Islamic caliphate,” he had no reason to expect that his rule would quickly become secure throughout the whole Islamic world. At the moment when he declared himself caliph, the political struggle had become so intense that the new state faced serious threats from every direction.

Muʿāwiya could rely on little beyond the people of Syria, both Muslim and non-Muslim, to withstand these threats. From the way events looked at the time, several outcomes must have seemed possible to him. We have strong reason to think that one of the most important was the possibility that his state would remain confined to its original stronghold: Syria. At that time, the Syrian region included what are now Syria, Palestine, and Lebanon.

These circumstances forced Muʿāwiya to work on two fronts that may at first seem contradictory, though in reality they were not.

On one side, he built a close alliance with the original inhabitants of Syria, especially the Christians. On the other, he formed an equally strong alliance with the most powerful Arab tribes whose main branches lived there.

These were the Qaḥṭānī, or Kalbī, tribes. They belonged to one of the two broad ancestral groupings into which the Arab people were traditionally divided: the Qaḥṭānī or Kalbī group, associated with southern Arabia, and the ʿAdnānī or Qaysī group, associated with northern Arabia.

Most of the Arabs of Syria were Kalbīs. Some were Christians who had adopted Christianity during the period of Byzantine rule.

When the Arab conquest of the region took place, the conquering forces included Arabs from both major groupings, Kalbī and Qaysī. At that stage, the common aims of conquest prevented their older rivalries and loyalties from coming openly to the surface.

Because Muʿāwiya belonged to the Umayyad branch of Quraysh, we might have expected him to side with the Qaysīs, since Quraysh itself was Qaysī. But Muʿāwiya was a skilled politician. Tribal loyalty mattered to him only when it helped his political aims.

He therefore had little difficulty forming an alliance with the Kalbīs against the Qaysīs. Through this alliance, he could win the support of the different important forces in Syria.

He strengthened the alliance through marriage. He married Maymūna1, a Kalbī woman, and later married their son Yazīd to another woman from the same tribal group.

By then, tribal rivalries had already begun to revive after the political struggle that erupted with the killing of ʿUthmān. Material conditions also played a part. The Kalbīs in Syria generally enjoyed better living conditions than the Qaysīs elsewhere, and this difference helped fuel jealousy and hostility between the two sides.

Muʿāwiya’s alliance with the Kalbīs gave the Qaysīs a further reason for resentment. The alliance included both Muslim and Christian Kalbīs in Syria.

From this point onward, the rivalry between these two major Arab groupings became less a spontaneous feature of tribal life and more an organized political force.

Muʿāwiya wanted to make the Arab population a basic source of support for both his own ambitions and those of the Umayyad aristocracy. His aim was to extend his new state into all the regions where Arabs had already established themselves, and both Kalbīs and Qaysīs could be found in most of those regions.

He understood that an alliance with the Kalbīs in Syria could help him win the support of Kalbīs wherever they lived. And the sharper the tribal struggle became between the two Arab groupings, the more strongly Kalbīs everywhere would rally around a ruler who had become their ally. His new state would itself become an important part of their strength against their Qaysī rivals.

Muʿāwiya eventually achieved what he wanted.

The Umayyad state he had founded moved beyond its original Syrian stronghold and soon became the sole Arab state for almost a century—eighty-nine years.

The Kalbīs remained one of its strongest sources of support. They even became the decisive force that saved the state from collapse after the death of Muʿāwiya II ibn Yazīd, the direct grandson of Muʿāwiya I.

At that point, the Umayyad state entered a crisis that nearly destroyed it. ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr claimed the caliphate for himself and won support among Muslims in the Hijaz and Iraq. The Qaysīs sided with him.

A fierce battle then broke out between the Qaysī and Kalbī tribes at Marj Rāhiṭ, near Damascus. The Kalbīs fought fiercely to defend the Umayyad state because their own interests were tied to it. They defeated their Qaysī opponents and restored the state’s strength.

But the result of the battle also transferred control of the Umayyad state from its founding family, the house of Muʿāwiya—the descendants of Abū Sufyān—to another branch of the Umayyads, the descendants of al-Ḥakam.

Immediately after the Battle of Marj Rāhiṭ, Marwān ibn al-Ḥakam took the Umayyad throne in Damascus. His branch of the family remained in power until the state finally fell.

Only three members of Muʿāwiya’s own line ruled the Umayyad state: Muʿāwiya himself, his son Yazīd, and his grandson Muʿāwiya ibn Yazīd.

3 — The Social System of the Umayyad State

We have seen that Muʿāwiya I relied on Arab tribes as a base of support for his rule.

Does this mean that the social system of the Umayyad state was itself based on tribal organization? Did Muʿāwiya turn society backward, restoring the tribal system that we saw already beginning to break apart even before Islam?

History cannot simply be turned backward by objective conditions. How, then, could it be turned backward by one person’s will?

In fact, Muʿāwiya had no such intention anyway. He was founding a state, and the creation of a state was itself historically more advanced than tribal organization.

The state he founded also met a historical need that had emerged as class divisions developed within society. A state required stability and accumulation, and both stood in a close, changing relationship with wider social development.

The conditions for this already existed in Syria when the Arabs conquered it.

By the time Muʿāwiya became governor there, the old natural economy had already been breaking down for a long time. New economic relationships were taking its place, not only in Syria but also in Mesopotamia and other parts of the eastern region.

Centers of exchange had appeared. At first they drew in local trade, then gradually expanded to serve a much wider region.

Historical development had therefore already moved a long way toward a social and economic system that went beyond the old natural economy.

Under Muʿāwiya, first as governor and then as caliph, the most important feature of this system across the region was its feudal character, combined with a strong military structure. This was a continuation of patterns that had developed under Byzantine and Sasanian rule.

Earlier, when discussing the caliphate of ʿUthmān, we saw how the Umayyad governors he appointed in the provinces quickly became landowners.

They had originally entered these regions not only as conquerors, but also as bearers of a new message that appealed to local people by promising an end to the oppression of their previous rulers. Once the new governors moved beyond that role and began acquiring land and wealth for themselves, the result was a social revolt that eventually led to the killing of the caliph himself.

The conduct of these Arab governors was not simply a matter of individual choices. It reflected their social and class position, but there were also objective historical forces at work.

Before the Arab-Islamic conquest, a particular form of military feudal relations had already developed in Syria and Mesopotamia. This had become the dominant feature of the social system in those regions.

That existing system inevitably influenced the form taken by Arab rule after the conquest, especially once Syria entered a period of stability under Muʿāwiya, first as governor and later as caliph.

The Umayyad ruling class also had a direct interest in making as much use as possible of a system whose roots and dominant relations of production were already firmly established. They therefore pushed further in the same direction, strengthening and deepening its foundations.

Their class interest had a very concrete basis.

Muʿāwiya and his family came into possession of large areas of land that had belonged before the Arab-Islamic conquest to the Byzantine emperor and the Byzantine aristocracy. Under the Islamic system of landholding, these lands should have become public property belonging to the Islamic state.

Instead, under Muʿāwiya and his relatives and close associates, they became private property.

Muʿāwiya employed Syrian experts to organize farming and irrigation on these lands. He and his closest relatives and supporters soon became some of the largest landowners in the region. Together they formed a new, semi-feudal aristocracy after the conquest.

Meanwhile, most other Arabs were occupied with military campaigns in distant regions or stationed in military camps to defend the state against uprisings and to fight political movements opposed to Umayyad rule in Iraq and elsewhere.

These conditions of conquest and internal political conflict gradually created certain habits among the Arabs.

One was their contempt for agricultural and craft work. The circumstances of conquest had left much of this work to slaves and to the original inhabitants of the conquered regions.

Together with surviving tribal traditions, these habits encouraged a sense of superiority over non-Arabs. The Umayyad state itself adopted this attitude and referred to non-Arabs as mawālī, or clients.

Under Umayyad rule, then, anyone who was not Arab could be described as a mawlā.

This kind of discrimination became one of the forces that helped destroy the Umayyad state before it had even completed a full century of existence.

When Muʿāwiya helped revive tribal loyalties early in his rule, however, he did not originally intend to make discrimination of this kind a permanent principle of Umayyad government.

His purpose at that stage was more immediate. He wanted to use the rivalry between the Qaysīs and Kalbīs to strengthen a throne that still faced serious danger after the caliphate had moved away from the political foundations of the Rightly Guided period.

The Umayyad caliphs who came after him went much further. They emphasized Arab privilege so strongly that they provoked resentment among the non-Arab populations of their state and encouraged an opposing form of ethnic hostility.

That counter-hostility later helped produce the movement that appeared toward the end of Umayyad rule and continued to develop under the Abbasids until it became hostile to the Arab people themselves, as well as to their history and culture.

Its hostility toward everything Arab eventually created an intellectual current that attacked Arab literature, thought, values, and traditions. This was the well-known Shuʿūbiyya movement.

In discussing the social system of the Umayyad period, we should also mention something else Muʿāwiya achieved as caliph: he gave the emerging Arab state a more concrete and developed administrative structure, helping turn it into a new feature of Arab civilization.

He established various dīwāns, which performed some of the functions that government departments or ministries perform today. There were offices for taxation and customs duties, accounts, official correspondence, the judiciary, and other areas of government.

At first, however, some of these offices kept their records in local languages: Persian in Iran and Iraq, Greek in Syria, and Coptic in Egypt.

The currency in circulation also remained much as it had been before the Arab conquest until the reigns of ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān and al-Walīd ibn ʿAbd al-Malik.

These two caliphs introduced important reforms in the organization of the state. They created a currency of its own, standardized systems of government administration, surveyed and registered land in Arabic, and replaced the older local languages with Arabic throughout the state’s administration and official offices.

The class character of the Umayyad state appeared in several other ways as well, apart from the general semi-feudal character of its social system.

The Umayyad government, and especially Muʿāwiya’s government, allowed the existing local ruling class to keep many of its old powers, including authority over courts and policing.

Later, when state institutions were Arabized under the Marwanid caliphs, these powers passed instead to groups close to the ruling class.

The form had changed, but the class character remained. Given the class character of the state itself, this was only to be expected.

During the early years of their rule, the Umayyads tried to offer some new advantages to the original inhabitants of the conquered regions.

In Iran, for example, they reduced some of the enormous inequalities in rights and duties that had existed under the old social order between the upper and lower classes.

They also reduced taxes on Nabataeans and Syriacs in Egypt and Syria, and they did not force them to convert to Islam.

But during the final decades of Umayyad rule, a combination of objective conditions and choices made by the rulers themselves changed this policy.

Harsh and arbitrary treatment of the lower social groups became increasingly common, both in setting taxes and in collecting them.

The Umayyads also changed an earlier rule introduced at the beginning of the conquests. At first, people who converted to Islam had been exempted from the jizya, while the kharāj, or land tax, was collected from those who owned or worked the land.

Later, people in this position were sometimes made to pay both taxes: the jizya and the kharāj.

This helped provoke repeated uprisings against Umayyad rule in several regions.

One example came in Central Asia in the year 73 AH (728 CE), followed by further revolts in the years that followed. These uprisings came close not only to destroying Umayyad rule in the region, but to ending the Arab presence there altogether.

Another important change under the Umayyads concerned land ownership among the conquering Arabs.

At the beginning of the conquests, under the Rightly Guided Caliphs and especially under ʿUmar, the Arabs had lived largely apart from the original inhabitants. They remained in the military cities that had originally been built for the armies.

Their children therefore took little part in production, and ʿUmar strictly prevented the Arabs from owning land in the conquered territories.

All of this changed under the Umayyads.

Arab communities that had arrived with the conquering armies were now allowed to acquire as much land as they wished in these regions.

Naturally, only some members of these communities could actually do so. They were, first, those wealthy enough to buy and develop land and, second, those with family or political connections to the Umayyad government.

The major Arabic historical sources—including the works of al-Ṭabarī, al-Balādhurī, and al-Yaʿqūbī—show that the estates acquired by Umayyad families and their supporters became so large and productive that enormous wealth became concentrated in the hands of a small new Arab class.

The same sources also show that by the late Umayyad period, conditions for the people working these large estates had become extremely harsh.

These workers included local peasants and enslaved captives. Their living conditions became so poor, and epidemic disease so destructive, that the system itself began to hold back further development of production.

This helped weaken the Umayyad state in its final years.

It faced repeated uprisings, first from groups whose anger came directly from social conditions; second from the political and factional opponents of the Umayyads; and third from non-Arab groups who remained deeply hostile to the Umayyads because of their policy of discrimination between Arabs and the mawālī.

4 — Agriculture and Industry

Before ending our discussion of the social system under Umayyad rule, a fair and objective account requires us to recognize other achievements of Muʿāwiya that contributed to development and relative progress.

One was his concern with developing both agriculture and industry in Syria throughout his rule there.

In agriculture, he worked to improve irrigation and increase the fertility of the land. As we have already seen, he made use of specialists from the local population.

In industry, he strengthened customs protections for locally produced goods. This helped local industries develop further, increased their contribution to public revenue and trade, and improved both the skills and the living standards of craftsmen.

Another historically important development began while Muʿāwiya was governor of Syria, during the caliphate of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb.

With Muʿāwiya himself taking a special interest in the project, the Arabs began building their first naval fleet.

Here again they made use of local specialists. They also used Lebanese cedar, just as the ancient Phoenicians had done.

The fleet was first used during the Arab conquest of Cyprus.

Later, under Muʿāwiya himself, it was used twice in campaigns against Constantinople. The first took place in 668 and ended in failure. The second began in 673 and succeeded in defeating the Greek fleet and entering the Bosporus and the Golden Horn. Constantinople was then besieged for around five years.

But all these reforms were also required by the way the productive forces were developing—first and foremost in agriculture, and then in craft production as its techniques became more advanced.

The social system represented by the Umayyad state was, through its own development, moving toward greater trade and toward more skilled forms of craft production.

The system itself was opening up new possibilities. Agriculture and irrigation, in particular, increasingly required more advanced tools.

At the same time, the ruling class, large landowners, wealthy merchants, and military commanders had growing resources of their own. They could afford expensive and technically advanced goods for consumption and private ownership.

And because the state was constantly expanding, weapons production also had to develop to meet its military needs.

5 — Uprisings Against Umayyad Rule

We have now looked at several features of the economic, social, and political conditions that accompanied Umayyad rule, from its foundation under Muʿāwiya to the period when the state began weakening under the combined pressures that eventually brought it down.

But for the purposes of our present study, we now need to identify some of the historical events that took the form of uprisings, rebellions, or organized opposition to Umayyad rule.

These events produced important effects in the world of ideas.

By the late seventh and early eighth centuries, they brought developing Arab thought directly face to face with social and political reality. They created a connection between thought and reality that could not be hidden even by the relative independence that thought can acquire when it becomes capable of dealing with abstract theoretical problems, or when artistic creation seems to rise far above the immediate world of everyday life.

These historical events followed one another rapidly and often overlapped in ways that were both striking and complex.

For now, we need to select the events most clearly connected with our subject, especially those involving the Shiʿa and the Kharijites, to whom this chapter is devoted.

First: The Shiʿi Uprising

We will not enter here into the familiar debate over when the term Shiʿa first appeared historically or as the name of a religious group.

Did it begin during the lifetime of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib? After the martyrdom of his son al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī at Karbala? Or even earlier, during the lifetime of the Prophet, as some modern writers on the subject argue?

In this study, by Shiʿa we mean those Muslims to whom the term later came to be applied without dispute because they supported—literally, took the side of—ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib.

They regarded him as the person with the legitimate, divinely sanctioned right to succeed the Prophet immediately as caliph, followed in turn by his direct descendants according to the recognized line of succession.

The Shiʿa in this sense launched several uprisings during the political, religious, and ideological struggles that followed the end of the period of the Rightly Guided Caliphs and continued throughout Umayyad rule.

Here, however, we are concerned specifically with the first Shiʿi uprising against Umayyad power.

After ʿAlī was killed in Kufa by one of the Khārijites, while Muʿāwiya escaped the attempt on his own life by another Khārijite, Muʿāwiya hoped to secure the caliphate for himself through political maneuvering rather than war. He achieved this when he reached an agreement with al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī, who, according to Shiʿi belief, should have become caliph after his father.

Under the agreement, al-Ḥasan gave up his claim to the caliphate in favor of Muʿāwiya, on the condition that the caliphate would pass to him after Muʿāwiya’s death. Muʿāwiya accepted this condition, but he already had another plan in mind and had begun preparing for it. He wanted to establish a hereditary Umayyad state, with the throne passing after him from one of his descendants to the next.

At the same time, he wanted to avoid any upheaval that might threaten his own rule. So he reluctantly accepted al-Ḥasan’s condition. “But Muʿāwiya could not rest easy while al-Ḥasan was alive and his pledge to him still stood.”2 Perhaps he had already decided that he would somehow free himself from this obligation so that nothing would stand in the way of his plan. Shiʿis believe that Muʿāwiya did in fact free himself from it by having al-Ḥasan poisoned in 49 AH/669 CE.

Whatever the truth of that claim, the death of the second Shiʿi imam left Muʿāwiya much more confident about the future of his plan. He was now free of his pledge to al-Ḥasan. The only remaining obstacle to naming his son Yazīd as heir to the throne was the reaction he expected from the leading Companions of the Prophet who were still alive, and from much of Arab-Islamic public opinion.

The idea itself was new and strange in Islam. And in the eyes of many Muslims, Yazīd was not fit for the position. But Muʿāwiya had such firm control over affairs that he was willing to go ahead despite the opposition he knew he might face.

Muʿāwiya was bold enough in confronting Arab-Islamic public opinion that he even had a number of prominent Companions of the Prophet killed, among them Ḥujr ibn ʿAdī and his companions. He showed no hesitation about this. In fact, during one meeting with al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī, he boasted about it in a mood of triumph and spite.3

With the same boldness, he named his son Yazīd as heir. Yazīd thus became the first designated heir to the caliphate in Islamic history. From that point on, hereditary succession became a normal practice under the Umayyad and Abbasid caliphs, and under later dynasties as well, apart from a few periods, down to the Ottoman revolution in Constantinople—Istanbul—at the beginning of the twentieth century, in 1908.

Muʿāwiya died in 680 CE, and Yazīd took the throne because his father had already made him heir.

Many people opposed this. The first open resistance to Yazīd’s caliphate came from the Shiʿa of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib in Kufa. They had learned that their third imam, al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī, who was then in Mecca, had refused to pledge allegiance to Yazīd as caliph. They sent delegations to al-Ḥusayn, inviting him to come to Kufa and lead their uprising against Yazīd and against the Umayyad caliphate itself.

Al-Ḥusayn accepted their invitation and decided to leave Mecca for Kufa. ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbbās, one of the leading Companions of the Prophet and a cousin of al-Ḥusayn’s father ʿAlī, advised him not to go. Ibn ʿAbbās told him:

“Go to Yemen. It is remote, and you have supporters and brothers there. Stay there and send out your callers.”4

But al-Ḥusayn believed that he had a duty to resist Yazīd and the Umayyad throne, especially now that he seemed to have the people he needed in Kufa.

When al-Ḥusayn reached Iraq on his way to Kufa, he learned that many of the supporters who had invited him to rise up and had promised to fight under his banner had lost their nerve. The governor of Kufa, ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Ziyād, who supported the Umayyads, had used threats and intimidation against some of them, and promises and bribes against others.

Al-Ḥusayn was now in a very difficult position. He could return to the Hijaz and risk being accused of weakness and of abandoning something he believed to be his duty. Or he could continue toward a battle with Yazīd’s army, even though he had brought women and children with him and now had only a very small number of supporters left.

He chose to go forward rather than turn back.

He continued until he met the Umayyad army at Karbala. The battle that followed became one of the most distinctive and powerful events of the period. It ended with the killing of al-Ḥusayn, his supporters, and some of his sons, while the women and children of his family were taken prisoner. This happened in 61 AH/680 CE.

At first glance, this first uprising against the first hereditary Umayyad caliph might seem, especially when told in such simple terms, like an ordinary event with little place in a discussion of historical movements that shaped the development of thought.

But that would badly distort the historical reality.

The uprising cannot be understood simply as the short battle at Karbala and its immediate result: the overwhelming victory that the Umayyad army won within a few hours over the small group of al-Ḥusayn’s supporters—some 300 fighters.

What defines this Shiʿi uprising historically is what happened after the battle of the tenth of Muḥarram in 61 AH, when its leader, the third Shiʿi imam, was killed. Its importance also comes from the political and intellectual effects that continued to spread, both deeply and widely, throughout the period we are discussing.

The lasting force of this uprising does not come simply from its tragic character. A modern view, no longer caught up in the intense emotions of the event itself, must look beyond the tragedy and reach the less dramatic forces underneath it.

Seen in that way, the following factors become clear.

The First Factor

We need to look closely at Muʿāwiya’s decision to change the caliphate from the consultative system associated with the Rightly Guided caliphs into a hereditary form of personal rule that was close to monarchy.

This was not a small change that could simply be imposed without expecting serious opposition from large parts of Muslim public opinion.

Muʿāwiya managed to carry it out during his lifetime by combining force with political maneuvering. But the fact that he avoided a major storm while he was alive does not mean that no storm was forming beneath the surface of Arab-Islamic society, waiting for something to bring it out into the open.

Large numbers of Arabs and Muslims, including leading Companions of the Prophet and the generation that followed them, did not find it easy to accept what Muʿāwiya had done, even if outward appearances sometimes suggested otherwise.

We can even say that generations of Muslim religious scholars, historians, and researchers continued, down to the modern period, to look on Muʿāwiya’s action with disapproval, or at least with genuine unease.

Al-Maqrīzī relates that one Muslim jurist, who lived much later than the Umayyad period, was once asked why Muslim kings so often failed to follow the right path and paid no respect to “covenant or sanctity.” He replied:

“That is because kingship has no place in our religious law. Our law recognizes only caliphs. Abū Bakr was the caliph of the Messenger of God, even though the Prophet had not expressly appointed him in a text. But people understood the matter that way and unanimously called him caliph.

“Then Abū Bakr appointed ʿUmar. In doing so, he took the office away from the path of kingship, in which a son inherits from his father, and placed it on the path of the caliphate, which rests on judgment and choice. He stated this clearly in his appointment.

“Then the people of the council agreed on ʿUthmān. The fact that ʿUmar moved the office away from the structure of kingship and placed it under consultation proves that it was not kingship.

“Then ʿAlī became the obvious choice, since no one like him remained. Those who preferred truth to desire and the next world to this one pledged allegiance to him. Then came al-Ḥasan in the same way.

“Muʿāwiya was the first to turn the caliphate into kingship, and austerity into ease. And after that, your Lord is indeed forgiving and merciful. He made the caliphate hereditary. Once he took it away from its proper form, no kingship remained upright.

“Do you not see that ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz—may God be pleased with him—was a caliph, not a king? No one ever followed the straight path except a caliph.”5

These words come from a jurist who lived long after the Umayyads, yet they show how deeply Muʿāwiya’s action continued to trouble Muslims across the generations.

The bitterness in his words is obvious. Even after so much time had passed, he still spoke with deep resentment about Muʿāwiya’s decision to turn the caliphate into hereditary monarchy.

If people felt this way generations later, what must Muslims have felt during Muʿāwiya’s own lifetime?

Was Muʿāwiya, from an objective historical point of view, actually wrong to do what he did?

I believe that a state with the historical weight of the Arab-Umayyad state could hardly have become stable, put down firm roots, and played its historical role if Muʿāwiya had not supported it with this bold political measure.

But that is another question.

The Second Factor

We also need to consider the fact that Yazīd himself happened to be the first man who would inherit Muʿāwiya’s throne under this new hereditary system.

That accident mattered.

It helped deepen the widespread resentment caused by Muʿāwiya’s change to the caliphate. It also helped give the Shiʿi uprising—and al-Ḥusayn’s death while fighting Yazīd’s army—a lasting presence in public life, political movements, and intellectual history.

Choosing Yazīd as the first heir gave the opponents of hereditary rule a powerful argument against the whole principle. It gave them a practical weapon with which to attack it.

The issue could no longer be limited to the Shiʿi claim that the caliphate was a divine right belonging to ʿAlī and his sons. It now reached the Sunnis as well. They believed that the caliphate belonged to the Muslim community, which should choose whoever was best qualified to carry its heavy responsibilities.

And Yazīd ibn Muʿāwiya had none of the qualities that would make him “the best qualified.”

First, he was a young man whose conduct and way of life were widely criticized.

Second, he was known for disregarding even basic standards of behavior and religious observance.

Third, he knew little about how to manage the public affairs of a state. Between Yazīd and the responsibilities he had been given stood a thick wall of isolation, together with his constant absorption in trivial daily amusements.

We should add a fourth point. People at the time may not yet have understood it clearly as a social issue, but that does not make it any less real.

Yazīd’s character and behavior were typical of the young men of the new aristocratic class. They looked down on ordinary people and immersed themselves in shallow material luxury. Their way of life separated them from the serious problems and everyday struggles that occupied the great majority of people.

This must have affected how people felt about them, even if that feeling had not yet developed into a clear social awareness.

The Third Factor

The first two factors pushed Muslims, especially after the killing of al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī, toward an increasingly negative comparison, whether they made it consciously or simply felt it.

It was a comparison between two men.

On one side stood Yazīd, with the character we have just described.

On the other stood al-Ḥusayn. Muslims knew that he was the grandson of the Prophet, the son of Muḥammad’s daughter. They knew that his father was ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, one of the Rightly Guided caliphs, whom Muslims in general regarded with great respect. They also knew al-Ḥusayn for his own personal qualities, and they knew that he had courageously accepted a tragic fate while defending what he believed to be his right.

The comparison left many Muslims with a deep sense of grief.

They grieved not only because of al-Ḥusayn’s terrible fate, but also because an army acting in the name of the Umayyad caliphate had killed him; because of the shocking way in which the killing had taken place; and because the Islamic caliphate itself now seemed to be passing into the hands of men of bloodshed who had opened their new era with an event of such horror.

A modern scholar of the Ashʿarī school, far removed from Shiʿi emotional attachment to the event, says that Muslims had never seen anything like it. He says that Muslims as a whole cursed Yazīd because of the massacre of 61 AH. This modern Ashʿarī scholar even describes the killing of al-Ḥusayn as “the greatest event in the political and spiritual history of Islam.”6

Together, these three factors, and others like them, helped the Shiʿi uprising continue far beyond Karbala.

At times it took the form of bloody uprisings and revolts. These began with the revolt of al-Mukhtār ibn Abī ʿUbayd al-Thaqafī, after the revolt of the Tawwābūn, or Penitents. The revolt of the Penitents was a direct and violent expression of the remorse felt by the people of Kufa for failing to support al-Ḥusayn in his struggle against Yazīd’s army. It was also, less directly, an expression of the effect that the factors we have just discussed had left on Muslim society.

At other times, the same Shiʿi uprising appeared in the form of intellectual movements. At first these took a purely religious form. Later they developed theological and philosophical forms as well, as we will see in the next chapter.

Second: The Uprising in Medina

We should add that many of the Companions of the Prophet and the generation that followed them in Medina had their own particular reasons for resenting Muʿāwiya’s hereditary system. The same was true in Mecca.

These were the two holy cities of Islam. Their people saw themselves as closely tied to Islam because they had personally nurtured its cause through their own lives and sacrifices. Islam had grown up among them and had remained closely connected with their lives.

For that reason, they were especially sensitive to anything they believed threatened it.

Some of them regarded Muʿāwiya’s transformation of the caliphate away from the model of the Rightly Guided caliphs as an innovation in Islam. In their view, it did not merely go against the practice of the early caliphs. More importantly, it went against the basic nature of the caliphate itself, as we have already explained.

Then there were the supporters of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib. They denied not only Muʿāwiya’s right to the caliphate, but even the right of Abū Bakr and ʿUmar. They believed that the caliphate was a divine office whose holder had to be named by God through the Prophet, and that such a designation had already been made in favor of ʿAlī immediately after the Prophet.

These were two religiously based positions toward Muʿāwiya’s caliphate that existed in Medina.

But there were other reasons for dissatisfaction as well. Some were personal and political. Others were social and class-based.

The first kind came from the ambitions of some of the sons of the Companions, such as Muṣʿab ibn al-Zubayr and his brother ʿAbd Allāh, who themselves hoped to become caliph.

The second kind came from the transfer of the center of the caliphate from Medina to Damascus.

This move cost Medina its almost central position in the Arab-Islamic world. It also cost the wealthy people of Medina, and those of Mecca, many of the benefits they had gained from that position. Their economic and political activity declined. Many of their ambitions were blocked. They found themselves pushed almost entirely away from the center of political and social life.

Several things had prevented Medina from rising against Muʿāwiya while he was alive: his wealth and political skill, the conflict between ʿAlī and Muʿāwiya, and the decision of many of the leading men we have mentioned to side against ʿAlī.

But as soon as Muʿāwiya’s son Yazīd inherited the Umayyad throne in Damascus, the resentment that had previously been held back began to move toward open revolt.

Again, Yazīd’s own character mattered greatly. The qualities we described earlier helped turn resentment into an explosion.

Yazīd was therefore left with little support except from those who had a direct interest in keeping him as ruler of the Muslims in Damascus—and, more broadly, in preserving the Umayyad throne itself.

These were, on the one hand, the representatives of the ruling class in Syria and, on the other, the Kalb tribes, who were allied with the Umayyads there.

Everything pointed toward an approaching revolt in Medina, and in Mecca as well. The wider explosion had in fact already begun after the killing of al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī in Iraq, where two movements hostile to the Umayyads were active despite their deep differences: the Shiʿa and the Khārijites.

Then the revolt came in Medina.

The people of the city openly rebelled and refused to pledge allegiance to Yazīd as caliph. Yazīd sent his Syrian army, made up of those allies, and crushed the rebellion.

His army then continued toward Mecca and placed the city under siege. During the siege, it committed an extraordinary act that shocked Muslims everywhere and continued to do so for generations: the army bombarded the Kaaba itself, along with the homes of the city’s inhabitants, and set fires around it.

Yazīd did not live long after this.

He died that same year, in 683 CE. His son, Muʿāwiya II, succeeded him, but remained caliph for only a few months and did not truly exercise power because of an illness from which he suffered. He then died of plague at the age of twenty.

With his death, the Umayyad throne passed to another branch of the family, that of Marwān ibn al-Ḥakam. Marwān became the first caliph after the three Sufyanids: Muʿāwiya I, Yazīd, and Muʿāwiya II.

Third: The Uprising of Ibn al-Zubayr in Mecca

Mecca experienced another of the major upheavals of the Umayyad period when ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr emerged as a claimant to the caliphate after the death of Muʿāwiya II.

His father, al-Zubayr, had been one of the leading Companions of the Prophet. As we saw earlier, he later fought against ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib in the Battle of the Camel at Basra. Together with ʿĀʾisha, he entered that war demanding revenge for the killing of the third caliph, ʿUthmān, and he was killed in the course of those events.

Now his son ʿAbd Allāh appeared in the Hijaz and declared himself caliph.

He saw that the Umayyad throne in Damascus had been shaken since the killing of al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī in Iraq. Then, after the deaths of Yazīd and his son Muʿāwiya II, the dynasty itself seemed in danger of disappearing.

The opportunity had arrived for these ambitious sons of the Companions, whom Muʿāwiya I had pushed away from the center of Arab-Islamic political life when he established the Umayyad caliphate in Syria, far from Mecca and Medina, the earlier centers of Arab and Muslim life.

These young men saw themselves as natural candidates for power because they came from the leading families of both Mecca and Medina. They even believed that they had a stronger claim than the descendants of Abū Sufyān, who had once fought against the Prophet and Islam while their own fathers had been among the Prophet’s leading Companions.

ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr now rose up in an attempt to return the caliphate to its original home in the Hijaz.

In doing so, he made use of the same old tribal rivalry that Muʿāwiya had previously exploited: the conflict between the Qays tribes and the Kalb tribes.

The Qays tribes, for their part, saw Ibn al-Zubayr’s movement as an opportunity to defeat the Kalb tribes and take from them the positions of power they had gained through their long alliance with Muʿāwiya.

Muʿāwiya was now gone, and the throne he had built seemed close to collapse. The Qays tribes therefore had every reason to move quickly, support ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr, and recognize him as caliph before a new Umayyad leader appeared in Syria and took the opportunity away from them.

The Qays-Kalb conflict thus erupted again.

The two sides met at the Battle of Marj Rāhiṭ near Damascus. It was a major battle, and the Kalb tribes won an overwhelming victory.

Then the new Umayyad leader whom the Qays tribes had feared finally appeared: Marwān ibn al-Ḥakam.

The Kalb tribes recognized him as the new caliph on the Umayyad throne in Damascus, a throne they themselves had helped save from collapse.

But ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr was not defeated simply because the Qays tribes had lost at Marj Rāhiṭ. Other Arab tribes in Iraq and Iran still supported him against the Umayyads.

At the same time, the supporters of ʿAlī were in no position to mount serious resistance to the Umayyads after the massacre at Karbala, and no Alid leader had yet emerged to lead a revolt against Umayyad rule.

Ibn al-Zubayr therefore still had enough support to maintain his claim to the caliphate in Mecca, where he had already taken control.

Marwān ibn al-Ḥakam, meanwhile, held power in Damascus.

Besides the Kalb tribes, he had the support of the wealthy class that controlled the great fortunes and large estates, and he himself was one of its representatives.

During the rule of the Rightly Guided caliph ʿUthmān, Marwān had already helped the Umayyads gain control over wealth and property and concentrate it in their own hands. His actions were also among the causes of the revolt against ʿUthmān.

Marwān had served as ʿUthmān’s secretary and exercised great influence over him. Some historians even describe him as the real ruler during that period.

This makes it easier to see how the political and social character of Umayyad rule continued under Marwān just as it had under its founder, Muʿāwiya.

Marwān did not appear merely as the man who saved Umayyad rule. He also came to protect the privileges of the wealthy, the great landowners, the leading Umayyads, and their allies—in other words, the local wealthy class and the Kalb tribes.

But Marwān did not rule for long.

His wife strangled him out of jealousy over one of his favored slave women. His son ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān then succeeded him on the Umayyad throne.

When ʿAbd al-Malik came to power, he faced two powerful movements that threatened his control over the Hijaz, Iraq, and Iran: the movement of ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr, who ruled Mecca, and the Khārijite movement.

There was also the revolt of al-Mukhtār ibn Abī ʿUbayd al-Thaqafī in Iraq. Al-Mukhtār had risen to avenge the blood of al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī and was hunting down those who had taken part in his killing in order to destroy them physically.

But Ibn al-Zubayr’s movement posed the greatest danger to the Umayyad caliphate. ʿAbd al-Malik therefore had to deal with that threat first.

Despite the strong position Ibn al-Zubayr had gained by attracting many of the forces opposed to the Umayyads, he does not seem to have had enough political skill or foresight to make good use of that support or even to keep it.

He committed acts that deeply offended believers, much as Yazīd ibn Muʿāwiya had done earlier when his army bombarded the Kaaba with catapults.

Ibn al-Zubayr ruled harshly and despotically. At the same time, while sitting in the Kaaba itself, he openly expressed irreligious views and contempt for religion.

Because of this, he could not withstand the Umayyad army that ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān sent to Mecca to bring him under control.

His own supporters deserted him because of the way he had behaved. By the time the Umayyad army arrived, he was already badly weakened.

He tried to take refuge in the Kaaba, but his mother, Asmāʾ bint Abī Bakr, encouraged him to face the Umayyads directly.

He went out to fight them in the streets of Mecca. Before long he was killed, and ʿAbd al-Malik’s army won the victory.

ʿAbd al-Malik then had to deal with the burning problems of opposition in Iraq.

There were the Khārijites and the Shiʿa. The Khārijites were disturbing the security of the Umayyad state. The Shiʿa were spreading ideas and an “ideology” hostile to the Umayyads, while their ally al-Mukhtār ibn Abī ʿUbayd al-Thaqafī7 was using armed force to kill everyone who had taken part in the killing of al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī.

The Umayyad governor of Iraq had also sided with Ibn al-Zubayr and then adopted positions that supported all the opposition forces, including both the Khārijites and the Shiʿa.

At this point al-Ḥajjāj ibn Yūsuf al-Thaqafī enters the story. We will return to him when we discuss the Khārijites.

Fourth: The Uprising of the Slaves

This time, the Umayyad throne, under ʿAbd al-Malik himself, faced a new kind of class uprising.

First, it came from inside the Umayyads’ own secure stronghold: Syria itself.

Second, it came from deep within society, from one of its poorest, most oppressed groups: the slaves.

The slaves of Damascus rose in rebellion. They went to the prisons and released everyone being held there. The slaves and the freed prisoners then withdrew to the mountain overlooking Damascus and took shelter there.

But like the slave revolts of earlier periods, this uprising had little chance of success.

The rebels did not even have the weapons they needed to defend themselves. Nor did they receive support from other oppressed social groups, such as poor peasants, artisans, and other exploited people.

Slavery still had an accepted place in the social order, and Islam itself recognized it. Islam even forbade slaves from leaving the ownership of their “masters” without those masters’ consent.

At the same time, Islam did introduce laws that required slave owners, in certain cases, to free some of their slaves as an act of atonement for particular sins.8

The slave revolt in Damascus therefore failed, and ʿAbd al-Malik’s army crushed it.

Yet the commander of that army ordered his soldiers not to kill the rebel slaves, out of respect for the property rights of their “masters”!.9

Fifth: The Uprising of the Turks

ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān and al-Walīd ibn ʿAbd al-Malik became known for major administrative and civil reforms in the history of the Umayyad state.

Among these were the minting of Arab coinage, the first measure of its kind; the Arabization of the state registers for the first time; an attempt to separate the powers of the different administrative departments so that each could be kept under better control; and the expansion of the conquests across large parts of Asia and Africa, and even into Europe.

These conquests expanded the Arab state and extended Arab and Islamic rule over many different countries and peoples. Their entry into Arab political history had a clear effect on Arab culture, making it more varied and enriching it.

But the conquests also had negative effects on economic, administrative, and social policy.

First, expansion weakened the central power of the state.

As conquest spread, the governor of each province began to behave almost like an independent ruler, or like the head of a state within the state. He might send only part of his tax revenue to the central caliphal government and keep the rest for himself.

The same was true of the spoils of conquest. He would send only one fifth to the central government and keep the remaining four fifths to use as he pleased.

Second, continued expansion required more spending on armies, on the defense of conquered lands, and on the administration of public affairs.

A state ruled by representatives of a wealthy class that exploits the majority naturally places most of its costs on that same majority.

This is exactly what began to happen more and more under the Umayyad state from this period onward, until the dynasty eventually collapsed under the pressure of social uprisings as well as political conflicts that had become deeply entangled with them.

One example was the uprising that took place in the lands of the Turks in Central Asia in 73 AH.

The works of Arab historians are full of accounts of what happened there during that year and the years that followed.

These accounts make it clear that Umayyad financial policy was the main cause of the resentment that built up and intensified until it became a series of armed uprisings that nearly destroyed Umayyad authority in the Turkic lands.

Many of the local people had converted to Islam.

But the Umayyad authorities continued to collect the jizya from them even after their conversion, and then added new taxes on top of it.

The Turkic kings, led by the “Great Khagan,” used the anger of the common people as an opportunity to recover their own power. They fought long and exhausting wars against the Umayyad state.

Some Arabs in the region who followed the movement known as the Murjiʾa10 sided with the discontented population. They supported the people’s demand that the Umayyad authorities reduce their tax burden and the harshness of tax collection.

We have presented this historical picture in some detail so that we can now see more clearly how political events and social conditions gave rise to intellectual movements.

Intellectual activity became so deeply mixed with political and social conflict that it is difficult to find any intellectual movement that appeared after the rise of Umayyad rule without finding roots in those events and conditions.

In some cases, particular parts of an intellectual movement were directly connected with a particular side of a political or social struggle.

We will point out these connections when we reach them.

B — The Shiʿa: A Position and a “Theory”

1 — The Position

We cannot completely separate a political or intellectual position from the theory behind it.

A position on any question, opinion, or movement is hardly worth serious attention unless it rests on some kind of theoretical thought or basic principle.

The reverse is also true. To accept a particular theory about a question is itself a position. Otherwise, the theory becomes a pure abstraction hanging in empty space.

So there is a dialectical relationship between position and theory. That relationship makes it impossible to separate them completely.

But for the sake of study and explanation, we need to make a formal distinction between them here.

With that in mind, we can say that Shiʿism, as a position within Islam, arose with the question of the caliphate immediately after the death of the Prophet.

That position then developed and interacted with events in Arab-Islamic life.

From it came a range of political and intellectual positions, including theological and philosophical ones. These eventually formed many different Shiʿi schools and sects.

Some gradually faded with time.

Some changed into positions very different from where they had begun.

Others grew stronger, developed a wider base, and still continue today with their original foundations largely intact.

However much the Shiʿi groups differed throughout history in their principles, interpretations, and degree of attachment to the basic teachings of Islam, most of them shared one thing: their position toward the person of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib.

That position often became, deliberately or otherwise, directly or indirectly, an expression of a political or class position toward one ruler or another under the Islamic caliphates, whether Umayyad, Abbasid, or something else.

Most often, this political or class position took the form of opposition.

And that opposition was often marked by bloodshed and violence: sometimes through battles and armed uprisings, and sometimes through political persecution so severe that it became outright massacre.

We have already discussed one of the earliest Shiʿi uprisings against the Umayyads.

Shiʿi political opposition to ruling governments continued through most of the Abbasid period. Political persecution of the Shiʿa also continued through different stages of Arab-Islamic political history, down to the end of the Turkish Ottoman caliphate in the early twentieth century.

The Shiʿi position shifted from opposition to support only during periods when Shiʿi rulers came to power, such as the Buyid state in Iran, the emirate of Sayf al-Dawla al-Ḥamdānī in Aleppo during the fourth century AH—the tenth century CE—and the Fatimid state in North Africa and Egypt during that same century.

There were also occasional periods of accommodation between Shiʿi groups and particular caliphs, such as the Abbasid caliph al-Maʾmūn.

Here we can see another important feature of Shiʿi history.

Political opposition often took on a social character as well.

In other words, the opposition was not always directed mainly at the form of government or at the individual rulers themselves. At a deeper level, it was often opposition to the way those rulers treated weak and oppressed social classes and groups.

It is quite possible that this had something to do with the position of ordinary Shiʿis themselves.

Many of them suffered social oppression alongside political persecution because they were themselves an organic part of the same social classes and groups that were being oppressed by the ruling classes.

2 — The Theory

It is difficult to give one complete and absolute definition of Shiʿi theory.

After the death of the fourth imam, ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn, known as Zayn al-ʿĀbidīn—the son who survived the massacre at Karbala in which his father al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī was killed—the Shiʿa began to divide into different groups.

At first there were three.

The first was the Imāmiyya, the followers of Imam Muḥammad al-Bāqir, son of Zayn al-ʿĀbidīn.

The second was the Zaydiyya, the followers of Zayd ibn ʿAlī Zayn al-ʿĀbidīn.

The third was the Kaysāniyya, the followers of Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥanafiyya, who was a direct son of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib and was known by the name of his mother, al-Ḥanafiyya.

As the first signs of theological and philosophical thought began to appear, Shiʿi groups continued to divide and develop.

This happened because new ideas kept entering Shiʿi theory from the wider intellectual movement that was beginning to take shape.

At first, this intellectual movement centered on the problem of divine decree, human responsibility for human actions, and the relationship between human action and divine action.

It was also closely connected with the political struggle over the caliphate, and especially with opposition to the Umayyad caliphate.

Later, these questions became more clearly developed as the growing movement of theological and philosophical thought gathered strength.

So it may be difficult to give one complete definition of Shiʿi theory.

But it is not difficult to identify its earliest foundations—the basic idea from which the many different Shiʿi religious and intellectual theories later developed.

Despite the differences between their sects and schools, Shiʿis begin from the belief that ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib was the Muslim with the first and strongest right to political authority after the Prophet.

They believe that this authority is a divine right, not something for people themselves to decide by choosing whoever they believe is best suited to lead.

Only God, they argue, knows where the true interests of human beings lie and what will bring them well-being in this world and the next.

For this reason, the Shiʿa regarded the imamate as one of the fundamental pillars of Islam—that is, as one of the basic principles of Islamic belief.

This is the firm foundation of Shiʿi theory, whatever differences later developed over the form and character of this authority, whether spiritual or political.

Beyond this point, Shiʿi groups differ greatly.

There are moderate Shiʿis, and there are those who went to extremes in the kind of authority they gave to the person of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib.

The latter are known in Islamic history as the ghulāt, the extremists, because they pushed their beliefs so far that some of them gave divine qualities to ʿAlī himself.

Moderate Shiʿis and Sunnis agree that these extremist groups fall outside the basic principles of Islamic belief.

Historians, however, often use the name “Shiʿa” for any group whose theory is fundamentally connected with the person of ʿAlī.

The Imāmiyya, the Twelvers, and the Zaydiyya reject this use of the term and deny that the extremist groups should be counted as Shiʿi.

Their rejection of extremism rests, first, on their Islamic belief in the absolute oneness of God: that God has no body and that nothing in creation is like Him. It also rests on their belief in Muḥammad’s prophethood, and in resurrection and life in the world to come.

Second, they point to a statement attributed to Imam ʿAlī in one of his sermons:

“Two kinds of people will be destroyed because of me: one who loves me so excessively that his love takes him away from the truth, and one who hates me so excessively that his hatred takes him away from the truth. The best position is the middle way, so hold to it.”11

Shiʿi sources also report the statement in another form:

“Two kinds of people are destroyed because of me: one who loves me to excess, and one who hates me with bitterness.”12

The fourth Shiʿi imam, ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn Zayn al-ʿĀbidīn, expressed the same idea:

“People, love us with the love that Islam teaches. Your love has kept growing until it has become a source of shame for us.”13

3 — The Theory of the Moderate Shiʿa

The full theory of the moderate Shiʿi groups rests, first, on the basic principles of Islamic belief that we have just discussed.

Second, it rests on the claim that the right to the caliphate after the Prophet belonged directly to ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, and then successively to his descendants.

This right is divine.

God chooses for it whoever He wishes from among those who are greatest in knowledge, character, and religion. Because God makes this choice, He must also identify the person He has chosen through the words of His Prophet Muḥammad.

To prove that ʿAlī himself was the person chosen by God, the Shiʿa use two kinds of argument.

The first they call rational proof.

The second they call transmitted proof, or proof from an authoritative text.

Their rational proof has three parts.

First, they argue that the imam14 must be protected from error, like the Prophet, so that he can safely carry the responsibility for preserving religious belief and law after the Prophet.

The Shiʿa then say that when the Prophet died, no one except ʿAlī possessed this protection from error. Therefore, ʿAlī had to be the imam.

Second, they argue that an imam must be someone who has never committed a sin. Since ʿAlī had never worshipped idols before Islam, they conclude that he must have been the imam.

Third, they argue that the imam must be more knowledgeable than anyone else in his own time. They believe that ʿAlī was exactly that. Therefore, in their view, he had to be the imam rather than anyone else.

Sunnis reject all three of these claims as rational proofs.

They argue that no one has proved that an imam must be protected from error, that he must never previously have committed a sin, or that he must be the most learned person of his time.

For Sunnis, it is enough that the person has the necessary qualifications to carry out the responsibilities of the caliphate. He is then chosen by the ahl al-ḥall wa-l-ʿaqd—those recognized as having the authority to choose a ruler.

The Shiʿa’s other proof for ʿAlī’s imamate comes from transmitted texts.

They cite several different examples.

One is the well-known Hadith of Ghadīr, also called the Hadith of Mawlā.

According to the report, the Prophet was returning from Mecca to Medina after his final pilgrimage when he stopped at a place on the road called Ghadīr Khumm. A group of Companions was with him.

He stood before them and delivered a speech. Among other things, he asked:

“Do I not have a greater claim over you than you have over yourselves?”

They replied:

“Yes, by God.”

The Prophet then took ʿAlī by the hand and said:

“God, whoever has me as his mawlā, ʿAlī is his mawlā. God, befriend whoever befriends him, oppose whoever opposes him, support whoever supports him, and abandon whoever abandons him.”

The Companions then came forward to congratulate ʿAlī, among them ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb.

ʿUmar himself said to him:

“Congratulations, ʿAlī. You have become my mawlā and the mawlā of every believing man and woman.”15

Sunnis do not deny this hadith.

But they interpret it differently from the Shiʿa.

The disagreement centers on the word mawlā, which is the key word in the Shiʿi argument.

The Shiʿa understand it as referring to wilāya—authority, rule, or the imamate.

Sunnis understand it as walāʾ in the sense of love, loyalty, and friendship.

Under the Sunni interpretation, the hadith no longer serves as proof that the Prophet appointed ʿAlī as imam and ruler of the Muslims after him.

4 — The Extremist Alid Theories

Al-Shahrastānī gives an initial definition of the religious and philosophical ideas that entered some Shiʿi beliefs about ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib and took those groups beyond the basic position we described above.

Their beliefs moved into ghulūw—extremism—especially in the way they understood the person of ʿAlī and the imams descended from him.

Al-Shahrastānī writes:

“The extremists are those who went so far in what they claimed for their imams that they took them beyond the limits of created humanity and gave them divine qualities.

“Sometimes they compared one of the imams to God, and sometimes they compared God to created beings. In this way they moved between extremes of exaggeration and distortion.

“Their comparisons came from the doctrines of divine indwelling, from the doctrines of the transmigration of souls—the passing of a soul from one being into another—and from doctrines found among Jews and Christians.

“The Jews compared the Creator to created beings, while the Christians compared a created being to the Creator. These forms of comparison then entered the minds of the extremist Shiʿa until they began to give some of the imams divine qualities.

“This kind of comparison originally appeared among the Shiʿa, and only later returned among the Sunnis.”16

Al-Shahrastānī therefore does more than give an initial definition of the theories of the extremist Alid groups.

He also tries to explain how these theories arose by tracing them back to their intellectual sources.

Does this mean, then, that ideas such as divine indwelling, the transmigration of souls, and similar doctrines already had a place in Arab thought during this period of Arab and Islamic history—or even before it?

We raise this question deliberately, because the answer will be useful when we later discuss the rise of philosophical thought and the development of Arab-Islamic philosophy itself. We will see that the theories mentioned by al-Shahrastānī also appear in some forms of that philosophy and in some of its ideas.

If our answer here shows that these theories already had roots in Arab-Islamic thought before philosophical thinking emerged, and before philosophy took shape as a distinct field, we will later be able to draw an important conclusion. Arab-Islamic philosophy, once it developed its own distinct place within Arab-Islamic thought, was not simply the result of importing Greek philosophy from outside. To a much greater extent, it grew out of a long historical process taking place within Arab life itself, as events interacted with religious thought and as that thought also came into contact with the achievements of world thought up to that time.

Let us now return to the question itself.

What we briefly discussed earlier, when looking at religious life in pre-Islamic Arabia, may help us answer it. We saw that Arab society at the time was already in contact with many of the religious ideas found among other peoples.

The Qurʾān itself provides evidence of this. It speaks about different religions and about various ways of explaining the universe, nature, and the realities of human life, whether through physical causes or unseen supernatural forces. The context makes clear that these were ideas already known among the pre-Islamic Arabs.

The Qurʾān mentions the “Magians” and the “Sabeans,” for example, in verse 17 of Sūrat al-Ḥajj:

“Those who believe, those who are Jews, the Sabeans, the Christians, the Magians, and those who associate others with God...”

Once we speak of the Magians and the Sabeans, we also have to remember the theories mentioned by al-Shahrastānī, including doctrines of divine indwelling, the transmigration of souls, and others like them.

We should also add what is historically known about the Arabs before Islam. They had already been influenced, though in a vague and unsystematic way, by Indian ideas and philosophy, as well as by ideas circulating in the Sasanian schools of Persia and Mesopotamia. This influence came through geographical contact and through trade, for which the Arabian Peninsula was one of the main routes in the pre-Islamic period.

Al-Yaʿqūbī confirms this when he discusses the religions of the pre-Islamic Arabs. Among them he mentions “dualism,” meaning the old Persian religion based on two divine principles. This was the doctrine of Manichaeism, which spoke of divine forces of good and evil. Al-Yaʿqūbī says that Ḥujr ibn ʿAmr al-Kindī followed this belief in the pre-Islamic period.17

In the Islamic period, we have a great deal of historical evidence showing that the theories mentioned above already had living and developing roots in Arab-Islamic thought at the early stage we are discussing here—that is, from the seventh century and the beginning of the eighth century CE.

One especially revealing example appears in Ibn Abī al-Ḥadīd’s commentary on Nahj al-Balāgha. He tried to explain why the more extreme doctrines of certain Shiʿi groups became more widespread in Iraq and Iran than elsewhere. His explanation is important because, whatever its weaknesses, he tried to connect the phenomenon with the real conditions in which it developed.

He writes:

“One difference that seems clear to me between these people and the Arabs who lived at the time of the Messenger of God is that these people are from Iraq and are inhabitants of Kufa. The soil of Iraq has always produced people of unusual doctrines and founders of novel sects.18 The people of this region are people of insight, close examination, reflection, and inquiry into ideas and beliefs, and into the objections raised against different doctrines. In the days of the Persian kings there had already appeared among them people such as Mani, Bardaisan, Mazdak, and others.

“The soil of the Hijaz is not like this, and neither are the minds of its people. The people of the Hijaz are generally marked by roughness, bluntness, and a certain harshness of character. Even those who live in its cities, such as Mecca, Medina, and Taʾif, have temperaments close to those of the neighboring Bedouins. Before this, there had been no sage or philosopher among them, no one devoted to speculation and debate, no one who raised such doubts, and no founder of a new doctrine.

“This is why we find that the teachings of the extremists appeared and developed only after ʿAlī settled in Iraq and Kufa, and not during the years he lived in Medina, which made up most of his life.”19

The value of this passage is that Ibn Abī al-Ḥadīd traces the rise of extremism within Shiʿi thought back to its historical setting and to the conditions of the society in which it appeared.

When he compares the Hijaz with Iraq and points to the differences between them, he is trying to show the effect of Bedouin conditions in the Hijaz and urban conditions in Iraq. Those urban conditions had deep roots in Iraq’s earlier history and in its relationship with Persian civilization before the Arab-Islamic conquest.

In modern terms, his argument is roughly this: people in Iraq were more prepared to accept complex forms of metaphysical thought, while people in the Hijaz were less prepared to accept ideas of that level of complexity. This, in all likelihood, is what Ibn Abī al-Ḥadīd meant.

We agree with the method behind this explanation, but not with the explanation itself.

It is true that some of the more extreme Shiʿi doctrines began in Kufa, but they soon spread to Medina, then to many parts of the Arabian Peninsula, especially Yemen. We have also already seen that Indian and Persian philosophical ideas had left traces in Arabia even before Islam.

5 - The Kaysāniyya

The name “Kaysāniyya” refers to the first of the Shiʿi groups regarded as extremist.

The group was named after Kaysān, a mawlā—a non-Arab client—of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib. After studying under ʿAlī, Kaysān became a follower of ʿAlī’s son Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥanafiyya.

Kaysān’s own followers were also mainly mawālī. They recognized Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥanafiyya as imam, holding that the imamate had passed to him from his nephew ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn Zayn al-ʿĀbidīn.

Within a short time, however, the ideas of this group moved far away from the original foundations of Shiʿism.

They began to attribute qualities to Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥanafiyya that went far beyond normal human limits. They claimed that he possessed hidden knowledge of everything that had happened and everything that would happen. They also said that religion consisted in obeying a man who possessed all knowledge and understood the secrets of interpretation and the hidden inner meanings of things.20

They later declared that Ibn al-Ḥanafiyya would never truly die and that, after his apparent death, he would return to the earthly world.

Two features of this movement deserve particular attention.

The first is that its beliefs, especially the ideas of immortality and return, arose mainly among the mawālī of Kufa.

The group was named after Kaysān, himself a mawlā, as we have seen. After him came the followers of Abū ʿAmra, who was killed during the revolt led by al-Mukhtār ibn Abī ʿUbayd al-Thaqafī against the Umayyads in revenge for the killing of al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī.

Abū ʿAmra’s followers were also mawālī of Kufa. At that time, they belonged to one of the lowest-ranking social groups in Umayyad society.

It was these followers of Abū ʿAmra who were the first to say that Ibn al-Ḥanafiyya would return after Abū ʿAmra was killed.

What makes this especially interesting is that they adopted this belief after their imam, Ibn al-Ḥanafiyya, had already made peace with the Umayyad caliph ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān, exchanged letters with him, and eventually recognized him as caliph. Earlier, he had also recognized Yazīd ibn Muʿāwiya.

The mawālī were angry that Ibn al-Ḥanafiyya had made peace with the Umayyads, whom they themselves had fought under the banner of al-Mukhtār al-Thaqafī. Al-Mukhtār had treated them as socially equal to the Arabs, without distinction.

They therefore saw Ibn al-Ḥanafiyya’s compromise as an abandonment of their cause, as well as of his own cause and that of the Prophet’s family.

Yet despite all this, they did not abandon their belief in him. On the contrary, their belief became more extreme.

They decided that he had committed a sin by making peace with the Umayyads, and that God had punished him by hiding him in a dark cave in Mount Raḍwā.

Before disappearing, they said, Ibn al-Ḥanafiyya passed the imamate to his son Abū Hāshim. Abū Hāshim therefore became, in their eyes, the “silent imam” after the disappearance of the “speaking imam,” Ibn al-Ḥanafiyya.

Abū Hāshim then appointed no successor of his own. God, they believed, would return the imamate to Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥanafiyya when he came back after the period of his punishment was over.

Abū Khalaf al-Qummī reports them as saying:

“They know no authoritative guide other than him, cannot distinguish truth from what merely resembles it, or certainty from confusion, until God raises up the knowing imam, Muḥammad, known as Abū al-Qāsim”—meaning Ibn al-Ḥanafiyya himself—“in spite of all who oppose him and in spite of hostile time itself. He will rule the whole earth and wrench it from every defender.”21

What can we learn from the story of these mawālī and from this belief of theirs?

Taken together, the details of the story and the belief in the imam’s return allow us to draw an important conclusion.

When the Kaysāni mawālī of Kufa—followers of Kaysān and Abū ʿAmra—joined al-Mukhtār’s revolt, they joined a movement that rejected the idea that their social position was naturally lower than that of the Arabs. Al-Mukhtār openly treated them as the Arabs’ equals.

On the surface, these men were fighting for the right of ʿAlī’s descendants to hold the imamate.

But beneath this visible political cause lay another form of social awareness. Without clearly realizing it themselves, they were also fighting for their own cause as an oppressed and despised group, subjected to many forms of humiliation and exploitation under the Umayyad state and under Arab tribal privilege.

That system of privilege was also used by the wealthy merchants and property owners of Kufa, many of whom descended from the rich merchants and property owners of pre-Islamic Mecca.

These mawālī saw in the descendants of ʿAlī, in their supporters, and in the Alid opposition to Umayyad rule a possible way out of the oppression and contempt they suffered.

Al-Mukhtār strengthened this hope within their still unclear social awareness. That hope first appeared in a religious and supernatural form, when they followed Kaysān and later Abū ʿAmra in supporting the imamate of Ibn al-Ḥanafiyya.

Then came a crushing disappointment.

First, they saw their military leadership collapse with the death of al-Mukhtār, followed by the death of Abū ʿAmra.

Then they saw their spiritual leader appear to abandon the cause when Ibn al-Ḥanafiyya made peace with the Umayyad ruler ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān.

The hope that had existed in the hidden depths of their still-unclear social awareness was shaken by these two blows. It began to collapse.

But their social awareness resisted complete defeat.

Instead, it turned toward a spiritual and supernatural escape from the unbearable feeling of hopelessness.

The belief that Ibn al-Ḥanafiyya would return was that escape. He had sinned, they believed, by making peace with the oppressive Umayyads, and God had temporarily hidden him away as punishment. But he would return.

For the Kaysāni mawālī of Kufa, this belief became a source of comfort.
