Did it not offer some relief from Umayyad oppression, and from the contempt shown to them by Kufa’s Arab merchants, landowners, and rulers, who controlled their livelihoods, their bodies, and their human dignity?

And what greater comfort could there be than the promise that God would one day:

“raise up the knowing imam, Muḥammad, known as Abū al-Qāsim, in spite of all who oppose him and in spite of hostile time itself. He will rule the whole earth and wrench it from every defender”?

The second striking feature of the Kaysāni movement is pointed out by al-Ṭabarī. He writes:

“Every extremist among the Shiʿa used to gather with Hind bint al-Mutakallifa al-Nāʿiṭiyya,22 and they would hold discussions in her house and in the house of Laylā bint Qumāma al-Muzaniyya.”23

Al-Ṭabarī is referring here to this same extremist Shiʿi group, the Kaysāniyya.

Both women were known historically to have been influenced by Kaysāni beliefs. They in turn influenced some of the women of Kufa, as well as a number of men who became active advocates of the movement.

One of these was ʿAbd Allāh ibn Nawf. Al-Ṭabarī himself tells us that Ibn Nawf left the house of Hind al-Nāʿiṭiyya when he went out to fight Muṣʿab ibn al-Zubayr.24

Al-Jāḥiẓ described both women as devoted worshippers and ascetics.25

It seems to us that the attraction of women in Kufa to the Kaysāni cause began, at first, as an emotional response to the killing of al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī and his family at Karbala.

Not long afterward, however, the movement to avenge al-Ḥusayn became linked with the movement of the Kaysāni mawālī. At that point, this emotional response developed into a religious belief centered on Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥanafiyya, the son of ʿAlī and brother of al-Ḥusayn, the martyr of Karbala.

This, in broad outline, is the picture of the Kaysāniyya as the first Shiʿi group to become known for extremism.

Before discussing them, we gave a broad picture of the more moderate Shiʿa, who stood closer to the original foundations of Shiʿism. Most of the other Shiʿi sects appeared later than the period we are examining here.

6 - The Question of Knowledge Among the Shiʿa

What we have discussed so far about the Shiʿi theory of the imamate, both in its moderate and extremist forms, should make it fairly easy to understand how the different Shiʿi groups approached the question of knowledge.

The Imami Shiʿa, and especially the Twelvers, held that the imamate was a divine right and that the imam’s authority came from God, not from the community. They also believed that the imam was protected from error and that he had to be the most knowledgeable person of his age.

The result is clear.

Knowledge of God, of the mysteries of the universe, creation, and the soul, and of the religious law that represents God’s law for humanity, comes first from the Prophet during his lifetime and then from the imam after the Prophet.

In every age, the imam is the authority through whom this knowledge is understood. There is no other authority equal to him, because the imam reports from the Prophet, and the Prophet reports from divine revelation.

Reason does have a role here, but only within strict limits. It may uncover arguments that support divine truths or prove them, but it cannot oppose those truths. Reason is unable by itself to reach the same level of knowledge about the truths of the universe and the mysteries of existence, much less the metaphysical mysteries of the universe and existence.

Here, as we saw in the first part of this study, knowledge remains tied to religious faith. It follows faith and is subject to what faith provides. Reason can operate only within those limits.

The moderate Shiʿa did accept ijtihād—independent reasoning—in matters of Islamic law. They never closed the door of ijtihād at any point in their history and continue to practice it today. This differs from the four main Sunni legal schools, which, according to this view, closed the door of ijtihād around the fourth Islamic century, or the tenth century CE.

But the continuing Shiʿi use of ijtihād does not change the basic religious character of their theory of knowledge.

This is because ijtihād is allowed only where there is no clear text in the Qurʾān, no clear statement from the Prophet, no clear statement from one of the Twelve Imams, and no established consensus among Shiʿi scholars.

When such a consensus exists, it means that the opinion of the infallible twelfth imam, Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan—the hidden and awaited imam—is understood to be present somewhere within the opinions that make up that consensus.

Only when there is no evidence from the Qurʾān, from the transmitted sayings, or from consensus does the fourth source come into play: reason.

This fourth source rests on basic rational assumptions accepted by common social reason—what is known as general custom.

Muslim jurists organized these principles into a systematic body of thought, creating a distinct field known as uṣūl al-fiqh, the principles of Islamic jurisprudence.

This field is not limited to the Shiʿa. Sunni jurists also use it, though with some differences. One important difference is that what the Shiʿa call the evidence of reason corresponds, among Sunnis, to the use of analogy.

7 - The Principles of Islamic Jurisprudence

There is no doubt that uṣūl al-fiqh played a distinctive rational role in the development of knowledge, at least because it relied on basic principles of common social reason.

Through this rational approach, it organized Islamic law according to rules and principles with some of the features of a science. It also allowed Islamic law to take part in the wider process of development affecting all areas of social life during the great historical period of Arab-Islamic civilization.

Uṣūl al-fiqh also differed from the formal structure of Aristotelian logic. Its conclusions began from living, particular cases rather than from abstract or hypothetical operations carried out purely in the mind.

But the underlying theory of knowledge still restricted religious and legal knowledge to a divine source. This greatly narrowed the room available to reason, even in legal matters.

As a result, ijtihād remained very limited. Jurists developed a deep caution toward using reason to change or renew the law as life itself changed.

The Muʿtazilites made a bold attempt to give reason greater freedom in this area.

They accepted, for example, a principle known as rational istiṣḥāb, or the rational presumption of continuity. This meant that reason could make an independent judgment about certain matters, and that this judgment could remain in force over time until transmitted evidence arrived—meaning a text received from a divine source—that overruled it.

Schools opposed to the Muʿtazila rejected this approach.

For example, after explaining the Muʿtazilite principle of rational istiṣḥāb, the judge Abū al-Ṭayyib writes:

“There is no disagreement among the Sunnis that one may not act on this basis, because reason has no authority in matters of revealed law.”26

What we are saying here about uṣūl al-fiqh applies equally to Sunnis and Shiʿa.

Even though this field had a rational foundation, the rational principles it used to derive legal rulings remained within the limits of the most basic assumptions of common social reason. They did not rise to the level of more developed rational principles that function as concepts in the philosophical sense and give reason room for a greater degree of independence and creativity.

In the later age of kalām, the study of uṣūl al-fiqh became intertwined with theology. This may be what led Muṣṭafā ʿAbd al-Rāziq to include uṣūl al-fiqh within what he called “Islamic philosophy.”

His argument makes this clear.

He says that the subjects discussed in uṣūl al-fiqh are, for the most part, similar to the subjects discussed in the study of the foundations of religious belief—that is, kalām. Books on uṣūl al-fiqh even sometimes refer to certain topics as “theological principles” because they belong to the field of kalām.27

But this similarity is not enough, by itself, to justify placing uṣūl al-fiqh within “Islamic philosophy,” unless we expand the meaning and subject matter of philosophy until it becomes as broad as it was among the ancients, when philosophy was considered the “science of the sciences.”

The overlap pointed out by ʿAbd al-Rāziq was not unique to uṣūl al-fiqh. It was a general feature of Arab-Islamic scholarship during the period when kalām and logic flourished.

Even Arabic grammar absorbed elements of kalām and logic. We can see this in the way grammarians tried to give theoretical reasons for many grammatical rules.

Yet grammar does not really require this kind of reasoning. Its rules are, after all, records and organized descriptions based on observing the language of poetry, its styles and structures, and the way Arabic words change according to meaning and the purpose of an expression.

Would it therefore make sense to classify grammar as philosophy simply because earlier grammarians sometimes used arguments borrowed from kalām when explaining its rules?

None of this means that we deny the highly rational method found in uṣūl al-fiqh. We have already emphasized that quality.

But the field remains within the limits of its own legal logic, which is tied to the concepts of Islamic law and to their connection with a divine source of knowledge.

At the same time, we should recognize something positive in the close interaction between the different branches of Arab culture at the time and the rational investigations of kalām. This interaction reflected one of the distinctive features of Arab thought: its tendency to treat different areas of thought as parts of a whole, rather than sharply separating speculative thinking from thinking based more directly on experience and practice.

C - The Kharijites: No Faith Without Action

1 - Their Origins and Their Name

As we mentioned earlier, the Kharijites emerged from the conflict between ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib and Muʿāwiya after the killing of the third Rightly Guided Caliph, ʿUthmān.

The conflict became an armed struggle at the Battle of Ṣiffīn. The fighting ended with the famous arbitration episode. One of the two arbitrators, Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī, deposed the man he represented, ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, while the second arbitrator, ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ, confirmed Muʿāwiya as caliph.

Al-Shahrastānī summarizes what happened as follows:

“The Kharijites first forced ʿAlī to accept arbitration. He had wanted to send ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbbās, but the Kharijites rejected this and said: ‘He is one of your own.’ They forced him instead to send Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī, on the condition that he judge according to the Book of God.

“But the outcome did not go as they had wanted. When ʿAlī then rejected the result, the Kharijites rebelled against him and said: ‘Why did you allow men to judge? Judgment belongs to God alone.’”28

This is how al-Shahrastānī explains both the rise of the Kharijites and the origin of their name. As he puts it:

“Anyone who rebels against the rightful imam whom the community has agreed upon is called a Kharijite.”29

2 - The Foundation of Their Theory

The first slogan raised by the Kharijites after the arbitration was:

“Judgment belongs to God, not to men.”

This was the first principle on which the rest of their theory was built.

“Right belongs to God.” No human being therefore has the right to dispose of it as he wishes, or to appoint another man to judge it according to personal desire.

This was the foundation of Kharijite thought.

From the moment they broke away from ʿAlī’s army at Ṣiffīn, they built their theoretical and practical positions toward every Islamic group and doctrine on this same principle.

Under this slogan, they went to Nahrawān and fought ʿAlī with the sword.

Applying the same principle, they argued that once a prophet had established a rule for his community, he could not turn back from it. Since ʿAlī had accepted arbitration over a right established by the Prophet, they argued that he had turned back from that right.

ʿAlī debated them on this point, but they refused to accept his argument.

They declared ʿAlī, ʿUthmān, and Muʿāwiya unbelievers. They did the same to everyone who had taken part in the Battle of the Camel and everyone who had accepted arbitration at Ṣiffīn.

They also publicly repented for their own sin in having accepted arbitration and raised the slogan of fighting all unbelievers.

Even after their defeat by ʿAlī’s army at Nahrawān, they did not abandon armed struggle.

They went so far as to assign two men from among themselves to carry out assassinations: one was to kill ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, and the other Muʿāwiya.

The first, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Muljam, succeeded. The second failed.30

After the death of ʿAlī, the Kharijites turned their struggle against the Umayyads.31

On what basis did the Kharijites declare ʿAlī and Muʿāwiya unbelievers and say that they had to be fought?

Here we come to the second main element of their theory: their understanding of faith.

Their definition of faith differed from that of other Muslims.

From the time of the Prophet until then, faith had meant first an inward belief and then an outward declaration of that belief in words.

The Kharijites added a third element: outward action.

For them, it was not enough for someone to hold a belief inwardly. Belief and action had to match.

No matter how sincere or deeply rooted a person’s belief might be, that person was not truly a believer until it was completed by action that matched it.

For the Kharijites, every person was therefore either a believer or an unbeliever. There was no third category.

Their reasoning led to an unavoidable conclusion: anyone who did not act according to what he believed was effectively contradicting his own belief. And someone who contradicted his belief could not be said to possess true faith. He was therefore an unbeliever.

Following this logic, the Kharijites believed that they themselves were required to wage jihad. They had to act according to their beliefs. If they failed to do so, then they too would cease to be believers.

The same reasoning led them to fight everyone they believed had violated this understanding of faith.

This applied to Muʿāwiya because he had rebelled against the Muslim caliph ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib even before ʿAlī accepted arbitration.

It also applied to the other Umayyad caliphs and to all the governors, officials, and propagandists who served them, because their actions violated what the Kharijites regarded as the Prophet’s appointment of ʿAlī to the caliphate—a matter they considered “God’s right, not the right of men.”

Later, they applied the same reasoning to the Abbasid caliphs.

This same logic also led them to declare that anyone who committed a major sin, such as murder, was an unbeliever.

This is why the history of the Kharijites became so violent. They rejected compromise and reconciliation with anyone who disagreed with them in theory or in practice.

The inseparability of theory and practice was at the heart of their doctrine.

In principle, this idea may have had a positive side.

But the Kharijites pushed it much too far. They became deeply involved in bloodshed. The means eventually took over from the goal, until they could no longer see beyond the means themselves.

Worse still, they reduced those means to one method alone: violent bloodshed.

This was another major mistake, and they persisted in it until violence itself came to dominate them.

It also made it difficult for many later researchers to see the more positive principles that were present in Kharijite thought or that developed during the course of their movement.

Yet it was precisely some of these principles that attracted support when the Kharijites first appeared on the political scene.

3 - “Democratic” Principles

On the question of the caliphate, the Kharijites disagreed with both the Shiʿa and the Sunnis.

Their original reason for breaking away from ʿAlī had been that “God’s right” was actually on ʿAlī’s side, and that he had violated that right when he accepted arbitration.

Later, however, their position changed.

They rejected the Shiʿi view that the caliphate should be restricted to ʿAlī and his descendants.

They also rejected the Sunni view that it should be restricted to Quraysh.

Instead, they argued that the caliph could come from outside the clans of Hāshim and Quraysh and even from outside the Arabs altogether. They went so far as to say that even an Abyssinian slave could become caliph.

For them, the caliphate belonged to the community, and the community stood above the caliph.

The community therefore had the right to choose whoever it believed was fit to hold the office and protect its interests.

And if the caliph departed from that duty, the community had the right not only to remove him but even to kill him.

They also rejected the Shiʿi belief that the imamate, or caliphate, was one of the essential foundations of religion.

This is one Kharijite principle that deserves attention when we consider the society and period in which they lived.

There was another positive side to the Kharijite movement as well.

They often defended the rights of ordinary people against oppressive authorities.

They did this, for example, in Iraq during the governorship of al-Ḥajjāj on behalf of the Umayyads. Kharijites took part in a peasant uprising in Basra against al-Ḥajjāj himself.32

They also gained supporters in the cities after peasants fled there from the countryside to escape state tax collectors, and after poor urban workers began to hear that the Kharijites were standing with oppressed rural people.33

But here too, the situation was not simple.

Although the Kharijites received support from oppressed groups in both the countryside and the cities, many members of those same groups were often repelled by the Kharijites’ methods of violence and bloody terror.

There was another positive feature of the Kharijite position: their relative tolerance toward ordinary non-Muslims and non-Arabs.

They were less burdened by religious and ethnic prejudice than many others around them. Relations among them could therefore be based on equality, without distinctions based on blood, ancestry, ethnicity, or religion.34

This is striking because it existed alongside their well-known religious rigidity.

Their freedom from these forms of prejudice may have had two causes.

First, after the killing of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, the Kharijites became united above all by one thing: opposition to Umayyad power. This became the main point around which their movement gathered supporters, regardless of identities that might otherwise have divided them.

Second, the Kharijite movement had from the beginning included members of several different tribes. Its organization therefore did not encourage the old tribal rivalries surrounding leadership.35

Even so, almost all of the support the Kharijites gained among oppressed Muslims and non-Muslims was concentrated in Iraq and parts of Iran.

In Syria, Umayyad control, together with the power of feudal landlords, large merchants, wealthy local families, and the Kalbite tribes, made it difficult for the Kharijites to build a social base.

In fact, the opposite happened.

The Umayyads used the people of Syria to fight the Kharijites in Iraq and Iran, just as they also used them to fight the Shiʿa there.

4 - The Kharijites and al-Ḥajjāj

When ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān became ruler of the Umayyad state, it faced two major dangers: the Kharijites in Iraq and ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr in Mecca.

ʿAbd al-Malik decided to destroy Ibn al-Zubayr’s movement first, so that he could then concentrate on the Kharijites.

That is what he did.

Once he had defeated Ibn al-Zubayr and destroyed the foundations of his movement, he turned to the other danger and confronted it through repression and terror—the same weapon used by the Kharijites themselves.

But Umayyad repression soon went far beyond the Kharijites. It spread across Iraqi society, especially among peasants and the poorest and weakest sections of the population.

Before this, Iraq had been governed on behalf of the Umayyads by a man who leaned toward Ibn al-Zubayr and was sympathetic to both Kharijite and Shiʿi opposition to Umayyad rule.

This led ʿAbd al-Malik to choose a new governor for Iraq who would be exceptionally ruthless and firmly loyal to the Umayyads.

He needed someone who would not be influenced by Iraq’s political environment, which at the time was divided among supporters of the Shiʿa, the Kharijites, and Ibn al-Zubayr—especially in Kufa, then the capital of Iraq.

Al-Ḥajjāj was the man ʿAbd al-Malik chose for this dangerous task.

First, al-Ḥajjāj was strongly loyal to the Umayyads.

Second, he had a forceful personality and was prepared to use violence against his opponents.

Third, he was a powerful speaker who knew how to play on the emotions of his listeners through the language of force and fear.

Al-Ḥajjāj began his rule in Kufa, then Iraq’s leading city.

Kufa was a center of the various forms of “counterrevolution” against the Umayyads. It was also a major center of intellectual life and a breeding ground for ideological conflict between political movements.

At first, al-Ḥajjāj succeeded in terrifying the people of Kufa.

He gathered their leaders in the historic mosque of the city and addressed them in a language of force and threat.

His first speech became famous in the political and literary history of Iraq. Its effect was so strong that no one present dared answer him. They responded only with complete silence.

But the effect did not last.

Political opposition, both Shiʿi and Kharijite, soon became active again. Even al-Ḥajjāj’s terror could not destroy it while he remained in Kufa.

Kharijite uprisings made his position there so insecure that he eventually moved his base to another location on the Tigris in southern Iraq, where he could establish a stronger strategic center for fighting the opposition.

There he founded the city that became permanently associated with his reign of terror: Wāsiṭ.

For twenty years, al-Ḥajjāj ruled the Iraqis through repression and fear.

When he died, Arab historians estimated that the prisons of Iraq held fifty thousand male opponents and thirty thousand women.

His strategy was to subject the entire population of Iraq to violent terror without distinction.

His rule resembled what we today might call martial law or a permanent state of emergency.

Every citizen was treated as guilty until proven innocent. In practice, no one was ever proven innocent.

Execution became al-Ḥajjāj’s preferred punishment.

It was even said that there were not enough executioners to kill the number of people condemned to death.

If we accept the figures given by Arab historians, around 130,000 people were executed in Iraq during his rule.

Peasants, agricultural workers, the urban poor, and craftsmen suffered most under al-Ḥajjāj.

They were crushed by arbitrary taxation, forced labor, imprisonment, and hunger.

Peasants abandoned the land and fled to the cities, only to find repression following them there.

Those who remained on the land were forced to work on irrigation systems. They were also prevented from selling their livestock even when they needed to sell them in order to pay their taxes or meet their most basic needs.

It is true that al-Ḥajjāj did a great deal to expand cultivated land and improve irrigation in Iraq.

But his oppression of the peasants undermined the purpose of those reforms.

The land was not developed enough even to provide the state with the agricultural taxes it needed. In this way, his policies slowed the development of the productive forces and even threatened them with collapse.36

This helps explain the peasant uprisings against al-Ḥajjāj.

It also explains why the Kharijite call to fight the Umayyads found such a wide response among the peasants.

The Kharijites were even able to lead some of these uprisings themselves.

But violent repression crushed every uprising that took place during al-Ḥajjāj’s rule.

It also weakened the Kharijites so badly that they were never again able to rebuild their strength or spread their movement on the same scale.

After al-Ḥajjāj, only weakened remnants of the movement remained. These later split into several separate groups, weakening them still further.

5 - The Intellectual War Against the Kharijites

Al-Ḥajjāj’s repression was not the only reason the Kharijites declined and their theory of faith failed to spread.

They were fought intellectually just as seriously as they were fought by the swords of al-Ḥajjāj and the Umayyads.

They faced both kinds of attack at the same time: polemical argument and theoretical criticism.

At first, their fiercest opponents were the Shiʿa.

One important Shiʿi opponent was al-Ḥasan ibn al-Ḥanafiyya, a son of Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥanafiyya and therefore a grandson of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib—the same ʿAlī whom the Kharijites had fought under their slogan:

“Judgment belongs to God, not to ʿAlī.”

Al-Ḥasan ibn al-Ḥanafiyya confronted the Kharijite theory of faith with an opposing principle.

The Kharijites argued that committing a sin destroyed a person’s faith and made the sinner an unbeliever, because for them faith did not exist without action that matched belief.

Al-Ḥasan ibn al-Ḥanafiyya answered that sin does not cancel faith.

Like the other Shiʿa, he did not consider action to be one of the elements that make up faith itself.

Someone who commits a sin, even a major one, has violated religious law. But that person remains a believer as long as he continues to believe in the basic principles of Islam.

Al-Ḥasan ibn al-Ḥanafiyya was not alone in holding this view.

What matters here is the active role he played in opposing the Kharijite theory.

He sent letters to people across the lands under Arab-Islamic rule, openly condemning the Kharijite position, calling on people to reject it, and defending the wider Muslim distinction between inward faith and outward action.

By the end of the first Islamic century and the beginning of the second—that is, between the seventh and eighth centuries CE—many jurists and theologians had joined the intellectual struggle against the Kharijites.

Historians of the period mention among the most important of them Abū Ḥanīfa al-Nuʿmān, the founder of the Sunni school later named after him, the Ḥanafī school, who died in 150 AH / 767 CE.

All of these thinkers agreed that a person who committed a major sin should not be declared an unbeliever or condemned to eternal punishment in hell.

6 - The Political Roots of the Theory of Faith

The debate over whether someone who committed a major sin should be declared an unbeliever became one of the central concerns of Arab-Islamic intellectual life between the seventh and eighth centuries CE.

This debate produced concepts and theories that continued to develop and become intertwined with other intellectual questions until they eventually helped prepare the ground for Arab philosophy.

The issue itself later became one of the central questions of kalām once theology had developed into a distinct field.

We have already seen that the Kharijite movement itself emerged from its position on this very question.

They fought ʿAlī and the Umayyads because this theory led them to declare both groups, and others as well, unbelievers and therefore legitimate targets of armed struggle.

The Shiʿa took a different position.

Other groups among the Prophet’s Companions also held different views on the status of someone who committed a major sin.

The debate over this question was therefore closely tied to the first divisions between Islamic schools and to the emergence of the earliest sectarian movements.

What can we learn from the fact that Arab-Islamic thought became so deeply occupied with this question that it became the first major center of intellectual debate at the time?

A first look at everything we have discussed so far is enough to show that real historical conditions were driving every position and every line of thought in this debate.

We will later see that even the Muʿtazilite movement originally grew out of the dispute over the person who commits a major sin.

Most historians trace the later beginning of the Muʿtazila to the moment when Wāṣil ibn ʿAṭāʾ withdrew from the teaching circle of his teacher al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī.

But even this later beginning, as we will see, had at its center the disagreement between teacher and student over the person who commits a major sin.

To understand why this question became one of the first major forces driving intellectual life at the end of the seventh century, we therefore need to return to the first historical event in which political conflict between the emerging parties became openly violent and bloody.

That event was the killing of ʿUthmān, the third Rightly Guided Caliph, followed by the transfer of the caliphate, through the principle of consultation, to ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib.

The debate over the person who commits a major sin began from this event.

At first, however, it was not expressed as a theoretical debate about the meaning of faith.

That happened only with the rise of the Kharijites. They were the first to turn the issue into an explicit theory of faith.

When Ṭalḥa and al-Zubayr went to war against ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib in the Battle of the Camel, their argument was that ʿAlī was one of those responsible for the killing of ʿUthmān.

He therefore had to be fought, because he was a killer, and killing was one of the major sins.

In other words, these two Companions were already thinking along lines that the Kharijites would later express in a more developed theoretical form.

It is true that Ṭalḥa and al-Zubayr’s decision to fight ʿAlī was fundamentally a political one. It was also shaped by their personal position toward ʿAlī himself, since he stood as the strongest obstacle to their own political ambitions.

But we also have to remember who Ṭalḥa and al-Zubayr were.

They had been close Companions of the Prophet and had reached leading positions within the Islamic movement.

Men of their standing could not easily go to war against someone with the standing of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib unless they could support their position with some principle drawn from Islam itself.

Otherwise, their action would have had no convincing religious justification.

Their claim that ʿAlī was one of those responsible for killing ʿUthmān, and that a killer had committed a major sin, therefore became the justification for launching the Battle of the Camel against him.

From this we can draw a broader conclusion.

The question of the person who commits a major sin first entered the arena as part of a political struggle. Only afterward did it move into the arena of theoretical and intellectual debate.

The same applies to Muʿāwiya’s position toward ʿAlī.

Muʿāwiya had spent twenty years as governor in Syria building the political position that would later support his ambitions.

But he could not openly pursue those ambitions without a justification.

He therefore used the same argument: ʿAlī was responsible for the blood of ʿUthmān, and anyone who took part in shedding the blood of a Muslim was a killer and therefore guilty of a major sin.

This, in turn, was used to justify rebelling against ʿAlī as caliph, fighting him, and eventually even challenging him for the caliphate itself, as Muʿāwiya ultimately did.

There was also another group of Companions who opposed ʿAlī politically, though less sharply than Ṭalḥa, al-Zubayr, and Muʿāwiya.

Their ambitions did not go as far as seeking the caliphate for themselves.

Their position on the person who commits a major sin therefore reflected a more middle-ground political position.

Among them were Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ, ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar, Muḥammad ibn Maslama, Usāma ibn Zayd, and others like them.

They refused to support ʿAlī in the conflict, but at the same time they also refused to fight him.

Al-Aḥnaf ibn Qays did the same in Basra, together with six thousand men under his command. Some members of the Azd tribe took a similar position.

Why did these men remain neutral during a conflict such as the Battle of the Camel, even though some of them could see the fighting with their own eyes and others were close enough to hear directly about it?

As leading Muslims and influential figures, the conflict concerned them. They might normally have been expected to enter it on one side or the other.

There is no doubt that political considerations lay behind their position.

But they could not appear before the wider Muslim community as neutral without giving any reason beyond their own political calculations.

That would not only have failed to persuade the public. It would also have exposed their political motives.

So once again, the issue of the person who commits a major sin appears.

There was a claim that ʿAlī was among those responsible for killing ʿUthmān—that is, a claim that he had committed one of the major sins. They could then tell the public that they were uncertain about the whole matter: they had no firm view on whether ʿAlī really was a killer, or on whether someone who committed murder—one of the major sins—should be fought with weapons or put to death. In other words, these “neutral” people justified their neutrality by saying they were unsure how to judge someone who committed a major sin. And being unsure in one’s judgment, just like reaching a firm judgment, was itself a form of independent reasoning. A Muslim had the right to form such a judgment and act on it.

Finally, what we want to show is this: the reason intellectual debate at the time became so absorbed first in the question of the person who commits a major sin, and then in the meaning of faith, was originally the political conflict over the caliphate—especially the different positions people took toward ʿAlī and Muʿāwiya.

The Kharijites insisted that anyone who committed a major sin was an unbeliever, and that actions were part of faith itself. From this, they concluded that they had to fight both ʿAlī and Muʿāwiya. This gave them a justification for the position they had taken after the arbitration at Ṣiffīn. The Shiʿa fought hard against the Kharijite theory because they knew that behind it lay an attack on Imam ʿAlī’s position, and even on the validity of his faith. Sunni scholars who also opposed the Kharijite view were, in practice, defending every Muslim caliph whom that theory condemned or discredited.

We do not deny that, during the intense debate surrounding it, the question of the person who commits a major sin—and the related question of what faith means—gradually developed an intellectual life of its own. It moved away from the immediate political conflict, or at least made those political positions harder to see.

Of course we do not deny this. But recognizing an intellectual phenomenon in its own right does not mean treating it as cut off from the political and social roots to which it is objectively connected, whether we want that connection to exist or not. Nor should the intellectual form of the debate prevent historians from seeing those roots or from examining the connection between them and the ideas that grew from them.

Summary of Chapter One

1 —

In Chapter Three of Part One, we saw how closely the historical development of Arab thought was connected with the political events surrounding the struggle over the caliphate after the Prophet.

By the final years of the Rightly Guided Caliphate—after the killing of ʿUthmān and the accession of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib under the system of consultation for which ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb had laid the practical foundation—it was already clear that this struggle was moving toward something new. Political divisions were beginning to develop into distinct schools and movements with their own theories, or their own “ideologies,” if we may use the term.

This became clear as positions toward ʿAlī’s caliphate began to take shape. Some of the Companions refused to pledge allegiance to him but did not go so far as to fight him. Others also refused allegiance and openly called for war against him. They then fought him in the Battle of the Camel at Basra and at Ṣiffīn.

At the head of this second camp stood ʿĀʾisha, daughter of Abū Bakr and wife of the Prophet, followed by Muʿāwiya ibn Abī Sufyān. At the time, Muʿāwiya governed Syria on behalf of the third caliph, ʿUthmān. He represented the economically dominant class in Syria and the leading Umayyad families. A third group supported ʿAlī. Most of them came from Iraq, especially Kufa.

From this point on, Arab-Islamic society began to divide into different tendencies and “ideologies.”

But if we wanted to understand the social roots of these divisions, we first had to return to the political and social setting in which they developed. It was there that they gradually took shape, acquired theoretical forms, and eventually became part of a much wider intellectual movement. Within that movement lay the earliest seeds of philosophical thought, which would later become a relatively independent field of philosophy in its own right.

2 —

The political and social setting we have in mind is the Umayyad period: the Arab-Islamic society ruled by the new state founded by Muʿāwiya, the first Umayyad ruler after the Rightly Guided Caliphs to take the title of caliph.

It was in this setting that the Shiʿa and the Kharijites emerged as the first two clearly distinct sects in Islam. Each developed its own view of political authority and the caliphate, as well as its own ideas about faith and knowledge. For that reason, we devoted the first chapter of this second part of our study to these two movements.

But before we could place the Shiʿa and Kharijites within the Umayyad world, we first had to give a clear picture of that world itself.

At the beginning of that picture, we drew attention to two features that marked Umayyad rule from the time of its founder, Muʿāwiya.

The first was the revival of tribal loyalties. Muʿāwiya strengthened his rule by allying with the Kalb tribes against the Qays tribes—the two main branches into which the Arabs were traditionally divided by ancestry. He hoped to give his new state a firm base in Arab tribal loyalty that could serve as its main protection against future upheavals.

The second feature was class division.

We reached this conclusion by examining the social order in Syria when Muʿāwiya governed it on behalf of the third Rightly Guided Caliph. The same basic social order continued to develop after Muʿāwiya became an independent ruler and founded the Umayyad state and caliphate.

This social order was feudal in character and had been inherited from the Sasanian and Byzantine periods. The Umayyads, with Muʿāwiya at their head, added something new that further strengthened the power of the landed elite. Muʿāwiya and his family themselves became major landowners. They used both slaves and free workers in agriculture and employed local specialists to organize farming and irrigation.

In this way, a new Arab Umayyad aristocracy of landowners emerged and allied itself with the existing local landed elite. It also formed alliances with major merchants and local Christian clergy against Christian clergy connected with the Byzantine Church.

Umayyad society therefore contained both a tribal alliance and a class alliance.

But the tribal alliance adapted itself to the class alliance, so no direct contradiction developed between the two. The allied tribes received special privileges, and over time these privileges themselves took on a class character.

When wealth becomes concentrated in this way, the result is predictable. A deep divide gradually opens between, on one side, those who hold economic and political power through the landed system, and on the other, the people who work the land, small craftsmen, and slaves.

Under the Umayyads, this process eventually reached an extreme point. The state placed a very heavy burden on the productive forces of society through taxation and harsh tax collection. This led to repeated uprisings in different parts of the Umayyad realm.

These uprisings also had intellectual effects. As we put it earlier in this chapter, they “brought the developing movement of Arab thought, in the late seventh and early eighth centuries, face to face with social and political reality.”

We discussed the most important of these uprisings in order to see how they were reflected in thought, and how those intellectual responses were connected with the social and political reality that produced them. Among them were Shiʿi uprisings and the uprisings of the Turks and the Kharijites, together with the forces that lay behind each.

The Shiʿa were the first to rise against Umayyad power, at the beginning of the reign of Yazīd ibn Muʿāwiya, the first heir to Muʿāwiya’s throne.

3 —

After giving a fairly detailed picture of the Umayyad setting in which the Shiʿa and Kharijites emerged as distinct movements, we turned to the positions and theories of each.

In discussing the Shiʿa, we began by defining the political and intellectual character of the Shiʿi position. From there, we moved to the theory that grew out of it.

We reached two conclusions.

The first was that the Shiʿa’s attitude toward ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, despite the differences among their various branches, expressed a political position toward different rulers of the Islamic caliphates. In most cases, this position was one of opposition.

The second was that this political opposition often also had a social character.

By this we mean that Shiʿi opposition was not limited to the form of government or to the people who ruled. It was often also directed against the way rulers treated weaker and oppressed social classes and groups.

We traced this social position to the fact that most ordinary Shiʿa themselves had suffered persecution throughout Arab-Islamic political history, as had their imams and leaders. It was therefore natural that they should also be affected by the persecution suffered by other weak groups in their society.

When we turned to Shiʿi theory itself, we tried to identify its earliest foundations, apart from the later developments and new ideas that appeared after the Shiʿa divided into a number of different sects.

We concluded that the basic ideas shared by the different Shiʿi branches were these:

First, political authority in Islam is a divine right. Authority belongs to God, not to the Muslim community.

Second, since authority belongs to God, the community does not have the right to choose the person who will hold it.

Third, God chose ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib as the designated successor, imam, and caliph after Muḥammad, and chose ʿAlī’s descendants after him. The different Shiʿi branches disagree over the exact line of succession among those descendants.

Fourth, the imamate—or caliphate—is a basic part of Shiʿi Islamic belief.

Not long after the first appearance of the Shiʿa, a more extreme group emerged whose view of ʿAlī raised him above the level of ordinary human beings. Some went even further and gave him divine qualities. These became known as the extremist Shiʿa, the ghulāt.

The more moderate Shiʿa continued to regard ʿAlī as an imam protected from error, much as the Prophet was protected from error. They also regarded him as the best and most knowledgeable person of his time. The same qualities were then applied to the imams descended from him: each was regarded as protected from error, and as the best and most knowledgeable person of his own age.

These more extreme ideas entered Shiʿi theory through the development of theological and philosophical debate, once that kind of thinking began to dominate sectarian thought and the questions raised by political conflict.

From al-Shahrastānī’s description of the doctrines of the extremist Shiʿa—al-Shahrastānī being one of the great historians of philosophy—we concluded that ideas such as divine indwelling, the transmigration of souls, and similar doctrines that had been prominent in Persian and Indian philosophy entered the beliefs of these groups.

In our discussion of the extremist Shiʿa, we also examined the doctrine of the Kaysāniyya, one of their branches. Here, for the first time in the history of Arab-Islamic thought, we find beliefs in divine indwelling and in rajʿa—the return to earthly life after death.

We also identified a class element in this movement: it was closely connected with a group of mawālī, non-Arab clients attached to Arab tribes.

After that, we discussed the Shiʿi “theory” of knowledge in general.

Our conclusion was that, for the Shiʿa, knowledge remained connected with a divine source. It came from God to the Prophet through revelation, and from the Prophet to the infallible imam whom God had appointed through the Prophet.

At the same time, however, we placed great value on the emergence of ijtihād, or independent legal reasoning, in Islamic law. This movement led to the development of a rational discipline: uṣūl al-fiqh, the study of the principles used to derive Islamic law.

In it we found a real effort to organize knowledge in a systematic way. We also found a move beyond the rigid abstract form of Aristotelian logic when drawing conclusions from premises.

Alongside this was another important feature: the tendency to treat thought as an interconnected whole. This can be seen clearly in the way the different Arab-Islamic sciences overlapped with one another—for example, the close relationship between uṣūl al-fiqh and rational theological debate.

4 —

In our discussion of the Kharijites, we first examined the historical origins of their movement.

At the beginning, they fought in ʿAlī’s army against Muʿāwiya at the Battle of Ṣiffīn. They then “withdrew” from ʿAlī’s ranks in anger after he accepted the idea of arbitration. That arbitration ended in a carefully arranged maneuver meant to remove ʿAlī from the caliphate while leaving Muʿāwiya in place.

The Kharijites justified their break with ʿAlī by developing a new theory of faith.

For them, faith had two parts: belief, and action in accordance with that belief. This led them to declare ʿAlī, ʿUthmān, Ṭalḥa, al-Zubayr, ʿĀʾisha, Muʿāwiya, and all later Umayyad and Abbasid rulers unbelievers. In their view, all of them acted against what was right, and therefore none of them could truly be believers.

On the basis of this theory, the Kharijites saw themselves as obliged to fight anyone who departed from the truth—which, in their words, was “God’s right, not the right of men.”

Their history was therefore filled with bloody violence, which was answered with violence in return, whether from the Shiʿa or the Umayyads. The greatest blow against them came when al-Ḥajjāj ibn Yūsuf al-Thaqafī took control of Iraq on behalf of the Umayyad caliph ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān.

Yet when we examined their principles in the abstract, we also found a positive side.

Unlike both the Sunnis and the Shiʿa, the Kharijites did not limit the caliphate to ʿAlī’s family, as the Shiʿa did, or to branches of Quraysh, as the Sunnis did.

They argued that the caliph did not have to be a Hāshimite or even a member of Quraysh. He could even be an Abyssinian slave. The caliphate, they said, belonged to the community, and the community had the right to choose whoever was worthy of carrying this responsibility and protecting Muslim interests, regardless of tribe, ethnicity, or class.

The Kharijites also often sided with the poor, peasants, workers, and the oppressed. They led some peasant uprisings against the terrible oppression that al-Ḥajjāj imposed on the people of Iraq.

There was another important feature of the Kharijite movement that had to be mentioned. Most of the religious and intellectual schools of the period fought them not only politically but also at the level of ideas. Their theory of faith—the theory from which they justified their violent struggles—came under sustained attack.

In discussing this conflict, we tried to uncover the political roots of the different theories of faith.

Our conclusion was that the huge debate which occupied intellectual life for so long—whether a person who committed a major sin should be declared an unbeliever or should remain a Muslim—had a political and partisan conflict behind it.

It was not an intellectual debate isolated from political reality.

That reality stretched from the killing of ʿUthmān through the rise of the Muʿtazila, the emergence of kalām, and eventually the development of Arab-Islamic philosophy itself.

Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

A — The School of Opinion and the School of Hadith

1 — Within the Political Struggle

While political conflict was developing along the lines we have described, another kind of conflict was developing alongside it. This second conflict followed much the same course, but with a degree of independence of its own. At first, it took the form of an intellectual dispute over Islamic law.

One striking feature of this legal and intellectual conflict was how deeply it was connected with the different social environments of the Arab-Islamic world.

We will see that these disagreements over legal questions became one of the forces driving the wider development of Arab-Islamic thought. Out of that development would come the rise of kalām: rational theological debate, and with it a growing form of philosophical thinking about the new questions confronting Muslim thinkers.

We have already mentioned more than once the use of independent judgment in matters of law.

We explained earlier that, in the first period of Islam, this was the main opening available to the developing movement of Arab thought after Islam had framed the question of knowledge in a way that tied reason very closely to faith.

In fact, independent judgment was already used during the Prophet’s lifetime. It continued under the Rightly Guided Caliphs, especially under ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb.

There was a major objective reason why ʿUmar became especially associated with this kind of flexible legal reasoning. There was also, of course, a personal factor: ʿUmar himself had a flexible and practical mind.

During the twenty years of ʿUmar’s caliphate, the Arab conquests brought the Arabs face to face with entirely new conditions in the conquered lands.

They now encountered situations, questions, and problems that had never arisen in the life they had known in the Arabian Peninsula. To deal with them, they had to apply Islamic law with skill, flexibility, and creativity. They needed rulings for circumstances they had never faced before and had never previously needed to regulate.

This is what we mean by the objective factor.

The Arab conquerors suddenly had to deal with new financial, administrative, organizational, military, social, and legal questions. They faced types of disputes unknown in their earlier, simpler society, as well as new questions of personal status.

Did the two main sources of Islamic law—the Qurʾān and the Sunnah—contain detailed ready-made rulings for every one of these matters?

Of course not.

No body of law, whether divine or human, can contain a detailed text for every new situation that life will ever produce.

So there was only one way to apply Islamic law to these new circumstances: the use of reasoned judgment, or ijtihād.

The Arabs responsible for governing the conquered lands therefore turned to this new source of legal judgment and used it extensively. Arab historical works and the large body of legal literature contain countless examples of rulings reached through rational reflection based on the general principles of Islamic law.

2 — The School of the People of Opinion

Out of the practical use of this legal method grew a distinct school known as the school of the “People of Opinion.”

It had become recognizable as a school with its own clear features by the middle of the first Islamic century, and its influence spread widely among jurists and judges during the first half of the second.

It had several distinguishing features.

First, its scholars did not limit themselves to giving legal judgments on real cases placed before them. They also imagined cases that had not actually happened and tried to work out what legal judgment should apply to each hypothetical situation.

Second, some of its representatives did not feel obliged to search first for a hadith from the Prophet before using their own judgment.

Some members of this school would even refuse to base a ruling on a prophetic hadith when a hadith directly matching the case was available. Their reason was the growing doubt, after some time had passed since the Prophet, about the reliability of hadith reports transmitted through chains of narrators.

“Al-Baghdādī attributed the rejection of acting on hadith to the Kharijites in his book Uṣūl al-Dīn.”37

There was another striking feature of the School of Opinion: it was especially widespread and firmly rooted in Iraq.

Aḥmad Amīn38 gives three reasons for this.

First, two of its most famous figures, ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd and later Abū Ḥanīfa, lived in Iraq and helped spread the use of personal judgment and analogical reasoning.

Second, Ibn Khaldūn noted that the people of “the Hijaz transmitted more hadith than the people of Iraq, because Medina was the home of the Hijra and the gathering place of the Companions. Those who later moved from there to Iraq were largely occupied with the great military campaigns.”39

Third:

“Iraq was a land of cities” and “had been deeply influenced by Persian and Greek civilization. Urban life constantly presents the law with many detailed questions requiring rulings, to a degree that cannot be compared with a largely nomadic region. Once this was combined with the amount of hadith that had reached Iraq, the result was inevitably a greater use of personal judgment.”40

This third reason is what we had in mind earlier when we said that intellectual conflict in this period was deeply connected with the different social environments found across the Arab-Islamic world.

This will become even clearer when we turn to the School of the People of Hadith.

3 — The School of the People of Hadith

This school arose in response to the School of Opinion and took the opposite position.

Its scholars rejected the use of personal opinion in legal judgment. If a case arose that required a ruling and they could not find one in the Qurʾān, they searched for a prophetic hadith that applied to it. If they could not find such a hadith, they stopped and gave no ruling on the case.

Some took this position so far that they placed hadith above the Qurʾān itself. Some jurists of the second Islamic century went even further and argued that the Sunnah—that is, prophetic hadith—could abrogate rulings in the Qurʾān.41

The features of this school were almost the exact opposite of those we described in the School of Opinion.

If the School of Opinion arose, became established, and spread in Iraq for the three reasons just given, then the School of Hadith arose, became established, and spread in the Hijaz for the same reasons in reverse.

Its best-known figures, such as Imam Mālik,42 lived in the Hijaz, the land in which the Prophet himself had lived. Hadith was also far more abundant there than in Iraq. And finally, the Hijaz was a largely “nomadic region” that had not been strongly affected by “Persian and Greek civilization,” to use Aḥmad Amīn’s explanation quoted above.

The difference between the two schools can also be seen in their attitude toward hypothetical cases.

The School of Opinion was willing to imagine situations that had never actually happened and then use reasoned judgment to work out the legal ruling that would apply.

The School of Hadith strongly disliked this practice. Its scholars refused to answer questions unless they concerned events that had really taken place.

At first, the conflict between these two opposing tendencies was mainly a conflict over law.

But it became increasingly intense and eventually expanded into a much broader intellectual struggle.

Later, we find each tendency taking a position in the major intellectual conflicts of the time that closely matched the position it had already taken in the legal debate.

From the legal tradition of the People of Opinion came intellectual figures such as al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī. It was from his teaching circle in the mosque of Basra that the well-known rationalist school of the Muʿtazila eventually emerged.

The People of Hadith, by contrast, entered the broader intellectual struggle with the same conservative attitude they had shown in legal matters. From their traditionalist school came figures such as Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal, who strongly opposed the principles of the Muʿtazila.

B — The Rise of the Arab Sciences

1 — Arab Sciences or Islamic Sciences?

Would it not be more accurate to call the sciences that arose in the early Islamic period “Islamic sciences” rather than “Arab sciences”?

After all, their development was directly connected with Islam—with its foundational texts, its leading figures, and the events of its early history. This was true both of the subjects these sciences studied and of the forces and purposes behind their emergence.

The question is entirely reasonable.

We have nevertheless chosen to call them the “Arab sciences,” even though we are fully aware of this historical fact and of how difficult it is to draw a sharp line between the two names.

From the moment Islam entered Arab life, it became one of the forces shaping that life. It became part of its events, interactions, conflicts, and cultural developments. In this way, Islam also became one of the most important forces shaping the course of Arab history across the different areas of social life.

So when we choose the term “Arab sciences,” we do not mean to deny, ignore, or move beyond this fact.

The distinction we are making is a different one.

Some sciences arose within the specifically Arab environment and dealt directly with the Arabic language, or with people who had lived through Islam’s beginnings and its earliest movement and events in its Arab birthplace.

Other sciences arose later in a much broader environment, where Arab life interacted with the life of many different peoples. These later sciences were the product of a much wider process of cultural exchange and interaction.

But distinguishing between these two kinds of science does not mean creating an artificial division inside the culture we call Arab-Islamic culture.

We can already state our position on this clearly. We will need to return to it in greater detail when we discuss Arab-Islamic philosophy, because there too we will face the question of whether it should instead be called “Islamic philosophy.” Our position there will be the same as it is here.

Put briefly, the culture produced by the living, dialectical relationship between Arab life and Islamic life, between Arab thought and Islamic thought, and between language and the thought expressed through that language, is an Arab-Islamic culture.

It cannot be divided neatly into something purely Arab, something purely Islamic, and something that is a mixture of the two.

Nor can it be divided between works produced by thinkers of Arab ancestry and works produced by Muslim thinkers of non-Arab ancestry.

They all belong to the same culture.

All of them developed their thought through the Arabic language—with its linguistic, expressive, and intellectual patterns. And in their cultural work, across its many different fields, they were all responding to the questions of a particular society: its social, political, and intellectual problems.

They all lived within that society, and they all formed their view of the world through its historical reality and its pattern of social relations.

The sciences we are discussing here, which we have chosen to call Arab rather than Islamic sciences, dealt with the Arabic language, its rules, and its literature; with Arab history before and after Islam; with the life of the Prophet and the lives of his Companions and successors; with reports of the Arab conquests; with the language of the Qurʾān and prophetic hadith and the meanings carried by that language; and with the study of hadith itself, including its transmission and its transmitters.

Their purpose also included using the language of the Qurʾān and hadith to draw out their teachings on belief and law.

More precisely, by the “Arab sciences” we mean those sciences connected most directly with the Arabic language itself: grammar,43 rhetoric, literature, history, Qurʾānic interpretation, hadith, and Islamic law, including both jurisprudence and the principles of jurisprudence.

All of these disciplines depended on knowledge of how Arabic works, because Arabic was the sole language through which the teachings of Islam were expressed.

We are not inventing the term “Arab sciences,” nor do we claim to be doing so. It was used in earlier times as well.

Al-Khwārizmī, for example, says while describing his book Mafātīḥ al-ʿUlūm:

“I divided it into two parts: one for the sciences of religious law and the Arab sciences connected with them, and another for the sciences of foreign peoples, including the Greeks and others.”44

Our reason for discussing these “Arab sciences” here is limited to one point.

Their rise in the early Islamic period, and especially during the Umayyad period, became a starting point for a wider movement of cultural development. That cultural development was itself one of the clearest expressions of the deeper changes taking place in the basic structures of the society ruled by the Islamic caliphate.

The rise of these sciences answered the needs created by that wider development.

The expanding state needed more organized forms of knowledge to support its economic, social, administrative, and financial organization.

At the same time, the Arab-Islamic conquests had spread across many countries and peoples. These populations now had to adapt to the language of the conquerors—to speak it and understand its meanings according to some organized set of rules.

There was also another problem.

As non-Arab peoples began speaking Arabic, and as Arabs mixed with speakers of other languages, it soon became clear that Arabic itself could lose much of its original purity, even among Arabs. Many Arabs were now living in new geographical and social surroundings far from the environment in which their language had originally developed.

From an Islamic point of view, this created a serious danger.

Muslims—including Arab Muslims—could gradually lose the ability to understand the beliefs and laws of Islam from what were then their only sources: the Qurʾān and the Sunnah.

Those sources used forms of expression regarded as among the highest achievements of Arabic in style, structure, and composition. Their contents also included metaphysical ideas, theories of knowledge, and legal concepts.

In the Qurʾān, these were often expressed in an artistic, suggestive, and indirect form. At other times, they were expressed very compactly, in language capable of carrying several possible meanings and intentions.

There was an additional difficulty.

At first, the texts of the Qurʾān and hadith were not generally available in written form. What had been written down circulated among only a limited number of the Companions. Most of these texts were preserved through oral transmission by people who had heard them from the Prophet.

Those people later scattered across different lands with the armies of conquest. Some were killed in those wars. Others gradually died, one after another, in widely separated regions.

All these factors, working together, created the need for the new sciences.

First came the need to establish the rules of Arabic grammar.

Second came the need to organize knowledge of the language’s rhetorical and expressive features.

Then came the need to interpret the language of the Qurʾān and explain its teachings on belief and law in the light of this organized linguistic knowledge.

There was also the need to collect prophetic hadith, verify different reports, distinguish one transmitter’s account from another, and study the life of each transmitter in order to judge how trustworthy that person was, whether he had actually been connected with the Prophet during the Prophet’s lifetime, and so on.

The early rise of these sciences created an active and energetic cultural life.

This helped the growing intellectual movement—which was itself developing alongside political conflict—gain access to a body of knowledge that had at least begun to be classified and organized.

At this stage, however, the classification was still basic and the organization still primitive. The full elements of specialized scientific study had not yet developed.

That kind of organization becomes possible only when knowledge has advanced and expanded enough for people to feel the need to classify it according to a common subject and to bring related material together in a coherent way.

The new sciences were still too young at this early stage of Islam for such classification to be complete.

For that reason, the “Arab sciences” remained closely intertwined. Clear boundaries between them did not emerge until the great flowering of Arab-Islamic culture in the late second Islamic century, during the early Abbasid period.

For the same reason, the intellectual questions produced by political conflict did not yet take the form of a clearly organized science with its own method.

That development came only in the later period we have just mentioned.

We are speaking here specifically of the questions that would eventually form the science of kalām.

From the beginning of the Umayyad period, debate had already arisen over the caliphate, the person who commits a major sin, and the meaning of faith. Later came debates over divine decree and human responsibility for action, followed by metaphysical questions about the attributes of God.

But for a long time, the intellectual material produced by all these debates remained scattered.

It had not yet been brought together into a single independent discipline with a clearly defined subject and its own rational method.

That happened only later, when philosophical thinking itself became the starting point and basic framework of Arab-Islamic thought across its different fields of activity.

This was the Abbasid period associated with the age of al-Maʾmūn.

There is one more point to make about these “Arab sciences.”

As soon as they had formed, become the center of a wide cultural movement, and begun developing toward greater maturity, the first signs of philosophical thinking were already entering Arab intellectual life from many directions.

The effect soon became visible inside these sciences themselves.

Even Arabic grammar and the study of language began to absorb this philosophical tendency. Their discussions started to take on a more rational and logical character, even though both disciplines had originally depended on transmitted reports and direct listening to pre-Islamic Arabic literature in order to establish the philological and grammatical features of the Arabic language.45

In the Basran school of grammar, for example, we find a strong tendency to use logical analogy.

De Boer’s explanation is not far from the historical reality: he connects this development with the influence of philosophical schools that appeared in Basra before they appeared elsewhere.46

2 — The Move from Oral Transmission to Writing

The development of written recording was closely connected, both historically and logically, with the rise of the “Arab sciences” we have just discussed.

This movement toward writing occupies a major place in the history of Arab-Islamic thought.

What we mean here is the historical process through which literary, religious, and scientific knowledge, along with reports about Arab history, began to be written down after having previously been transmitted mainly by speaking and listening rather than by reading.

Written recording in this sense is not the same as authorship.

It means the transition from an age in which knowledge was passed on orally to an age in which it was preserved in writing.

So when exactly did this transition begin?

Some historians believe that it began around the middle of the second Islamic century, in other words during the second half of the eighth century CE.

This view does not fit the historical evidence.

There are clear signs that both the Qurʾān and prophetic hadith were already being written down during the earliest period of Islam.

Ibn al-Nadīm, the author of al-Fihrist, reports that ʿUbayd ibn Shariya al-Jurhumī wrote down a Book of Proverbs and a Book of Kings and Accounts of Earlier Peoples during Muʿāwiya’s reign.

He also reports that Ṣuḥār al-ʿAbdī, who was a Kharijite, wrote another work called The Book of Proverbs during the same period.

Elsewhere in al-Fihrist, Ibn al-Nadīm tells us of a man from al-Ḥadītha named Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥusayn who collected books.

His library contained Arabic works on grammar, language, and literature.

Ibn al-Nadīm says that among them he saw a copy of the Qurʾān written in the hand of Khālid ibn al-Hayyāj, a companion of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib. He also saw examples of the handwriting of al-Ḥasan and al-Ḥusayn, the sons of ʿAlī.

The collection also contained guarantees and agreements written in ʿAlī’s own hand and in the hands of other secretaries of the Prophet, as well as writings by scholars of grammar and language such as Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ and Abū ʿAmr al-Shaybānī.

In al-Ṭabaqāt al-Kubrā, Ibn Saʿd reports that Hishām ibn ʿUrwa ibn al-Zubayr said:

“My father burned some books on jurisprudence that he owned on the day of al-Ḥarra. Afterwards he used to say: I would rather still have those books than possess the equivalent of my family and all my wealth.”47

Abū al-Faraj al-Iṣfahānī gives us another vivid picture.

He tells us that ʿAbd al-Ḥakam ibn ʿAmr ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ṣafwān al-Jumaḥī, a man of the Umayyad period, turned one of his rooms into something rather like a public club in our own time.

He placed chess sets and dice there, together with “notebooks containing material from every branch of knowledge.” He put pegs into the walls so that anyone who came in could hang up his clothes, take down a notebook and read it, or choose one of the games and play.48

This shows that written notebooks were already available for people to read at an earlier date.

Ibn Khallikān also tells us about Ibn Shihāb al-Zuhrī:

“When he sat at home, he would place his books around him and become so absorbed in them that he forgot everything else in the world. His wife once said to him: By God, these books are harder for me to bear than three rival wives.”49

Ibn Shihāb died in 124 AH/741 CE.

This indicates that written books had already been common during the Umayyad period for some time.

Ibn Khallikān confirms the point again when speaking about ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ, who was born in 70 AH/689 CE:

“The books in which he had written down material from the eloquent Arabs filled one of his rooms almost to the ceiling.”50

All these historical examples show clearly that the movement toward written recording developed alongside the rise of cultural activity and the emergence of the Arab sciences.

It also developed alongside the intellectual movement that had begun, in its earliest stage, as a reflection of the intense political conflict of the early Umayyad period.

It was therefore natural for writing to become another force helping cultural exchange between the Arabs and the peoples of the vast Arab state.

This exchange would later bear fruit in the development of Arab-Islamic thought.

Written transmission also played an important part in spreading the rational thought of the Muʿtazila, which was becoming increasingly active within these same political and cultural developments.

3 — Centers of Intellectual Life

The main centers of cultural activity, including intellectual activity in particular, shifted from one period to another.

These changes followed developments in Arab political life and the movement of political capitals. They also reflected the influence of the older intellectual traditions of the different lands brought into the Arab-Islamic empire.

For this reason, the main centers of intellectual life in early Islam were different from those of the Abbasid period.

Further changes took place within the Abbasid period itself, continuing through the age of the regional dynasties,51 the Crusades, the Mongol invasions, and finally the period later described as the “age of decline.”

But during the early Islamic period, including the Umayyad age that still concerns us here, the main centers of intellectual activity were Mecca and Medina in the Hijaz; Basra and Kufa in Iraq; Damascus in Syria; and Fusṭāṭ, now Cairo, in Egypt.

In Mecca and Medina, the main fields that flourished were jurisprudence, hadith, and history.

This was because the Hijaz was the birthplace of Islam. From there, the new religion had spread through all the educational means available to it.

Mecca and Medina remained the main centers of the Prophet’s mission and of the Rightly Guided Caliphate, apart from the caliphate of ʿAlī, who made Kufa his center.

Basra and Kufa,52 by contrast, arose after the Arab conquest of Iraq during the caliphate of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb.

Both quickly became major centers of the most advanced forms of cultural activity then available.

In these two cities, the practical experience of people from the Hijaz combined with their knowledge of Islam, gained from having lived through its development from the beginning. Many of these people migrated to Kufa and Basra after the conquest.

This was joined by the much older civilizational experience of the people of Iraq.

They had inherited, or lived within, the cultural legacy of Babylon, Persia, and Assyria. The city of al-Ḥīra had also been influenced by these civilizations.

Some knowledge of Greek philosophy had reached Iraq through Christian monasteries in the north and through certain Persian schools.53

All these different forms of experience met in a region already marked by a rich cultural life and helped by rapid urban and economic development.

Before long, a sharp rivalry developed between Basra and Kufa.

This rivalry became one of the forces encouraging intellectual growth in both cities.

It eventually produced a division between a Basran school and a Kufan school. Each developed its own distinct approach to questions of jurisprudence, grammar, and literature, and later to questions of kalām as well.

Basra and Kufa remained among the most important centers of Arab thought for several generations, even after Baghdad had emerged as the unrivaled capital of Arab culture. We can see this in the deep and powerful effects they had on the development of Arab thought. They became starting points for some of the boldest and most independent schools of thought, such as the Muʿtazila, as well as for social movements with an intellectual basis, such as the Qarmaṭians and the Brethren of Purity.

It seems to me that the conditions that placed Basra and Kufa in political opposition from the time the conflict between the Alids and the Umayyads became intense may have helped these schools of thought and social movements emerge in those two rebellious cities. Both cities also had large populations of mawālī, non-Arab clients and converts, who were among the strongest opponents of the Umayyads because the Umayyads stood for the idea of Arab supremacy.

Damascus, meanwhile, rose to great importance when it became the capital of the Umayyad caliphate. Scholars and writers came there from across the Arab state. Yet its cultural influence never reached the level of Basra or Kufa. Political conflict took up so much of the Umayyads’ attention that they devoted less effort to developing scholarship in their capital. Instead, they gave considerable attention to literature and writers, especially poets, whom they used to support their policies and attack their political opponents among the Anṣār, the Alids, and the Kharijites.

This does not mean that Damascus had no intellectual life. Serious debates took place there over some of the questions raised by contact between Islam and Christianity. But these discussions remained within the limits of the official debate allowed in the Umayyad capital.

Take the problem of divine decree and the question of whether human beings are compelled to act or free to choose. Damascus could hardly have avoided discussing it when it had become the leading subject of intellectual debate in the schools of Iraq and the Hijaz. What mattered, however, was the position taken on the issue. In Damascus, the dominant position was the same as that of the Umayyad government: it supported the view that human beings do not have freedom of choice in their actions. We will later see how fiercely the Umayyad rulers fought the idea of free choice, and why.

As for Fusṭāṭ, from the Arab conquest of Egypt in 20 AH/640 CE under ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb until the final years of Umayyad rule, it remained a center of learning dominated by the purely religious sciences, especially hadith and law. Its intellectual life therefore developed mainly through Islamic religious studies and the schools of law.

C — Early Signs of Philosophical Thought

First: Questions of Faith

How did philosophical thought arise around Islamic beliefs?

Many later researchers, both Eastern and Western, have approached this question from only one side, although they disagree over which side matters.

Some explain the rise of philosophical thought around Islamic beliefs entirely through outside influences. The historian of philosophy T. J. de Boer is one of the clearest examples.

First, he denies that the Qurʾan itself brought Muslims a body of doctrine. His argument is that the Qurʾan “gave Muslims a religion, not theories; they received rules, but they did not receive doctrines.”

Second, he argues that once Muslims conquered other lands, “they found before them a fully developed Christian theology, as well as the doctrines of the followers of Zoroaster and the doctrines of the Brahmins.”

De Boer therefore has no doubt that the theological doctrines of the Muslim mutakallimūn were deeply influenced by Christian ideas. In his view, Islamic doctrine took shape under the influence of the Melkites and Jacobites in Damascus, and under the influence of Nestorian and Gnostic teachings in Basra.54

De Boer finally concludes that, alongside the considerations he has already described, there are “scattered indications that some of the earliest Muslims who defended free choice had Christian teachers. Purely philosophical elements then came first from the Gnostic schools, and later from translated books. These joined the Christian influences that had themselves been shaped by Greek philosophy in its final Eastern form.”55

Taken together, these views of De Boer—and they represent the position of many Western researchers—treat the philosophical discussion of Islamic beliefs among Arab Muslims as something that came entirely from outside.

They give no real place to internal causes.
