Nor do they see any connection between the rise of philosophical thinking about Islamic beliefs and the actual conditions of Arab-Islamic life: not when these debates first appeared, not when they developed into the discipline known as kalām, and not when they later became fully philosophical questions with the emergence of Arab philosophy as something independent of kalām.

It should be clear that views of this kind conflict, at least in one respect, not only with the facts of history but also with a sound scientific method of research. No sound method can accept that a particular kind of thinking simply appears in a society while remaining cut off from the internal conditions of that society at a particular stage of its development.

What Engels wrote to Conrad Schmidt on 5 August 1890 applies to our subject to a large extent:

“The whole of history must be studied anew, and the conditions of the different social formations must be examined in detail before any attempt is made to derive from them the political, legal, aesthetic, philosophical, and religious forms of thought that correspond to those conditions.”56

Another group of researchers on Arab-Islamic thought approaches the question in a way that comes closer to a sound method, but still does not examine social and political reality deeply enough to carry the logic of scientific inquiry through to its conclusion.

This second group explains the rise of philosophical thought around Islamic beliefs through a very broad theory: that in its search for certainty, human thought passes through three stages—absolute belief, inner doubt, and finally rational conviction.

When one representative of this view tries to apply this pattern to Arab-Islamic thought, however, he finds that he must qualify it:

“Islamic thought was not primitive. Its acceptance in the first stage was therefore not naïve acceptance, but submission after resistance. Its doubt in the second stage was not hesitation over whether to believe, but uncertainty over whether the intended meaning had been fully understood. Most early Muslims therefore accepted the Qurʾanic verses according to their literal meaning. But some reflective minds began to doubt whether their first understanding had gone far enough. They returned to the text, considered its other possible meanings, and eventually settled on a view that gave them a form of rational certainty.”57

This view, in one form or another, also appears in the work of other modern historians of Arab thought, especially Arab historians.

Its weakness is not only that it relies on broad generalizations. It also fails to begin from the ground of real social life and ask what actually drove this development.

Why did early Muslims move from accepting Qurʾanic verses in their literal sense, to doubting whether they had fully understood them, to rereading the text and considering other possible meanings, and finally to reaching a view that gave them a form of rational certainty?58

Was this gradual change purely internal and reflective? Or was it connected to changes in the social and political life of Arab-Islamic society?

If it was connected to those changes, how? Which events shaped its direction? And how closely were these changing intellectual positions connected to changes in the society itself?

Those who take this view give us no answer to any of these questions. Their explanation therefore remains, on one side, broad and abstract and, on the other, idealist in the way it approaches the subject.

If we compare these first two positions with that of a third group of major modern researchers, such as Muṣṭafā ʿAbd al-Rāziq and Aḥmad Amīn, we find an approach much closer to a scientific method because it avoids looking at the problem from only one side.

Muṣṭafā ʿAbd al-Rāziq, for example, writes about matters of belief under the Rightly Guided Caliphs:

“Questions of belief under the Rightly Guided Caliphs remained much as they had been in the time of the Prophet. But the Prophet proclaimed the word of revelation, and no believer could turn away from it. Any disagreement among Muslims was settled by referring it back to the Messenger of God.

“Under the Rightly Guided Caliphs, disagreements did arise over questions that required independent judgment. Although these questions were connected to practical rulings, they became important enough to form the basis of lasting divisions among Muslims. Their importance grew until they became connected to questions of belief, and many Islamic sects were built on their foundations.”

ʿAbd al-Rāziq then traces these disputes in concrete historical terms, beginning with the disagreement over the caliphate after the Prophet’s death, moving through the events that followed, and then through the rise of different schools and factions. He finally concludes:

“Although the arguments between these schools were based mainly on transmitted religious texts, they were also mixed with rational inquiry.”59

This account places the rise of “rational inquiry” within real historical conditions. Its starting point was the first dispute over the caliphate. That dispute then developed until it produced schools that were political in content but religious in form. Debate between those schools created an intellectual basis from which rational inquiry—or what we have called philosophical thought—could begin.

We agree with this concrete account of the conditions in which this kind of thinking emerged. But, as we have repeatedly stressed, this does not mean ignoring outside influences, especially cultural ones. Those influences helped philosophical thought move beyond its first simple beginnings and develop into more complex and mature forms. In other words, they helped move it from the concrete level of social and political reality to the level of theoretical awareness.

Aḥmad Amīn also traces the beginnings of these debates—which later took on a rational and theoretical form in kalām—back to their first political roots in Arab-Islamic life. At the same time, he does not ignore the part played by outside influences in helping these debates develop into the more systematic theoretical form they reached under the Abbasids.

It is true that Aḥmad Amīn also uses the same broad theory we saw in the second group of researchers. He expresses it by saying that every religious belief begins as a simple but powerful faith. At first, it pays little attention to disagreement or investigation. It accepts the foundations of religion and believes in them fully, without much desire for analysis or philosophy.

Then comes the stage of investigation and reflection. Religious questions begin to take on a scholarly and philosophical character, and religious thinkers turn to philosophy to strengthen their arguments and support their proofs.

Aḥmad Amīn writes:

“This happened in Judaism, this happened in Christianity, and this happened in Islam. The first Islamic age nearly passed in a state of faith with little argument. Then, once people had settled down, they began to examine and investigate. They widened the scope of their inquiry, compared similar cases, distinguished differences and points of agreement, and this necessarily led to different ways of looking at things, and therefore to differences of opinion and doctrine.”60

It is true that Aḥmad Amīn uses this general theory in an idealist form. But he does not leave it floating in abstraction or push it further into idealism. He connects it to real historical factors. Whether he intended this or not, that connection helps strip away its idealist shell.

This becomes clear when he discusses internal causes, including political ones. Speaking of those political causes, he writes:

“Sometimes a teaching belonging to one of the different sects is described as though it were purely religious doctrine, a question of belief and nothing more. But if we examine its origin carefully, we find that it was political. Take the question of the Muslim who commits a major sin: is he an unbeliever or a believer? It seems that this was not originally a purely theological debate. Its source was the judgment that the political parties passed on one another…”

He goes on to say that political disagreement became “a major cause of religious disagreement, and a cause of doctrines and sects.”

After describing the political conflict in detail and identifying the different sides—the Shīʿa, the Umayyads, the Kharijites, and the neutral party, the Murjiʾa—he reaches this conclusion:

“This political conflict, which took on a religious form, also contributed to disagreements over the meaning of faith and unbelief, major and minor sins, the status of the person who commits a major sin, and similar questions. They were then drawn into disagreements over secondary matters as well, until each group gradually became a separate sect with its own disagreements over both fundamental and secondary questions.”61

This way of analyzing the problem closely agrees with the analysis we adopted in an earlier chapter.62 In our view, it identifies the indirect political and social roots from which philosophical thinking about Islamic beliefs emerged.

What remains is to trace the historical course through which this kind of thinking began to develop.

We do not say that we must identify its “direct causes.” Intellectual developments, like historical stages in the development of society, cannot be assigned simple direct causes. There are no sharp boundaries separating one stage from another. Two stages may coexist for a long time, and intellectual developments are even more complicated in this respect.

So if we want to identify the historical course of this development, or the point at which that course began to take shape, we have to look at particular historical events and ask how they affected the general climate of thought during this period rather than another.

We must also look at what was distinctive about those events, at the kind of effect they had on the dominant intellectual questions of the time, at the internal forces working beneath the surface, and at the way those internal forces interacted with influences coming from outside.

Second: The Problem of Divine Decree

1 — Its Historical Emergence

The problem of divine decree was one of the first major questions through which Arab thought began moving toward the kind of rational inquiry that prepared the way for philosophical thought.

We have a great deal of historical evidence showing that discussion of divine decree and predestination among Arab and Muslim thinkers had already become an intellectual debate about the responsibility of the individual for his own actions around the middle of the first Islamic century—that is, around the middle of the seventh century CE.

Al-Isfarāyīnī, for example, writes:

“In the later days of the Companions, disagreement appeared with the Qadarites. They discussed divine decree and human power—the ability of a person to act through his own power—as did Maʿbad al-Juhanī, Ghaylān al-Dimashqī, and Jaʿd ibn Dirham. The Companions who were still alive rejected their views: ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbbās, Jābir, Anas, Abū Hurayra, ʿUqba ibn ʿĀmir, and others of their generation. They advised those who came after them not to greet these men, not to visit them if they became ill, and not to pray over them when they died.”63

If we add to this what we know about the deaths of these Companions—Jābir died in 50 AH/670 CE, while Anas, the last of them, died in 93 AH/712 CE—we can reasonably conclude that the issue was already being widely discussed in intellectual and religious circles before the 50s AH, that is, before the 670s CE.

This conclusion is supported by Ṭāshkubrīzāda, who says that:

“The disagreement”—meaning the disagreement over divine decree—“developed gradually until the final days of the Companions. Then Maʿbad al-Juhanī, Ghaylān al-Dimashqī, Wāṣil ibn ʿAṭāʾ, ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd, and Yūnus al-Aswārī appeared. They disagreed over divine decree and over attributing all things to God’s determination, and so on, until the principles of Muʿtazilism emerged.”64

This passage suggests that the issue was already being discussed even before Maʿbad and Ghaylān, whom some researchers describe as the first people to speak about divine decree.

The view that comes closest to the historical evidence, then, is that the question had already been raised before either man appeared. Ṭāshkubrīzāda’s wording itself points in that direction: “The disagreement developed gradually until the final days of the Companions, then Maʿbad appeared…”

This not only fits the historical evidence. It also fits the way history itself develops.

Intellectual movements do not normally begin at a sharp and precisely identifiable point. We cannot usually say that a particular intellectual development was created by one person, or by a few people, at one exact moment.

First, intellectual developments do not appear suddenly and spontaneously without earlier developments preparing the way for them.

Second, intellectual developments do not arise apart from social developments. They are connected to them in one way or another, sometimes directly and sometimes indirectly.

Third, as we will soon see, the debate over divine decree in particular was connected to a position that was political in substance even though it appeared in religious form.

Once we take these three points into account, we have good reason to reject the common claim made by many historians of Arab philosophy that discussion of this problem began with Maʿbad al-Juhanī.65

There is another historical reason for rejecting that claim.

It is well known that the Sunnis regarded ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib as the first of their theologians. They say that he debated the Kharijites over God’s promise and threat, and debated the Qadarites over divine will and human power.66 Here “divine will” means God’s will, while “human power” means a person’s ability to act by choice.

It is also reported that ʿAlī himself knew of a well-known Qadarite in the time of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb named ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ṣayfī, who argued about divine decree. ʿAlī is said to have reported how ʿUmar prevented ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ṣayfī from publicly arguing for his view.67

This would mean that the issue was already being raised in the time of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb.

There is even reason to think that it had been raised during the Prophet’s lifetime. We may recall what we discussed in Chapter Two of Part One:68 the Prophet was said to become extremely angry when he heard people arguing—that is, arguing about divine decree.69

We also have a report attributed to the Prophet:

“No people went astray after having been rightly guided except that they were given to argument.”70

Much of the argument referred to in this report, as well as in other reports mentioned in that earlier chapter, concerned questions such as the relationship between divine decree and human will and action.71

Muslim historians have also preserved examples of debates over this very question during the time of the Rightly Guided Caliphs. Here are two of them.

They report that a man came to ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib and asked:

“Commander of the Faithful, tell me about divine decree.”

ʿAlī replied: “It is a narrow path. Do not walk it.”

But the man did not stop. He said again: “Commander of the Faithful, tell me about divine decree.”

ʿAlī replied: “It is a deep sea. Do not enter it.”

The man was still not satisfied. Once again he asked: “Commander of the Faithful, tell me about divine decree.”

ʿAlī replied: “It is a hidden secret of God. Do not uncover it.”

The man again said: “Commander of the Faithful, tell me about divine decree.”

ʿAlī then asked him: “Did God create you as He wished, or as you wished?”

The man said: “As He wished.”

ʿAlī asked: “And on the Day of Resurrection, will God raise you as you wish or as He wishes?”

He replied: “As He wishes.”

ʿAlī then said: “Do you possess a will alongside God’s will, above His will, or below His will? If you say that your will exists alongside His, you claim to share His authority. If you say that it exists below His will, you claim that you can do without His will. And if you say that it is above His will, then your will would overpower His.”

Then ʿAlī asked: “Do you not ask God for well-being?”

The man replied: “Yes.”

ʿAlī asked: “From what do you ask Him to protect you? From an affliction He has placed upon you, or from an affliction placed upon you by someone else?”

The man answered: “From an affliction He has placed upon me.”

ʿAlī said: “Do you not say, ‘There is no power and no strength except through God, the Most High, the Almighty’?”

He said: “Yes.”

ʿAlī asked: “Do you know what that means?”

The man said: “No, Commander of the Faithful. Teach me from what God has taught you.”

ʿAlī replied: “It means that a servant has no power to obey God and no power to disobey Him except through God Almighty. Questioner, God makes people ill and He heals them. From Him comes the illness and from Him comes the cure. Understand this from God.”

The man replied: “I understand.”

ʿAlī said to him: “Then have you now become a Muslim? Stand up and take the hand of your Muslim brother.”

ʿAlī then said: “If I found a man from among the Qadarites, I would seize him by the neck and keep striking him until I broke it. They are the Jews of this community.”72

Another report, also attributed to ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, tells the story differently:

“When ʿAlī returned from Ṣiffīn, one of his followers stood up and asked him: ‘Tell us about our journey from Syria. Was it by divine decree and predestination?’

“ʿAlī replied: ‘By Him who split the seed and created life, we did not descend into a valley or climb a hill except by divine decree and predestination.’

“The man said: ‘Then I leave my hardship with God’—meaning that his effort had been wasted—‘and I have no reward for it.’

“ʿAlī replied: ‘On the contrary, old man. May God greatly reward you for your journey while you were travelling and for your rest while you were resting. In none of these situations were you forced or compelled.’

“The man said: ‘But how can that be, if divine decree and predestination drove us and our journey came from them?’

“ʿAlī replied: ‘Perhaps you think that divine decree means an unavoidable command and predestination an inescapable fate. If that were so, reward and punishment would become meaningless, God’s promise and threat would have no purpose, no sinner could be blamed and no good person praised. The person who did good would have no greater claim to reward than the person who did evil, and the person who did evil would have no greater claim to punishment than the person who did good.

“‘That is the teaching of devils, idol worshippers, enemies of the Merciful, false witnesses, and those blind to what is right. They are the Qadarites of this community and its Magians.

“‘God commanded while leaving people a choice, and He prohibited as a warning. He did not impose duties on people while compelling them, nor did He send the prophets in vain. That is what those who disbelieve imagine, and woe to those who disbelieve because of the Fire.’

“The man asked: ‘Then what are the divine decree and predestination that led us here?’

“ʿAlī replied: ‘God’s command and His will.’

“Then he recited: ‘Your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him, and that you show kindness to your parents.’”73

There is an obvious difference between ʿAlī’s answer in these two reports.

In the first, he seems to affirm absolute compulsion. In the second, he interprets divine decree and predestination in a way that rejects absolute compulsion and leaves room for human choice.

This difference gives us reason to doubt whether both reports really go back to ʿAlī himself.

But our main concern here is not to investigate the authenticity of the reports. What matters more is what they show us about the history of the question: people were already thinking about divine decree in the period of the Rightly Guided Caliphs. The uncertainty surrounding the problem troubled them, and they tried to overcome that uncertainty by asking questions, pressing for answers, and debating the issue.

Our doubts about whether these two reports can really be attributed to ʿAlī do not make us doubt that they arose out of the period of the Rightly Guided Caliphs. The style of the questions and answers, and the way the issue itself is expressed, seem to us to belong to that period.

Even so, the first report appears more likely than the second to preserve something genuinely connected to ʿAlī. The wording of the second almost seems to have been composed according to the later Qadarite interpretation of divine decree, after the period of the Rightly Guided Caliphs.

Those who created the report seem to have tried hard to make it fit not only the language of that earlier period but also its historical events. That is why the story is placed specifically in the context of the Battle of Ṣiffīn.

In any case, despite the obvious signs of later invention, the report still has historical value.

By this we mean that it supports what many other sources also show: debate over this question was common during the period of the Rightly Guided Caliphs, and people were eager to know what those caliphs thought about the effect of divine decree and predestination on their lives and on the consequences of their actions.

There is another piece of evidence that gives even stronger support to our account of the historical setting of the problem.

Aḥmad Amīn quotes Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā al-Murtaḍā, author of al-Munya wa-l-Amal fī Sharḥ Kitāb al-Milal wa-l-Niḥal, as saying that Muʿtazilism goes back to the earliest period of Islam.

Al-Murtaḍā places the four caliphs, ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbbās, ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd, and others in the first generation of Muʿtazilites. In the second generation he places al-Ḥasan, al-Ḥusayn, Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥanafiyya, Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib, and others. In the third he includes al-Ḥasan ibn al-Ḥasan, ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Ḥasan, and Abū Hāshim ʿAbd Allāh ibn Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥanafiyya, from whom Wāṣil is said to have learned. In the fourth he places Ghaylān al-Dimashqī, Wāṣil ibn ʿAṭāʾ, and others.

Aḥmad Amīn comments:

“What appears from his words is that he wants to count as a Muʿtazilite anyone among the Companions or Followers from whom a statement has been reported showing either that human beings possess freedom of will or that moral good and evil can be known by reason.

“For example, Ibn al-Murtaḍā argues that Abū Bakr and Ibn Masʿūd held the Muʿtazilite position because, in the case of a woman whose marriage contract left her dowry unspecified, they gave judgment according to their own reasoning. In other words, he takes this as evidence that they believed moral good and evil could be known rationally.

“He also argues that Ibn ʿAbbās held this position because he debated the Syrian supporters of compulsion and defeated their argument.

“Ibn al-Murtaḍā does not mean that Muʿtazilism, under that name and as a fully formed school, already existed in the time of Abū Bakr.”74

The conclusion we draw from all this historical evidence is the point we have been trying to establish: the problem of divine decree was already being argued over and discussed from the earliest period of Islam, before Maʿbad al-Juhanī, Ghaylān al-Dimashqī, and Wāṣil ibn ʿAṭāʾ.

Ordinary Muslims already felt a need to decide where they stood on the issue. They raised it with the Prophet during his lifetime, with the Rightly Guided Caliphs after him, and with the Companions.

The caliphs and Companions themselves did not all take the same position. We have seen this in the positions attributed to ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb and ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, and in the report about ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbbās, one of the greatest and most respected Companions, who is said by Ibn al-Murtaḍā to have “debated the Syrian supporters of compulsion and defeated their argument.” In other words, he defended human choice rather than compulsion.

All this means that the problem of divine decree already existed whether or not Maʿbad al-Juhanī and Ghaylān al-Dimashqī had ever appeared, and whether or not they had raised the banner of human freedom in action.

The conditions surrounding the problem were already capable of producing that position. They were also capable of producing the opposite position and of driving the two into conflict.

That conflict would naturally lead to the emergence of two opposing schools on the question, just as it eventually did with the rise of the Muʿtazila and their opposite, the Ashʿarites.

Our final point is this: the historical setting shows that the problem had an objective reality of its own, independent of Maʿbad al-Juhanī and Ghaylān al-Dimashqī, their personal wishes, or their individual thinking.

Their decision to openly reject predestination and defend human freedom in action was therefore a response to an existing historical reality.

Of course, this does not mean that we deny the part played by personal choice and individual commitment in what they did. Otherwise, how could we explain their willingness to endure different forms of persecution for publicly defending a view that deeply angered the ruling authorities, until both men were eventually killed in acts of violence and revenge?

2 — The Social and Political Roots of the Problem of Divine Decree

What we have said so far raises a further question:

  • What kind of conditions first produced Maʿbad al-Juhanī, and then Ghaylān al-Dimashqī, as open defenders of the view that human actions are not predetermined? What made them victims of that position? What then produced al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, who held the same view, and after him Wāṣil ibn ʿAṭāʾ, with whom this question and several others began to form the foundation of a rational school of Islamic doctrine? And what allowed that school—the Muʿtazila—to become a real turning point in the development of Arab thought toward philosophy?

To answer this question, we turn again to Eastern and Western researchers. What we find is that most of them see only one side of the conditions that produced this development. And when some of them do notice another side, they do not place it where it actually belongs in historical reality.

Earlier, we discussed De Boer’s view of the origins of philosophical thought around Islamic beliefs. We may recall his claim that there are “scattered indications that some of the earliest Muslims who defended free choice had Christian teachers…”

From this, he concludes that the earliest Muslim defenders of free choice had no real objective conditions within their own society that led them to discuss the idea of divine decree—or at least none worth considering. The explanation is reduced instead to the influence of Eastern Christians, who “almost all believed in free choice.”75

Other Western researchers deal with the question in much the same way.

Macdonald, for example, says that the problem of human freedom arises from a “philosophical necessity of the human mind.” That is his general explanation.

When he turns to the concrete historical case, however, he argues that the doctrine of free will in Syria under the Umayyads arose under the influence of Christian ideas, especially the writings of John of Damascus. Those writings, he says, show that compulsion and freedom of the will were among the most important points of disagreement between Islam and Christianity.76

Goldziher, meanwhile, quotes the researcher Kremer as saying that early Muslim scholars learned from Christian theologians in a way that caused them to question their previous belief in absolute eternal predestination.77

Goldziher himself appears to see the main source of the Qadarite movement in the efforts of pious Muslims under the Umayyads to reconcile Qurʾanic passages that seemed to conflict over the relationship between God’s will and human will.78

These examples from Western scholarship explain the rise of debate over divine decree among Arab thinkers through one factor or another, but always from only one side.

Either they explain it entirely through the influence of Christian theology or some other outside source; or they appeal to a broad and abstract principle such as Macdonald’s “philosophical necessity of the human mind”; or they explain it as an attempt to reconcile Qurʾanic passages that appeared to contradict one another.

What they do not ask is what social or political ground led early Muslims to make that attempt at reconciliation in the first place. Nor do they ask what led one group to defend predestination while another rejected it and defended human freedom of will and action.

Muslim historians themselves often explained the origins of the problem in the same way.

They too tended to trace it entirely to the influence of Christian theology.

In his Tahdhīb, for example, Ibn ʿAsākir does not limit this Christian influence to the Umayyad period. He takes it back as far as the time of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb.

He reports that while giving a sermon at al-Jābiya, ʿUmar said that God “guides whom He wills and leads astray whom He wills.”

A Christian Catholicos was present—a Catholicos being a Christian ecclesiastical title that entered Arabic usage—and he muttered something in his own language.

ʿUmar asked what he had said and was told that the Catholicos was saying: “God does not lead anyone astray.”79

Ibn ʿAsākir appears to have seen this report as an example of an indirect debate between “official” Islamic thought, which attributed human action to God, and Christian theology, which defended human choice and denied that God Himself causes people to go astray.

From this point of view, exchanges of this kind would have been what first stirred discussion of divine decree among Muslims.

We find the same idea in other Muslim historians who say that Maʿbad al-Juhanī was the first person to teach the doctrine of free will.

According to them, he took the idea from—or was influenced by—a Christian named Sinsawayh, who had converted to Islam and then returned to Christianity, as Ibn Saʿd reports in his Ṭabaqāt.80

According to these historians, this Christian influence then passed from Maʿbad to al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī in Iraq,81 and to Ghaylān al-Dimashqī in Syria.

If we take all these views together, we are left with the conclusion that the problem which, as these same researchers rightly say, had already begun stirring Arab thought in the time of the Prophet and later emerged in an especially sharp form under the Umayyad caliph Hishām ibn ʿAbd al-Malik, whose reign began in 106 AH/724 CE, is explained from a single source.

That source is either abstract rational reflection, driven by what Macdonald calls the “philosophical necessity of the human mind”; or what Aḥmad Amīn means when he says that this question “occupied philosophers and religious thinkers in every age”;82 or else the influence of Christian theological thought.

But limiting the question to this framework alone goes against historical reality. It also goes against the dialectical relationship between intellectual developments and social developments. That relationship exists objectively, whether researchers notice it or not.

What is striking is that some of these same researchers, in their own studies of the problem of human freedom and divine decree, actually give us excellent material for seeing this relationship. But they present it only as historical information. They do not use it as the basis for a scientific analysis that would trace the problem back to its real roots in the society where it took its particular forms.

Take Goldziher, for example. As we saw earlier, he explains the rise of the Qadarite movement as an attempt to reconcile apparently conflicting passages in the Qurʾān. He stops there, without asking what forces lay behind this attempt. Yet elsewhere in the very same book,83 when he discusses the rise of the Murjiʾa, he uses a very different kind of explanation.

Goldziher explains the Murjiʾa doctrine, and what he sees as its tolerance toward the Umayyads, by the political need for such a doctrine at that particular time. In the eyes of much of the Muslim community, he says, the Umayyads had seized power illegitimately. A doctrine was therefore needed which taught that judgment on a Muslim’s faith should be postponed and left to God. This would prevent Muslims from quickly declaring the Umayyads unbelievers and would postpone that judgment until God Himself decided it. Otherwise, such an immediate judgment by Muslims might encourage them to rise against their rulers.

Here Goldziher gives a sound explanation. He connects the Murjiʾa doctrine directly to the political circumstances in which it appeared.

But when he turns to the Qadarites, his treatment splits in two.

On the one hand, he explains their origin simply as an attempt to reconcile passages in the Qurʾān. On the other hand, when he discusses the attitude of the Umayyad rulers toward the Qadarites, he says that the Umayyads hated those who defended human free choice. Their hostility, he adds, did not come from any dislike of theological debate as such. It came from their belief that the disappearance of the doctrine of divine compulsion would threaten their rule.84

Yet Goldziher makes this observation separately from his discussion of how the Qadarite movement arose. He never makes it part of that explanation.

This last point gives us excellent material for seeing the social and political ground from which the Qadarite movement grew. But Goldziher does not use it when he explains the movement’s origins, even though he does exactly that when explaining the rise of the Murjiʾa.

Even more surprising is the response of a modern Arab scholar known for the depth and range of his analysis. He quotes Goldziher’s remarks about the attitude of the Umayyad rulers toward the Qadarite movement and then comments:

“There is no doubt that the Umayyad state benefited from the ideas of the determinists, who saw the Umayyad caliphate, and the oppression produced by it, as a divine decree that human beings had no power to resist or rebel against. But the connection between the theoretical principle of free will and its practical consequences was not something the Umayyad caliphs understood in the way Goldziher imagined. The sacrifice of Maʿbad or Ghaylān was not caused by fear that their rule might collapse. It was simply a campaign against a new religious innovation, carried out in the name of the religion whose guardians they had made themselves.”85

The Theoretical Principle and the Practical Position

There are several problems with this comment.

First, it accepts the basic point that the Umayyad state benefited from the views of the determinists, and it gives a realistic explanation for why.

If that is so, then the views of those who defended human choice—the Qadarites—must have meant more than simple opposition to the injustice of the Umayyad state. Those views also posed a serious danger to its power.

If the Qadarite idea spread among the people, it opened a door of hope for those suffering under oppression. They would come to understand that this oppression was not a divine decree that they had no choice but to accept. Its removal could depend on their own will and choice, if they rose to resist it and put an end to it.

It is hard to believe that the Umayyad rulers could not see this danger. They were known for their political skill and for the care with which they protected their rule, especially at a time when opposition movements were becoming stronger and developing new intellectual weapons that could spread quickly.

Even some early Muslim writers support this view. Qāḍī ʿAbd al-Jabbār, for example, says that “the first person to openly preach compulsion was Muʿāwiya.” He adds that Muʿāwiya claimed that whatever he did happened by God’s decree and was created by God. In this way, he could use divine decree as an excuse for his actions, make people think he was right, and suggest that God Himself had appointed him as ruler and entrusted authority to him. ʿAbd al-Jabbār says that this idea later became widespread among the Umayyad kings.86

Second, even if we accepted for the sake of argument that the Umayyad caliphs did not understand the connection between the theoretical principle and its practical consequences in the way Goldziher did—and that would hardly fit their reputation for political cunning—there is another point that requires no extraordinary insight into the connection between theory and practice.

The same researcher mentions it himself when he adds:

“But alongside their theoretical belief in free choice, the Qadarites also expressed opposition to the state.”

He gives the example of Khālid ibn Maʿdān, one of Maʿbad’s students, who said as his teacher was being taken away to be killed:

“The greatest calamity is when the rulers come from among them,”

meaning the Umayyads.87

Despite the depth we usually find in this researcher’s work, there is an attempt here to separate the Qadarites’ theoretical doctrine from their opposition to the state. It is almost as if he is saying that the Umayyads killed Maʿbad not because of Qadarite doctrine, but because he opposed the government.

Such a separation does not fit a sound method of research.

Dr ʿAbbās tries to support this distinction by referring to Khālid ibn Maʿdān’s remark about the Umayyads when he saw Maʿbad being taken to his death. He argues that Khālid did not say this because he was a Qadarite. Many people who believed in divine compulsion said similar things.

But first, this explanation concerns Khālid ibn Maʿdān alone. Does it mean that the Umayyads killed Maʿbad because he was a Qadarite?

Second, what exactly does the argument prove?

Does it mean that opposition to Umayyad rule was not limited to the Qadarites and that many determinists also opposed the Umayyads?

That is true.

The opponents of the Umayyads belonged to many different political parties and religious schools. Each had its own intellectual weapons for fighting Umayyad rule. The Qadarite doctrine was not the only intellectual weapon used against them.

The determinists themselves were not one single group. Al-Shahrastānī lists three main kinds: the pure Jabriyya, the moderate Jabriyya, and those who allowed created human power some degree of influence over human action. He also divides the Najjāriyya, one branch among them, into three groups.

Another branch, the followers of Ḍirār ibn ʿAmr, held a particularly interesting position on political leadership. One of their principles stated:

“The imamate may belong to someone who is not from Quraysh. If a Qurashī and a Nabataean are both available, we should choose the Nabataean, because he has fewer supporters and weaker backing, and we can remove him more easily if he violates the religious law.”

The Muʿtazila also allowed the imam to come from outside Quraysh, but they did not go so far as to say that the Nabataean should be preferred over the Qurashī.88

So there were determinists whose ideas posed an even greater danger to Umayyad rule than those of the Muʿtazila, even though the Muʿtazila adopted the Qadarite idea of human freedom.

The claim that the imam did not have to come from Quraysh—the Umayyads themselves being Qurashī—and that even a Nabataean could be preferred over a Qurashī posed a direct threat to the Umayyad caliphate. It is no exaggeration to say that this threat was even greater than the one posed by Qadarite doctrine.

So saying that many determinists spoke about the Umayyads in the same way as Khālid ibn Maʿdān does not prove what Dr ʿAbbās wants it to prove. Not every determinist held ideas that suited Umayyad policy.

Even if we assumed that all the determinists thought alike, we could still say, first, that although their ideas might have suited Umayyad policy, the Jabriyya were not an Umayyad party and were not a political alliance supporting the Umayyad family.

They were an independent group with their own religious, intellectual and political positions. Those positions did not simply reproduce the positions of the Umayyad state.

Otherwise, how could we explain the killing of Jahm ibn Ṣafwān, the leading figure of the “pure Jabriyya”?

The Umayyads certainly did not kill Jahm because he believed in compulsion. They themselves supported that doctrine and protected it. They killed him because he joined those who rebelled against Umayyad rule.89

Nothing in Jahm’s belief in compulsion required him to obey the Umayyads or prevented him from rising against them.

That is one point.

There is another. Despite his belief in compulsion, Jahm had a strongly rational tendency in his thinking, as we will see at the end of this chapter.90 The Umayyads were hostile to people with this kind of rational approach.

That is the first answer.

Second, does the fact that many determinists shared Khālid ibn Maʿdān’s hostility toward the Umayyads prove that Qadarite doctrine was not an intellectual expression of the interests of a social group, and therefore did not pose a danger to Umayyad rule?

Third, does it provide convincing evidence that the Umayyad rulers did not kill Maʿbad because he was a Qadarite, but only because he joined Ibn al-Ashʿath’s rebellion?

Before accepting that, would we not first need to know why Maʿbad opposed the Umayyads and why he joined Ibn al-Ashʿath against them?

One further claim remains to be discussed: that the Umayyads killed Maʿbad and Ghaylān not because they feared for their rule, but because they were suppressing a new religious innovation in the name of the religion whose guardians they claimed to be.

There are several problems with this argument.

First, the Umayyad caliphs—with the exception of ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz—committed many serious and well-known religious violations and introduced innovations of their own. The fact that they presented themselves as guardians of religion did not stop them, nor did any wish to respect the religious feelings of ordinary Muslims.

Second, the doctrine of compulsion itself was, like Qadarite doctrine, regarded by Muslims as a “new innovation.”

Most of the leading figures of the major schools of law and theology rejected it, from Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq and Abū Ḥanīfa to Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal.

Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq and Abū Ḥanīfa both rejected the extremes of Qadarite free choice and Jabriyya compulsion with the well-known formula:

“No compulsion, no complete delegation, and no absolute empowerment,”

followed by the rest of the familiar report attributed to Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq.

Then we come to the fourth great imam of Sunni Islam, Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal (d. 241 AH / 855 CE). He wrote an entire work entitled Refutation of the Heretics and the Jahmites concerning the Ambiguous Verses of the Qurʾān Which They Questioned and Interpreted Incorrectly.91

Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal places the Jahmites alongside the heretics and refutes them together. In his eyes, therefore, they too were followers of religious innovation.

So the doctrine of compulsion was regarded by most of the leading figures of the Islamic schools as a “new innovation,” just as Qadarite doctrine was.

Why, then, did the Umayyad caliphs persecute one innovation but not the other?

Why distinguish between one “innovation” and another if their real concern was simply to defend the religion whose guardians they claimed to be?

A much better answer comes from one of the leading Muslim scholars of our own time. No one could reasonably doubt that he is a major conservative Islamic scholar, and he is certainly not someone who approaches Islamic history with our particular concern for connecting theoretical principles with practical circumstances.

Writing about the Muʿtazilite hatred of the Umayyad state, he says:

“Perhaps the Muʿtazila inherited their hatred of the Umayyads from these teachers of theirs”—meaning Maʿbad al-Juhanī and Ghaylān al-Dimashqī among the Qadarites, and Jahm ibn Ṣafwān among the determinists. “The Umayyads, it seems, disliked the doctrine of free will not only for religious reasons but for political reasons as well, because compulsion served their policy. The result of the doctrine of compulsion was that God, who causes all things, had imposed the Umayyads on the people just as He imposed everything else. Their state existed by God’s decree and destiny, and people therefore had to submit to that decree and destiny. Jahm, although a determinist, joined those who rebelled against the Umayyads. He also held views which caused ordinary people to resent him, so Umayyad policy took advantage of the people’s hatred and killed him.”92

As for Jahm and the views that made people resent him, we believe that this question goes beyond the problem of compulsion and leads us to the rational tendency for which Jahm was known.

Third, it is difficult for anyone studying the Umayyad period to accept the claim that the Umayyad caliphs did not fear that Qadarite doctrine might threaten their rule.

When Qadarite doctrine appeared in connection with Maʿbad al-Juhanī, the Umayyad state was going through an intense crisis. Political, social, class and religious tensions between rulers and ruled had all become severe.

Ideas directed against the rulers therefore found a wide and powerful response among the populations living under Umayyad rule, whatever the precise religious form of those ideas might be.

Any idea that directly, or even indirectly, challenged some part of Umayyad rule could spread quickly among the people. It could attract preachers, supporters and even people willing to fight for it.

That is exactly what happened when Qadarite doctrine took its later form through Maʿbad al-Juhanī.

Historical sources tell us that Maʿbad went to the Hijaz carrying his Qadarite message to a region whose people were generally more conservative in religious matters than the people of Iraq.

There he met the scholars of Medina and explained his doctrine to them. The scholars of Medina were known for being among the strictest Muslim scholars on questions of religion and belief.

What response did Maʿbad find among them?

One of the great historians of Islamic beliefs gives us the answer. He was himself a major Sunni scholar and an opponent of Qadarite doctrine, yet he openly admits how widely the doctrine had spread at that time.

Speaking specifically about the Qadarites, he says:

“…and among those who escaped these false doctrines, there remained only a small group from among the most distinguished scholars and the righteous early generations whom God protected from deviation and error…”93

He says this because the historical record tells us that Maʿbad influenced the scholars of Medina, who adopted his doctrine, just as he influenced many people in Iraq, a region strongly hostile to the Umayyads.

This historical reality shows very clearly that the Qadarite idea could appeal even to conservative religious scholars who held great influence over public opinion.

So we have to ask: what was it about Qadarite doctrine that attracted these scholars and so many other people?

Was it simply the “philosophical necessity of the human mind”?

Was it simply an attempt to reconcile passages in the Qurʾān?

Or was it simply the result of Christian theological influence transmitted through the man said to have been called Sansawayh, or Sawsan as Ibn Qutayba calls him in al-Maʿārif, and who is also mentioned in Mīzān al-Iʿtidāl? He was said to have been a Christian, then to have converted to Islam, then returned to Christianity, and to have influenced Maʿbad al-Juhanī.

If “philosophical necessity” alone explains the doctrine, why did this necessity appear at this particular moment rather than before or after it?

Why did this particular side of the attempt to reconcile Qurʾānic passages—the side supporting human freedom—appeal to so many people in Iraq and the Hijaz, and later in Damascus?

By contrast, the doctrine of compulsion first appeared through Jahm ibn Ṣafwān in Tirmidh, in the region of Marw in Persia, and through al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Najjār in Rayy, also in Persia.94

Why, then, did Qadarite doctrine flourish in Arab regions closely connected, directly or indirectly, to the political struggle between the Umayyad party and the various political forces opposed to it, while the doctrine of compulsion first grew in a different, Persian environment?

And how could the limited personal influence of one individual—Maʿbad al-Juhanī’s supposed influence from Sansawayh—turn into a broad intellectual movement that rapidly spread among people from many social groups outside the ruling class, including religious scholars in a conservative region such as the Hijaz?

If that personal influence really occurred, how could it grow into such a wide and powerful intellectual phenomenon unless another factor—social or political—helped produce that transformation?

Five Pieces of Historical Evidence

Early historians and later researchers give us historical material that can shed a great deal of light on all these questions.

This material allows us to reach a more realistic understanding of the problem than the one usually found in the studies available to us.

We call these “historical materials” because the historians and researchers who recorded them generally treated them simply as pieces of information. They did not use them to build a broader interpretation beyond the historical narrative itself.

We will now present five of these pieces of evidence, one by one and without comment. After that, we will draw the conclusions that we believe follow from them.

1. Historians tell us that Maʿbad al-Juhanī and ʿAṭāʾ ibn Yasār came to al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and said:

“Abū Saʿīd, these kings shed Muslim blood and take Muslim wealth, and then they say, ‘Our actions happen only by the decree of God Most High.’”

Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī replied:

“The enemies of God are lying.”95

He meant the Umayyads.

2. Ibn Saʿd96 reports from Ayyūb al-Sakhtiyānī, a Basran who strongly opposed the Qadarites, that he argued with al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī more than once about the question of divine decree.

Al-Ḥasan did not change his position until Ayyūb threatened him with the Umayyads. Only then did al-Ḥasan stop speaking in this way.

Maʿbad al-Juhanī, as is well known, was a student of al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī.97

3. Al-Shahrastānī says:98

“…I saw a letter attributed to al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī which he wrote to ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān after the caliph asked him about free choice and compulsion. In it, he gave an answer consistent with Qadarite doctrine, supporting it with verses from the Qurʾān and arguments from reason. Perhaps the letter was really written by Wāṣil ibn ʿAṭāʾ, since al-Ḥasan was not someone who would disagree with the early authorities on the principle that divine decree, both good and bad, comes from God Most High. These words were almost universally accepted among them.”

4. Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā al-Murtaḍā99 gives us a fascinating account of Ghaylān al-Dimashqī.

After Maʿbad, Ghaylān was the second major early figure to develop Qadarite thought into a more complete doctrine and theory.

According to Ibn al-Murtaḍā, Ghaylān wrote to the Umayyad caliph ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, calling on him to accept Qadarite doctrine. In the letter, he described the condition of Islam and the Muslims under Umayyad rule and the damage that had been done, to the point that:

“The learned man is frightened into silence, while the ignorant man is not allowed to ask.”

The account suggests that ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz was not convinced by Ghaylān’s doctrine. Even so, he summoned him because he trusted his integrity and the sincerity of his religion.

When Ghaylān arrived, the caliph asked him to help reform the affairs of the Muslims.

Ghaylān agreed, on the condition that he be allowed to sell the treasures accumulated by the Umayyads and return people’s rights to their rightful owners. The caliph accepted.

When Ghaylān took charge of the sale, he called out to the people of Damascus:

“Come to the possessions of the traitors!”

meaning the Umayyad rulers who had come before ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz.

“Come to the possessions of the oppressors! Come to the possessions of those who succeeded the Messenger among his community but did not follow his way or conduct!”

As he sold the Umayyad possessions, he said to the crowd around him:

“What can I say to those who claim that these men were rightly guided leaders, when this is what they owned while people were dying of hunger?”

Ghaylān meant that the Umayyad rulers had enjoyed enormously valuable possessions while ordinary people were starving.

According to the account, Hishām ibn ʿAbd al-Malik passed by while Ghaylān was speaking in this way.

Hishām said:

“This man is insulting me and my fathers. By God, if I ever get hold of him, I will cut off his hands and feet.”

Later, when Hishām became the Umayyad caliph, Ghaylān fled to Armenia. From there he continued spreading reports of Hishām’s faults and of the injustice committed by Hishām and the Umayyads.

The Umayyads, he argued, claimed that they ruled by God’s decree and destiny and that no one could escape that decree.

Hishām ordered Ghaylān and his companion Ṣāliḥ to be brought before him. After keeping them imprisoned for several days, he ordered their hands and feet to be cut off.

Ṣāliḥ died before Ghaylān.

Ghaylān then turned to the people and said:

“May God destroy them”—meaning the Umayyads—“How many rights they have put to death! How much falsehood they have brought to life! How many people despised in God’s religion they have raised up, and how many people honored in God’s religion they have humiliated!”

The Umayyads who heard him became angry and went to Hishām.

They said:

“You cut off Ghaylān’s hands and feet, but you left his tongue free. He has made the people weep and awakened them to things they had not noticed before. Send someone to cut out his tongue.”

Hishām did so.

Ghaylān died as a martyr to his defense of the rights of the oppressed and to his belief in human freedom.

5. Historical works mention a third important figure who raised the banner of Qadarite doctrine and died for it: ʿAmr al-Maqṣūṣ.

According to the historical account, he was the first person to preach Qadarite doctrine openly in Damascus, before Ghaylān al-Dimashqī.

He was also the teacher of Muʿāwiya II—Muʿāwiya ibn Yazīd ibn Muʿāwiya I, the founder of the Umayyad dynasty.

ʿAmr influenced his student so strongly that Muʿāwiya II became a Qadarite like his teacher.

When his father Yazīd died and the Umayyads wanted to pledge allegiance to Muʿāwiya as his successor, following the hereditary system created by his grandfather Muʿāwiya I, the young man consulted his teacher ʿAmr.

ʿAmr advised him:

“Either rule justly, or step down.”

Muʿāwiya II then considered his position.

How could he choose? And if he remained caliph, how could he rule justly?

He concluded that he would not be able to achieve the justice his teacher required of him.

So he decided to step down from the caliphate.

He announced his decision in a speech to the people of Damascus:

“We have been tested through you, and you have been tested through us. My grandfather Muʿāwiya fought over authority with someone who had a greater right and stronger claim to it”—meaning ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib—“and he took upon himself what you know. He has now gone to meet the consequences of what he did.

“Then my father Yazīd inherited it, though he was not worthy of it. He followed his own desires and thought his errors were right.

“I do not wish to meet God carrying responsibility for you. So your affair is now yours. Give it to whomever you wish.

“By God, if the caliphate is a prize, our family has already received its share. And if it is an evil, then the family of Abū Sufyān has already had enough of it.”

Historians say that after giving this speech and giving up the caliphate, Muʿāwiya II withdrew from public life.

He died forty days later.

The Umayyads then seized ʿAmr al-Maqṣūṣ and told him:

“You corrupted him. You taught him this.”

They buried ʿAmr alive.

He died for his Qadarite doctrine, which stood against an Umayyad system that claimed to rule in the name of divine right—that is, in the name of God’s decree and destiny, or the doctrine of compulsion, as the Umayyads presented it.100

What We Can Learn from These Five Pieces of Evidence

These are five examples of the “historical materials” given to us by early historians and later researchers.

Yet they usually pass over them without trying to use them to uncover the social and political roots of the problem of human freedom and divine decree.

Maʿbad al-Juhanī and al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī raised the question in Iraq. Ghaylān al-Dimashqī and ʿAmr al-Maqṣūṣ raised it in Damascus. From there, the question helped set Arab thought as a whole moving further along the road toward philosophical thinking.

Now that we have presented these examples in their bare historical form, we can ask what objective connection existed between them and the social and political conditions that gave them their historical meaning.

We will examine them in the same order.

— 1 —

Was it simply a coincidence that Maʿbad al-Juhanī and his companion ʿAṭāʾ ibn Yasār came to al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and said:

“Abū Saʿīd, these kings shed Muslim blood and take Muslim wealth, and then they say, ‘Our actions happen only by the decree of God Most High’”?

Of course not.

There was nothing accidental about it.

Maʿbad al-Juhanī and ʿAṭāʾ ibn Yasār came to al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī complaining about and protesting against “these kings.”

Who were “these kings”?

They were the rulers of the Muslims themselves: the Umayyad rulers. At that time, Muslims had no other kings.

What were Maʿbad and ʿAṭāʾ protesting against?

What exactly were they complaining about?

The historical evidence is perfectly clear. It answers the question without any need for interpretation.

“These kings shed Muslim blood and take Muslim wealth.”

And they did not stop there.

They justified these acts of oppression by saying that they “happen by God’s decree.”

In other words, they shed blood and seized property, then attributed their actions to God—to God’s decree and destiny, to a divine compulsion imposed on Muslims from which there was no escape.

Here we can clearly see that the question of divine decree had acquired a direct political and social meaning.

There is no ambiguity about it.

This meaning shows, first, how useful the doctrine of compulsion was to Umayyad power.

It helped support the existence of the regime itself.

At the same time, it closed the door on any hope among Muslims that they might free themselves from Umayyad oppression.

If Umayyad rule came through an irresistible divine decree, then human beings had no power to resist God’s authority or free themselves from God’s decree.

They had no real choice over their actions.

Muslims therefore had to submit to Umayyad rule because, in doing so, they were supposedly submitting to God’s decree.

That was the political equation behind Umayyad reasoning.

But the same political and social meaning also tells us something about the Qadarite movement itself.

When Qadarite doctrine appeared as a developed theory through Maʿbad al-Juhanī, its call for human freedom became closely tied to opposition to Umayyad rule for two connected reasons.

First, the Umayyads shed Muslim blood and seized Muslim wealth.

Second, they claimed that this injustice had been imposed on people by God.

It would be more accurate to go even further.

The Qadarite call for freedom of human will and action carried, in its very meaning, a call for the oppressed to use that freedom of will and action to free themselves from the oppression of “these kings.”

The Qadarite doctrine therefore opened the door to hope.

Liberation was possible because human beings were not completely compelled by divine decree.

— 2 —

What do we learn from Ayyūb al-Sakhtiyānī’s debate with al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī over the question of human freedom?

Ayyūb was unable to persuade al-Ḥasan through argument, so in the end he threatened him with the Umayyads if he did not give up his Qadarite position.

Of course, Ayyūb had every right to debate al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, or anyone else, over a doctrine with which he disagreed.

What goes beyond that right is replacing intellectual argument with a threat involving Umayyad power.

And this brings us directly to the heart of the matter.

Why threaten him specifically with the Umayyads?

The answer is clear.

The historical account itself gives it to us through both its wording and its meaning.

It is almost as if the report were saying directly that the Umayyads were watching for anyone who accepted Qadarite doctrine.

They were even prepared to punish people simply for believing it.

We can see this because Ayyūb did not merely ask al-Ḥasan to stop publicly preaching the doctrine.

He argued with him over the belief itself.

He wanted al-Ḥasan to abandon that belief completely.

When he could not persuade him through argument, he threatened him with the Umayyad authorities. According to the same historical account, al-Ḥasan then did in fact stop.

This shows that the Umayyads fought Qadarite doctrine relentlessly.

They fought it through intellectual argument, using people such as Ayyūb al-Sakhtiyānī and other supporters of compulsion.

They fought it through intimidation and terror.

And finally, they fought it by killing people such as Maʿbad al-Juhanī, ʿAmr al-Maqṣūṣ, Ghaylān al-Dimashqī and others.

As for why the Umayyads fought Qadarite doctrine, we have already explained this clearly, and we will return to it again elsewhere.

— 3 —

We now need to draw some conclusions from the letter that al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī wrote to ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān after the caliph asked him about human freedom and divine compulsion.

We also need to consider al-Shahrastānī’s claim that the letter was not really written by al-Ḥasan but by Wāṣil ibn ʿAṭāʾ.

The fact that ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān, while caliph, specifically asked al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī for his opinion on free choice and compulsion deserves serious attention.

We see it as an attempt by the Umayyad ruler to obtain an authoritative Islamic opinion from a major religious scholar whose views carried great weight among the educated people and intellectuals of Basra.

It seems to us that ʿAbd al-Malik hoped this opinion would condemn the Qadarites.

He could then use it as a religious weapon to defend the doctrine of divine decree and compulsion—in other words, to defend the ideology of Umayyad rule itself.

At the same time, he could use religion as a weapon against the Qadarite movement.

But how could ʿAbd al-Malik expect such a ruling from al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī himself, who was widely known at the time as one of the leading teachers of Qadarite thought in Basra?

We believe there are two reasons.

First, ʿAbd al-Malik would probably not have asked al-Ḥasan about such a sensitive issue unless he expected an answer that suited him.

Second, al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī was known to fear the power of the state.

Although he was then one of the leading teachers and advocates of Qadarite doctrine—perhaps its most important theoretical teacher—it was quite possible that fear of political authority would prevent him from stating his position openly.

Historical sources describe several situations that suggest this.

We have already mentioned the story told by Ayyūb al-Sakhtiyānī. He said that he argued with al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī about Qadarite doctrine several times but could not change his opinion until he frightened him with the threat of political authority. Al-Ḥasan then promised to abandon the view.101

It appears that he did finally move away from it toward the end of his life.

There are other signs of his fear of the authorities.

Historians tell us that when Ibn al-Ashʿath rose against the Umayyads, al-Ḥasan urged people not to support him, even though al-Ḥasan himself strongly opposed Umayyad rule.

He took a similar position when Ibn al-Muhallab rebelled against the Umayyads in Basra. Again, al-Ḥasan called on people not to support the revolt.

It is difficult to explain these two positions except through his desire to protect himself from the punishment of the authorities.

Some have tried to use them as proof that al-Ḥasan was not really a Qadarite.

But this goes against the historical evidence.

Most of the reports describing his Qadarite views come from his own students, including Qatāda ibn Diʿāma al-Sadūsī, ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd and Ayyūb al-Sakhtiyānī.

Al-Dhahabī102 also reports that al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī said that both good and evil occur within divine decree. In other words, neither good nor evil should be attributed to God in a completely unrestricted way.

Al-Sayyid al-Murtaḍā reports from Abū al-Jaʿd that he heard al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī say:

“Whoever claims that acts of disobedience come from God will come on the Day of Resurrection with a blackened face.”

And Dāwūd ibn Abī Hind reports hearing al-Ḥasan say:

“Everything is by decree and destiny except acts of disobedience.”103

This last sentence appears word for word in the letter attributed to al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and addressed to ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān.

That supports the conclusion that the letter really was written by al-Ḥasan, not by Wāṣil ibn ʿAṭāʾ as al-Shahrastānī suggests.

Al-Shahrastānī gives no evidence for rejecting al-Ḥasan’s authorship except his own belief that al-Ḥasan would never have disagreed with the early Muslim authorities, who, as al-Shahrastānī puts it, held that divine decree, “both its good and its evil,” comes from God.

The claim that Wāṣil ibn ʿAṭāʾ wrote the letter is even stranger, because a simple historical calculation makes it impossible.

Wāṣil was born in 80 AH and died in 131 AH.

ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān became caliph in 65 AH—fifteen years before Wāṣil was born.

ʿAbd al-Malik ruled for twenty years.

This means that Wāṣil was only about five years old when ʿAbd al-Malik died in 85 AH.

How could he possibly have written a letter to him?

There can be little doubt, then, that al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī held Qadarite views during an important and productive period of his intellectual and teaching career.

Nor do we doubt that he wrote the letter to ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān.

The only serious objection comes from al-Shahrastānī, and he offers no convincing evidence for it. The historical evidence, as we have seen, actually destroys his suggestion that Wāṣil was the author.

Dr Iḥsān ʿAbbās was therefore right to say that there is more reason to attribute Qadarite views to al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī than to deny them completely.

The reports come from his own students, some of whom disliked the Qadarites and their doctrine. If they had been able to clear al-Ḥasan of the accusation, they would have done so. And if they had known of any reason for caution in attributing those views to him, they would have mentioned it.104

That leaves one likely explanation for al-Ḥasan’s more hesitant positions, including his possible abandonment of Qadarite views late in life: his fear of persecution by the ruling authorities.

There is considerable evidence for this fear, some of which we have already mentioned.

If our discussion were not already so long, we could give more examples.

For now, one story reported by Ibn ʿAsākir will be enough.105

He says that al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī once fled from al-Ḥajjāj’s soldiers and took refuge with Ḥabīb al-ʿAjamī, a Sufi and one of al-Ḥasan’s students.

Trembling with fear, al-Ḥasan said:

“Abū Muḥammad, protect me from the police! They are right behind me!”

Ḥabīb replied:

“Abū Saʿīd, I am ashamed for you. Do you not trust your Lord enough to pray to Him and ask Him to hide you from them?”

Some details in this story may be doubtful.

But the fact that the story was widely repeated tells us two things.

First, it adds to the other evidence showing how strongly al-Ḥasan feared the ruling authorities.

Second, it suggests that the Umayyad authorities were not satisfied simply because al-Ḥasan had warned people against supporting Ibn al-Ashʿath.

That was not enough while he continued to hold his position on human freedom.

The spread of Qadarite doctrine in Umayyad society posed a greater danger to the regime than al-Ḥasan’s personal support for the revolt of Ibn al-Ashʿath would have done.

Al-Ḥasan was a man whose words carried enormous influence among the people.

When his opinion on human freedom became known, it could spread more widely among the public and have a deeper effect in encouraging the oppressed to rebel.

There is one more point to consider about al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī’s letter to ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān.

As we have argued, ʿAbd al-Malik knew about al-Ḥasan’s fear of political authority.

That is why, we believe, he asked him for his opinion on free choice and compulsion. He expected al-Ḥasan to be too frightened to state his true position openly.

Perhaps, he thought, al-Ḥasan would give an obscure or ambiguous answer that could then be used as a weapon against the Qadarites.

But this time al-Ḥasan did not completely give way to fear.

His reply to ʿAbd al-Malik contains language which, in our view, did more than simply state the theoretical position of the Qadarites.

It also contained an indirect criticism of the Umayyad caliph.

This is the third point we wanted to make.

When al-Ḥasan wrote:

“Everything is by God’s decree and destiny except acts of disobedience,”

he was not simply stating an abstract theory.

We can also hear in these words an allusion to the sins committed by the Umayyad rulers.

And by “acts of disobedience,” we should not understand only their personal violations of religious or moral rules.

The term also includes social injustice, the shedding of Muslim blood and the seizure of Muslim wealth.

This is exactly what Maʿbad al-Juhanī and ʿAṭāʾ ibn Yasār had in mind when they came to al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and said:

“Abū Saʿīd, these kings shed Muslim blood and take Muslim wealth, and then they say, ‘Our actions happen only by the decree of God Most High.’”

— 4 —

Let us now return to Ibn al-Murtaḍā’s account of Ghaylān al-Dimashqī.

We saw Ghaylān call on the righteous Umayyad caliph ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz to accept Qadarite doctrine.

We then saw the caliph summon Ghaylān and ask for his help in repairing the damage done by earlier Umayyad rulers, even though he himself disagreed with Ghaylān over the question of human freedom.

We also saw Ghaylān take charge of selling the treasures of the Umayyad rulers.

As he did so, he raised slogans with a clear social and class meaning.

Indeed, we can say that their content was directly concerned with class inequality.

While selling the Umayyad possessions in Damascus, he called out:

“Come to the possessions of the traitors! Come to the possessions of the oppressors!”

And again:

“What can I say to those who claim that these men were rightly guided leaders, when this is what they owned while people were dying of hunger?”

What can we conclude from this account?

The answer seems natural and logical.

We cannot separate the “theoretical principle” from the “practical position.”

Anyone following the logic of the evidence must see the real and direct connection between Ghaylān’s Qadarite doctrine and his position toward the Umayyads—between his ideas and his political conduct.

There is no split in Ghaylān’s personality here.

A split would exist only if his theory contradicted his actions, or if his principles contradicted his conduct.

But once we reject that contradiction, we can see that the two sides fit together completely.

They are two sides of the same thing: one theoretical and one practical, one expressed as principle and one expressed through action.

The same was true of Maʿbad al-Juhanī.

And it was also true of ʿAmr al-Maqṣūṣ.

All this leads us to a necessary conclusion.

Qadarite doctrine took the particular theoretical form in which it appeared through the school of al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī in Basra, then in Damascus, and then in Medina in the Hijaz, because it gave religious expression to an ideology growing on the opposite side of the struggle from the ideology of Umayyad rule: the doctrine of compulsion.

This conclusion does not mean that Qadarite doctrine had no connection with what has been called the philosophical needs of the human mind.

Nor does it deny the importance of attempts to reconcile Qurʾānic passages.

Nor does it deny the influence on Arab-Islamic thought of Christian theology, Persian religious thought or ancient Indian thought.

Our point is simply that none of these factors was the fundamental cause of the rise of Qadarite doctrine.

Different Western and Eastern scholars have taken one or more of these factors and treated them as the original source of Qadarite thought.

We believe they were not the original source, although they certainly helped shape some of the ideas that later entered Qadarite doctrine when it became one of the foundations of Muʿtazilite thought.

Take, for example, the “philosophical necessity of the human mind” discussed by Macdonald, which he treats as the source of Qadarite doctrine.

In reality, this philosophical form was the higher stage to which Qadarite theory later developed.

Before reaching that stage, it had remained closely connected for a long time to the realities of social and political struggle, from the killing of the third caliph, ʿUthmān, through the rise of Umayyad rule.

The Umayyads gradually established a system that was almost a hereditary monarchy, with increasingly clear foundations that revealed the real character and content of the regime.

This character and content were rooted in class relations.

The Umayyad aristocracy gave them a religious form by adopting the doctrine of compulsion.

In time, this doctrine itself became one of the clearest features of Umayyad ideology, as we have already explained.

The Umayyad rulers used it first as an intellectual weapon in the name of religion, and then as a weapon of violent repression against opponents from every political camp.

The attempt to reconcile Qurʾānic passages, which De Boer treats as the origin of Qadarite doctrine, was in reality a result, not a cause.

When social and political conditions produced the Qadarite movement, the Qadarites naturally turned to the Qurʾān in search of religious support.

There they found passages that appeared to point in different directions.

Some could support human freedom.

Others could support divine compulsion.

The Qadarites therefore had to interpret passages that seemed to support compulsion in a way that brought them into harmony with passages that appeared to support human freedom.

In this way, all the passages could be read as supporting one overall meaning consistent with Qadarite doctrine.

The supporters of compulsion did exactly the same thing, but in the opposite direction.

That is why we say that the attempt to reconcile Qurʾānic passages was a result, not a cause.

As for the influence of Christian theology, this cannot be denied.

But it was an outside influence that helped internal, objective forces already at work.

It also helped develop Qadarite theory and raise it toward a more philosophical level, especially once Qadarite thought entered its Muʿtazilite phase.

— 5 —

Finally, let us look at the story told by al-Maqdisī about ʿAmr al-Maqṣūṣ, the first Qadarite martyr in Syria.

Let us also consider the speech given by Muʿāwiya II to the people of Damascus when he decided to give up the Umayyad throne after taking the advice of his teacher, ʿAmr al-Maqṣūṣ.

Once again, this confirms our conclusion: Qadarite theory was connected, in both its origins and foundations, to social and political reality.

When Muʿāwiya ibn Yazīd asked his teacher ʿAmr al-Maqṣūṣ whether he should accept the inherited Umayyad caliphate, what advice did ʿAmr give him?

As we saw, he told him to accept it only if he could rule justly—and here he meant social justice.

Otherwise, he should step down.

What does this tell us?

In our view, justice was the central concern in ʿAmr al-Maqṣūṣ’s thinking when he had the chance to advise an Umayyad heir whom he himself had taught Qadarite doctrine.

Muʿāwiya II’s speech announcing his abdication also makes it clear that his decision came from his judgment of the mistakes made by his predecessors.

He believed he could not take responsibility for those mistakes or for the unjust conditions he had inherited from his grandfather Muʿāwiya I and his father Yazīd ibn Muʿāwiya.

Under those inherited conditions, he did not believe he could achieve the justice demanded by the principle he had learned from his teacher, ʿAmr al-Maqṣūṣ.

Can we really say, then, that neither the teacher nor the student understood any connection between this “practical position” and their theoretical principle?

The objective relationship between thought and action makes such a separation impossible.

Thought and action are connected in the first place.

And secondly, the connection exists objectively whether or not the people involved are consciously aware of it.

So whether ʿAmr al-Maqṣūṣ and his student Muʿāwiya II clearly understood this connection or not, the connection itself still existed.

And because it existed, it affected their practical behavior even if it had not entered their conscious awareness.

After all this, we need to know something about the personal lives of the three major early Qadarites: Maʿbad al-Juhanī, ʿAmr al-Maqṣūṣ and Ghaylān al-Dimashqī.

This will help us understand what these three men were really trying to achieve through Qadarite doctrine in both its theoretical and political forms.

A researcher might wonder whether their preaching concealed some deeper position against Islam itself.

Perhaps Qadarite doctrine was only a cover for that position.

Some opponents of the Qadarites at the time called their doctrine a “religious innovation” that violated the accepted foundations and principles of Islam.

We saw an example of this in al-Shahrastānī’s earlier remarks, when he doubted that al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī had written the letter attributed to him and addressed to ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān.

There, al-Shahrastānī clearly treats Qadarite doctrine as something opposed to the position of the early Muslim authorities, who, in his words, believed that divine decree, “both its good and its evil,” comes from God.

So do we find anything in the lives of these three Qadarites, all of whom died while holding their doctrine, that could be used to cast doubt on their commitment to Islam?

Would there be any basis for concluding that their Qadarite preaching was really aimed against Islam itself?

I wanted to investigate this question in the historical sources for the period.

What I found was the opposite.

The historians’ accounts of all three men show not only that they were sincere Muslims, but that they were known for serious religious devotion and trusted for it.

I found no historian of Islamic sects—not al-Shahrastānī, al-Baghdādī or al-Isfarāyīnī—who attacked the personal religious commitment of any of the three.

As for Maʿbad al-Juhanī, al-Isfarāyīnī speaks of him in a way that shows he was a transmitter of sayings from the Prophet.106

That alone gave him a respected religious standing and makes it difficult to accuse him of hostility toward Islam.

It was even said that Ibn Mājah, one of the well-known transmitters of hadith, narrated some reports from him.107
