The Qurʾān as something read and written, however, is unquestionably something that came into existence and was created, just as the Muʿtazilites say.

Every spoken word ends as soon as the next word is pronounced.

Each word therefore comes into existence in time, and the complete sequence formed from those words does as well.

The written and recited Qurʾān can still be called “the speech of God,” but only figuratively rather than literally.286

There is something valuable and surprisingly deep in this Ashʿari discussion of human speech.

Whatever we may think of its metaphysical foundation, it comes fairly close in some respects to modern discussions of the relationship between language and thought.

It also begins from concrete human experience rather than from a purely metaphysical world.

But al-Shahrastānī reports an even deeper Muʿtazilite treatment of the relationship between language and thought, one that comes closer to the scientific reality of that relationship.

Speaking for the Muʿtazilites, he writes:

“We do not deny the thoughts that arise within a person’s mind. We may sometimes call them inner speech.

“But in reality, these thoughts are anticipations of the expressions that the tongue will later pronounce.

“A person who does not know a single word of Arabic does not have Arabic speech arising in his mind.

“The thoughts and inner conversations a person has depend on the expressions he learned from the beginning of his development.

“Those expressions are the basis from which the thoughts arise and to which they return.

“We therefore know that real speech is the ordered letters pronounced by the tongue.

“Among speakers of a language and among rational people generally, what comes from the tongue is what is normally called speech.

“Someone who can produce it is called a speaker; someone who cannot is called mute.

“This shows that speech is not in itself a separate rational essence or category like other abstract meanings.

“It consists of expressions, words and similar signs, and these differ according to convention, agreement and common usage.

“If a group of people agreed instead to communicate through taps, gestures or symbols, they could understand one another through these just as they understand one another through words.”287

To pose the relationship between language and thought in this way shows a remarkable degree of theoretical awareness among the Muʿtazilites.

For a modern researcher, it is striking evidence of how important and innovative their contribution to knowledge was in their own time.

Before leaving the question of the created Qurʾān, however, we should record one final point about the Ashʿari current.

Despite its Salafi roots, it used rational methods just as the Muʿtazilites did.

C — The Question of Seeing God

This is another issue on which the Muʿtazilites took a distinctive position because of their rational understanding of divine unity and, in turn, their denial of separate divine attributes.

The denial that God can be seen is therefore a consequence of a consequence of their basic principle.

Even so, it became an important issue both for the Muʿtazilites and for their opponents and generated a great deal of theoretical debate.

The question concerns whether God can be seen with the physical eyes on the Day of Resurrection.

The Muʿtazilites denied this, despite Qurʾānic verses whose literal wording seems to suggest it.

One example is:

“Faces on that day will be radiant, looking toward their Lord.” (Sūrat al-Qiyāma, verses 22–23)

The source of the Muʿtazilite position is clear.

As al-Shahrastānī says, they wanted to remove from God every possible resemblance to created things: direction, place, form, body, spatial position, movement, disappearance, change and being affected.

They therefore considered it necessary to reinterpret the ambiguous verses that seemed to suggest otherwise.288

To see God with the eyes would obviously require Him to have a direction, a place, a body and so on.

Without such things, visual sight is impossible.

But all of these would contradict the Muʿtazilite understanding of divine unity.

The Muʿtazilites therefore reinterpreted the Qurʾānic verses whose literal wording appears to allow the sight of God.

Take again:

“Faces on that day will be radiant, looking toward their Lord.”

They argued that “looking” here means waiting, expecting and hoping for God’s pardon and mercy.

Al-Zamakhsharī follows this interpretation in his commentary and supports it by an example from ordinary speech.

He writes:

“At noon in Mecca, when people had closed their doors and gone inside to rest, I heard a woman begging and saying: ‘My little eyes are looking toward God and toward you.’

“What she meant was that the people of the Resurrection expect blessing and honour from no one but their Lord, just as in this world they feared and hoped in no one but Him.”289

Al-Ashʿarī reports that the Muʿtazilites were unanimous that God:

“cannot be seen with the eyes.”

They disagreed, however, over whether He could be “seen by the heart.”

Abū al-Hudhayl al-ʿAllāf and most Muʿtazilites said that we do see God with our hearts, meaning simply that we know Him through our hearts.290

The Muʿtazilites also found Qurʾānic support for their rational rejection of physical vision.

One example is:

“Eyes do not grasp Him, but He grasps all eyes.” (Sūrat al-Anʿām, verse 103)

Two Muʿtazilites belonging to al-Naẓẓām’s school, Aḥmad ibn Khābiṭ and al-Faḍl al-Ḥadathī, approached the problem through Neoplatonism.

Like the other Muʿtazilites, they denied that God Himself could be seen.

But they interpreted prophetic traditions that speak of seeing God in a different way.

One such tradition says:

“You will see your Lord on the Day of Resurrection just as you see the full moon, without crowding one another in order to see Him.”

They argued that what will actually be seen is the First Intellect, the first thing brought into existence, which is also the Active Intellect.291

From this intellect, forms flow out toward created beings.

According to them, it is this intellect that is meant by the prophetic saying:

“The first thing God created was the intellect. He said to it, ‘Come forward,’ and it came forward. Then He said, ‘Turn back,’ and it turned back.

“God then said: ‘By My might and majesty, I have created nothing better than you. Through you I honour, through you I humble, through you I give, and through you I withhold.’”

Ibn Khābiṭ and al-Faḍl held that this intellect will appear on the Day of Resurrection.

The barriers between it and the forms that flowed from it will be removed, and people will see it as clearly as they see the full moon.

But the giver of the intellect—that is, God Himself—can never be seen.292

This is the first case we find of an explicitly Islamic question tied directly to a prophetic tradition being studied through the metaphysics of Neoplatonism.

That metaphysics was built around the theory of the ten intellects and the theory of emanation: the idea that existence flows into our natural world from the Active Intellect.

Here there is no reason to deny direct influence from the Alexandrian philosophical school and the application of its ideas to the prophetic tradition about vision.

These two Muʿtazilite thinkers seem to lack the characteristic originality of the Muʿtazila.

In some Islamic questions they imported philosophical and Christian ideas into Muʿtazilite thought in a rather mechanical way.

For example, they also interpreted Qurʾānic verses that seem to describe God in bodily form.

One such verse says:

“And your Lord comes, with the angels rank upon rank.” (Sūrat al-Fajr, verse 22)

They explained such passages by saying that Christ clothed himself in a physical body and that Christ was the eternal Word embodied in flesh, as Christianity teaches.

They also connected this with sayings attributed to the Prophet such as:

“God created Adam in the image of the Merciful,”

and:

“The Almighty places His foot in the Fire.”293

The Ashʿaris take a different position on the vision of God.

They argue not merely that seeing God is possible, but that it necessarily occurs.

Abū al-Ḥasan al-Ashʿarī, founder of the school, tried to prove this rationally through an argument based on Aristotelian logic.

His argument was:

Everything that exists can, in principle, be seen.

What makes sight possible is existence itself.

God exists.

Therefore God can be seen.

Al-Ashʿarī then supported this rational argument with the Qurʾānic verse:

“Faces on that day will be radiant, looking toward their Lord.”

The Muʿtazilites, as we saw, rejected the literal meaning of this verse and interpreted it differently, as al-Zamakhsharī did.294

Finally, we should remember that Jahm ibn Ṣafwān had already raised the question of seeing God before either the Muʿtazilites or the Ashʿaris.

D — The Question of Atomism

1 — How Atomism Entered Arab-Islamic Thought

By this question we mean what is known as atomism: the doctrine of the “indivisible part,” or the “individual substance.” This doctrine was known in Greek and Hellenistic philosophy, and was associated above all with the Greek philosopher Democritus.

At first sight, then, atomism seems out of place in the Islamic intellectual setting we are discussing here with the Muʿtazilites and the Ashʿarites.

It seems out of place for two reasons.

First, atomism originally arose as a theory for explaining the natural world. At first it remained within philosophy, and later it became part of more specialized scientific attempts to discover the laws of nature. But with the Muʿtazilites and the Ashʿarites, we are dealing here with a purely metaphysical realm.

Second, our present subject, both with the Muʿtazilites and with the Ashʿarites, is the question of God’s attributes. So what does atomism have to do with the divine attributes? And how did the “atomic question” enter the discussion in the first place?

Both questions are entirely reasonable.

The answer lies in an intellectual development that marked the age of the Muʿtazilites.

We have seen that the Muʿtazilites emerged from earlier Qadarite and Jahmite currents that had discussed Islamic questions on a direct social and political level. Gradually, however, the same questions began to move away from that immediate setting and into a more independent field of intellectual and theoretical inquiry.

This shift was strengthened by the wider development of Arab culture during the Muʿtazilite period. Arab culture as a whole was changing rapidly, both in scale and in character. It was becoming more complex, more highly developed, and more abstract as it interacted dynamically with the other cultures that people in that period were able to encounter.

But none of this could separate Muʿtazilite or Ashʿarite thinkers from the original Islamic questions they had inherited from their predecessors. Nor could it separate them from the metaphysical framework in which those questions had first appeared, even when they were still closely tied to the realities of political and social struggle.

This helps explain what happened whenever something new entered Arab-Islamic thought and became part of the wider current of Arab culture.

These thinkers would subject the new idea to a process of adaptation and transformation. They would reshape it so that it could fit within the distinctive world of Islamic metaphysics. At the same time, they would turn it into a flexible tool for giving theoretical support to one position or another within that metaphysical system.

Indeed, the same older philosophical idea—Greek or otherwise—was often used to support two opposing positions within Islamic metaphysics, as happened with the Muʿtazilites and the Ashʿarites.

2 — The Connection Between Atomism and the Divine Attributes

This is how atomism entered the subject we are discussing with the Muʿtazilites, and later with the Ashʿarites as well.

In fact, we are still dealing with the commitments that followed from the Muʿtazilite view of God’s attributes.

To make this clear, we need to return to three divine attributes: eternity, knowledge, and power. We must also remember the opposite of “eternal,” namely created in time.

All Muslim thinkers, not only the Muʿtazilites, reserve eternity for God alone. In fact, all non-pagan religious doctrines do the same. The natural world, by contrast, is not eternal. It came into existence because it was created.

That is the first point.

The second concerns knowledge and power.

As we have seen, the Muʿtazilites understood these attributes, like all the other divine attributes, as identical with God’s own essence. Since God’s essence is infinite and encompasses all beings without exception, his knowledge and power must also be infinite and must include everything that exists.

From this, the Muʿtazilites concluded that created beings themselves must be finite.

If they were infinite, this would mean, first, that they too were eternal—and nothing is eternal except God, who created them.

Second, it would mean that God’s knowledge and power did not fully encompass them, because one infinite thing cannot completely encompass another infinite thing.

These were basic starting points for Muʿtazilite thinkers and, later, for the Ashʿarites as well. At their root, they came directly from Islamic belief.

The earliest Muslims, and especially the traditionalists who followed the teachings of the early generations, accepted these principles simply as matters of faith required by the religious texts. They did not think rational or theoretical proofs were needed. In fact, they resisted attempts to provide such proofs.

But from the ninth century onward, Arab-Islamic culture entered a period of intense intellectual development. Thinkers could no longer be satisfied with statements of faith alone. They increasingly felt the need to give those beliefs a theoretical foundation.

For the material needed to build that foundation, they turned to the body of philosophical knowledge reaching them from the different intellectual sources available in their society and their time.

This was the setting in which the new rational schools arose, above all the Muʿtazila.

They examined each new philosophical idea and asked whether it contained something that could be absorbed, transformed, and made into part of the theoretical foundation for one of their religious or doctrinal positions.

Abū al-Hudhayl al-ʿAllāf was the first Islamic thinker—not merely the first Muʿtazilite—to find in atomism, or the theory of the individual substance, a theoretical basis for several key beliefs.

The theory had reached Muslim thinkers from ancient Indian and Greek philosophy.

Al-ʿAllāf used it to support the belief that God alone is eternal while the world came into existence; to explain how God’s infinite knowledge and power encompass all finite individual things; and to explain the relationship between God and the world.

So what exactly was this atomic theory?

3 — The Greek Source of Atomism

In its Greek form, atomism goes back to its first founder, Leucippus, and to Democritus, who developed it further.295

Democritus developed the theory at a time when the ideas of the Eleatic philosophers, especially Zeno, were influential.

The Eleatics denied that motion really existed. They even denied that motion could be thought about consistently. Zeno believed that existence involved contradictions, and that sensory knowledge and rational knowledge stood in conflict with one another.

Leucippus, Democritus, and Anaxagoras therefore opposed the Eleatic teachings. They developed theories meant to show that motion does exist in the natural world and that sensory and rational knowledge do not necessarily contradict one another.

Atomism emerged in this setting.

These thinkers assumed that there were infinitely many material particles. But they also assumed that empty space existed, and that the particles moved through this void eternally, without beginning or end.

In one surviving passage from his works, Democritus presents the theory through three basic ideas: the principles of the universe, the atoms, and the void.

“Atoms” was the name that Democritus and his teacher Leucippus gave to these particles. The Greek word atom means something that cannot be divided.

Leucippus and Democritus believed that these particles were infinite in number and could not be divided. This is why their theory became known as the doctrine of the “indivisible part,” or the “individual substance.”

Their atoms therefore had three basic features.

First, they were infinite in number.

Second, they were indivisible.

Third, they were completely solid: there was no empty space inside them.

Democritus also held that atoms had so many different outward forms that they could not be counted or fully grasped by the mind.

Atoms differed from one another in shape, size, position, and arrangement.

They could also interact in different ways. Sometimes they met and became intertwined. At other times they repelled one another and moved apart.

Their shapes varied. Some were spherical, others rounded, others pyramid-shaped, and so on.

They also varied in size, from small to smaller and smaller still, until they reached a size too small to be seen.

They differed in position as well. Democritus illustrated this through the numerals 6 and 2: if the orientation of the numeral 6 is reversed, changing the direction of the angle it forms from left to right, it becomes 2.296 The reverse is also true. The same idea can be illustrated by reversing the direction of the Arabic letter ʿayn.

Atoms also differed in arrangement, rather as the position of the Arabic letter bāʾ differs in the words ab and bāʾ.

For Democritus, the way atoms sometimes join together and sometimes move apart explains how bodies are formed in the natural, material world.

He says:

“Atoms are basically small bodies with no particular quality. The void is the space in which they move eternally, from above to below. As they move, they either become intertwined in one way or another, or they collide and push one another apart. They separate, then come together again in new combinations. In this way they produce other complex bodies, including our own bodies, together with their states and sensations.”297

Other statements by Democritus tell us that as atoms move, they meet and combine to form a particular body. They remain in that arrangement for a certain period, then separate again.

How long a particular combination lasts depends on how long the body formed by those atoms continues to exist, or how long the larger unit formed by those particles remains together.

Another statement gives us a clearer picture:

“The atoms move rapidly through infinite empty space, where there is no above or below, no middle, no end, and no boundary. They move through this space in such a way that collisions cause them to hold together. From this arise everything that exists and everything that can be sensed.”298

4 — The Atomic Explanation of the Material World

From this account of Democritus’s atomism, we can see that the phenomena of the natural world are explained through atomic combinations.

If matter is analyzed far enough, it eventually resolves into an infinite number of atoms moving eternally through an infinite void.

One conclusion follows directly from this: motion is the natural state of matter.

This was the opposite of what the Eleatics, and especially Zeno, had argued.

Both ancient and modern accounts of Democritus often describe the atoms themselves as being, while the void is described as non-being.

But for Democritus this does not mean that the void is somehow less real than the atoms.

Rather, atoms and void form a kind of unity of opposites.

The Eleatic philosophers had reasoned about motion in the following way:

There can be no motion without empty space. But empty space does not exist. Therefore motion does not exist.

Democritus approached the problem differently.

He accepted the first statement: there can be no motion without empty space.

But he began from a different basic assumption—the fact that motion exists.

If motion really exists, then empty space must exist as well.299

Democritus also included in his atomism the idea that being itself does not change.

He took this idea from the Eleatic philosophers. It stands in contrast to Heraclitus’s view that things continually arise and disappear through a process of becoming.

Democritus believed that the existence of many different things did not contradict the unity of being. For him, there could be no multiplicity without unity.

When Aristotle explained the atomism of Leucippus and Democritus in his Metaphysics, he said that they accepted both the full and the empty—being and non-being—as the two basic elements from which reality is composed.

According to Aristotle, this meant that for Leucippus and Democritus, being was no more real than non-being, just as solid body was no more real than empty space.

These, Aristotle said, were the purely material causes of existing things.

He then made a comparison.

Some philosophers recognized only one basic substance from which everything was made. They explained the different phenomena of the world as different changes in that one substance.

Leucippus and Democritus did something similar. They took fullness and emptiness as the two basic principles and explained all other phenomena through changes in the atoms.

But they reduced the differences between atoms themselves to three things: shape, position, and arrangement.

5 — Matter and Motion

To complete our account of the different sides of atomism, we should also note Democritus’s insistence that motion cannot be separated from matter.

For him, the motion of atoms had no beginning.

In this sense, he was explaining nature through nature itself.

Through this theory, Democritus became the first thinker in the history of Greek science to raise the problem of space and time in this form.

Space was the vast void through which atoms had moved from eternity.

Time was contained in the very idea of motion.

Democritus also believed that empty space existed inside bodies, allowing them to contract and expand.

He regarded space as discontinuous. At the same time, he denied that it could be divided physically and practically into an infinite number of parts.

This did not mean that infinite division was impossible in geometry or mathematical operations, where the process could be repeated endlessly through an unlimited series of hypothetical divisions.

Here Democritus’s mathematical view of infinity met his atomic theory.

Democritus’s advanced theories provoked the hostility of the Greek aristocracy, whose outlook found expression in Plato’s idealism. Plato himself came from the highest ranks of the nobility.300

From Plato onward, idealist thinkers tried to distort Democritus’s theory and reduce its importance in the history of philosophy.

Yet the importance of Democritus’s view of the universe can also be seen in the way it explained generation and destruction—the coming into existence and passing away of things.

His account of the universe, based on the atomic structure of matter, contains a rich element of spontaneous dialectical thinking.

For Democritus, the motion of atoms through the vast void explains how worlds arise and disappear.

And there is not just one world. The universe contains an immeasurable number of worlds.

An infinite number of atoms move eternally through infinite space. In different parts of that space, they gather into whirlpools. Through their motion and gathering, different worlds are formed.

As groups of atoms swirl together, they collide sideways. This produces an outer shell that separates the newly forming world from the other parts of the universe.301

6 — Epicurus’s Theory of Atoms

Epicurus (341–270 BCE) agreed with Democritus that nothing exists except atoms and the void.

Everything else, including all the phenomena of nature, consists of different combinations of atoms.

The appearance and disappearance of any particular thing is simply the result of atoms coming together or moving apart.

Nothing comes from nothing, and nothing becomes nothing.

Epicurus explained the point in this way.

Nothing can arise from something that does not exist. If it could, then anything could arise from anything else, without any need for seeds or beginnings.

The reverse is also true. If things that disappear simply ceased to exist altogether—if they became nothing—then everything would have vanished long ago.

The universe would then have remained forever without change, because there would be nothing for it to turn into, and nothing outside the universe that could enter it and cause change.

Although Epicurus took many ideas from Democritus, especially the idea that all things and events are governed by causal necessity, he also introduced a number of new ideas.

In doing so, he tried to overcome some of the historical limits of Democritus’s atomism.

Democritus had not solved the problem of the weight of atoms, and he had restricted their movement to a straight line.

This gave his atomism a somewhat deterministic character.

Epicurus therefore insisted that atoms have weight.

It is worth noting here that when the weight of atoms was discovered in the nineteenth century, Engels commented that Epicurus had already known that atoms had weight, although he had understood it in his own particular way.

For Democritus, the movement of atoms through the void came from mechanical necessity.

Epicurus introduced the weight of atoms into the theory. This opened a new way of looking at the problem.

He began to look to the weight of the atom itself for the source of its movement through empty space. In other words, he treated weight as an internal property of the atom.

That was the first result of Epicurus’s idea.

It had a second result as well.

Epicurus argued that the number of atoms was the only thing about them that was infinite.

The number of possible atomic shapes, by contrast, was finite. An atom’s shape depended on its weight, and its weight remained within certain limits. Its possible shapes were therefore limited as well.

More important, however, Epicurus’s introduction of weight allowed him to consider two closely connected questions at the same time: what causes atoms to move, and what path does that movement take?

As he developed the argument, he reached the following conclusion.

If atoms have weight, there is no reason to accept Democritus’s claim that they can move only in a straight line.

Instead, Epicurus argued that their spontaneous motion, arising internally from their own weight, can take the form of a swerve away from the straight line.

The angle of this swerve, he believed, was determined by the atom’s weight.

Epicurus made a rather simple assumption when he thought that this atomic swerve could help explain human freedom.

In this way he tried to escape the determinism of Democritus, who had completely denied that atoms could depart from a straight path.

But however simple Epicurus’s assumption may have been, his idea that atoms could swerve away from a straight line made a notable contribution to the development of ancient Greek materialism.

In it we can see an attempt to find the source of matter’s motion within matter itself.

This was understood as a challenge to the idea of a divine mover, or a divine source responsible for the motion of all things.302

In short, Epicurus’s philosophy held that the world is material.

It denied the existence of immaterial spirits.

Everything in the world is made from eternal and indestructible atoms.

Nothing comes from nothing, and nothing ends in nothing.

7 — Atomism in Indian Philosophy

So far, we have looked at atomism in its Greek forms, especially in the work of Leucippus, Democritus, and Epicurus.

This account shows that Greek atomism had a materialist direction in the way it understood the origin of the world, its motion, its development, and its fate.

In Indian sources, atomic ideas appeared in a different form.

We find some version of these ideas in a number of Indian philosophical schools. But atomism reached a more complete and distinctive form in one school in particular: the Nyaya–Vaisheshika school.

According to Deliprasad Chattopadhyaya and other historians of Indian philosophy, including Radhakrishnan—one of India’s most prominent philosophers and the author of History of Indian Philosophy—Nyaya–Vaisheshika had several features that set it apart from other Indian schools.

One of these was its special interest in atomism.

The school’s name combines the names of two earlier schools that merged in the third century BCE and became a single tradition.

One was the Nyaya school. The other was the Vaisheshika school.

Their doctrines were set out in two works, the Nyaya Sutra and the Vaisheshika Sutra.303

The strong interest in atomism within this combined school was something new in Indian philosophy. From there, atomic ideas began to spread from one school to another.

Some historians date the emergence of this development within Nyaya–Vaisheshika to the second century BCE, around the same period in which atomism was taking a more developed form in Greek philosophy.

Because of this, many scholars of Indian philosophy argued that Indian thinkers had borrowed atomic theory from the Greeks.

Among them was the British scholar Keith, who presented this view in his book Indian Logic and Atomism, published by Oxford University Press in 1921.

But Chattopadhyaya, whom we mentioned above, tried to challenge this explanation.

He wrote:

“Quite apart from the possibility that philosophical ideas may develop independently and in parallel in different countries with similar social conditions—a possibility that this hypothesis clearly ignores altogether—there is another point to consider.

“For a foreign, ‘borrowed’ idea to take root in new soil, that soil must already be prepared to receive it.

“So even if we accept that Greek influence helped shape the ideas of Nyaya–Vaisheshika, we still have to study the social conditions in India—conditions which, in their general features, may have resembled those of Greece. Only those conditions could have made the acceptance and further development of these ideas possible.

“There is another point as well. Those who support the idea of complete and wholesale borrowing ignore the fact that the Nyaya Sutra and the Vaisheshika Sutra, although they remind us in some respects of Democritus, Plato, and Aristotle, contain a great deal more than we find in those thinkers.

“Moreover, those three ancient Greek philosophers did not, in the final analysis, represent the same philosophy that appears in Nyaya–Vaisheshika. Nor did they hold the same atomic theories, the same related ideas, the same judgments and conclusions, or the same philosophical categories. These things are not simply the same as they were in Greek philosophy. Here, in Nyaya–Vaisheshika, they appear as parts of a new Indian philosophy.”304

8 — The Main Ideas of Ancient Indian Atomism

We therefore need to look at Indian atomism in its own right, rather than treating it in exactly the same way as Greek atomism.

Two questions need to be answered.

What were the main ideas in the atomic theories of Nyaya–Vaisheshika?

And how did this school understand essence?

Indian thinkers spoke of nine kinds of essence.

The first four, however, had a special place in their philosophy: earth, water, fire, and air.

Each of these four essences could be understood in two forms: an eternal form and a non-eternal form.

Chattopadhyaya explains the distinction as follows:

“By the eternal form of these essences they meant their atoms. By the non-eternal form they meant the combinations formed from those atoms.

“According to the Nyaya–Vaisheshika theory, atoms are not all alike in quality. Atoms of earth differ qualitatively from atoms of water and from the atoms of the other essences. The same is true of the atoms of water, fire, and air.”305

Here we can see one difference between the atomism of Democritus and that of Nyaya–Vaisheshika.

But there was also another intellectual current in India, known as the Jaina tradition, which was interested in atomism.

Its interest was less intense than that of Nyaya–Vaisheshika, but the Jaina current had already taken shape several centuries before that school.

It also differed from Nyaya–Vaisheshika in an important respect: it accepted the idea that atoms were qualitatively alike.

So the disagreements over atomism did not exist only between Indian and Greek philosophy. They also existed among the different Indian atomic schools themselves.

In any case, the followers of Nyaya–Vaisheshika tried to prove that atoms differed qualitatively.

They argued in roughly the following way:

Even the tiny particles that we can see only in a beam of sunlight entering a room through a small opening are not ultimate particles. They too are made up of smaller parts.

But this process of division cannot continue forever. There must be some point at which it ends.

They therefore rejected infinite division.

Their reasoning was that if division were truly infinite, size itself would ultimately disappear as a meaningful difference. We could then say, for example, that an atom and a mountain were equal, since there would be no real difference in size between them.

From the claim that the chain of smaller parts must eventually come to an end, and that atoms can no longer be divided beyond that point, they concluded that atoms are not eternal.

Following this logic, the question of the creation of the world could be raised only together with the question of its disappearance, because if we accept disappearance, we must also accept coming into existence.

On this question of coming into existence and passing away, they reasoned as follows:

If atoms are infinite, there is no need to ask when they began.

But all ordinary things are temporary.

This means that they have both a beginning and an end.

9 — Indian and Greek Atomism Compared

If we now compare the atomism of Nyaya–Vaisheshika with that of the ancient Greek school, what do we find?

Let us look again at Chattopadhyaya, who states the issue very directly:

“Our view of the atomic theory of Nyaya–Vaisheshika must be connected with our view of its relationship to the corresponding theory in ancient Greece.

“In the history of ancient Greek philosophy, Democritus proposed the atomic hypothesis as a rational way of solving the problems of his age, especially problems that had already been raised by thinkers such as Parmenides and Heraclitus.”

Chattopadhyaya continues:

“Parmenides, to some extent, has a parallel in the idealism of the Upanishads,306 since he recognized one reality: a single, unchanging being.

“Heraclitus, on the other hand, was in some respects like our early Buddhists. For him, the only reality was change, or becoming.”

We can understand Chattopadhyaya’s point in the following way.

In Greece, atomism first appeared as an attempt to solve the problems raised by two opposing views.

On one side stood Parmenides, who spoke of true being and denied change.

On the other stood Heraclitus, who recognized nothing except change.

India had something similar.

The Upanishads insisted on a single, unchanging being.

Buddha, by contrast, recognized only change.

Buddha used the image of a candle flame to describe this constant change, just as Heraclitus used the image of flowing river water.

If this is what Chattopadhyaya means, then the comparison leads to a further conclusion.

Just as the ancient Greek atomists tried to find a way of reconciling the view of Parmenides with that of Heraclitus, the Indian atomists tried to find a way of reconciling the Upanishadic view with the early Buddhist view.

Chattopadhyaya continues:

“It is not difficult to see the strong similarity with the situation faced by the followers of Nyaya–Vaisheshika.

“On one side stood the teaching of the Upanishads, with its eternal and unchanging Brahman. On the other stood the Buddhist doctrine of a continuous stream—the stream of change.

“The followers of Nyaya–Vaisheshika found a way out of this contradiction through atomic theory.

“They argued that eternal, unchanging atoms could explain being, while the different ways in which those atoms combine, separate, and recombine could explain becoming.

“But the Nyaya–Vaisheshika system lacked many important elements of Democritus’s theory, especially one of its central elements: the motion of atoms.”307

Chattopadhyaya then comments on this last point:

“Nyaya atomism developed, to some extent, in the opposite direction.

“Kanada, one of the founders of the Nyaya school, did not even mention God. He was most likely an atheist.

“Later philosophers who followed this method, however, were not merely believers in God. They found themselves in the front ranks of those who offered proofs for his existence.

“Why did our atomism meet this particular fate?

“Perhaps we can trace it back to the level of technology through which Nyaya thinkers tried to understand the problem of creation.

“As we noted earlier, they understood the creation of a thing as the result of bringing together the parts from which it is made. Their standard example was the production of a pot by joining its parts together. This method of production is called kabala and is still used in our country in pottery.

“Because the followers of Nyaya tried to understand the production of everything through this same model, they also explained the creation of things made from atoms as basically a process of combining atoms.

“But if this is a process of bringing things together, then there must be someone who brings them together.

“Who is that?

“In this way, a place was opened within the Nyaya system for ‘God,’ who was called upon to fill this gap in the atomic hypothesis.”

10 — The Relationship Between Material and Intellectual Production

There is no doubt that Chattopadhyaya’s way of framing the question deserves attention. But if we look at the issue more broadly, on the level of society as a whole, it is useful to remember what Marx said on this subject:

“Historical periods differ from one another not in what they produce, but in how they produce it. So there is nothing unreasonable about connecting the way ideas are produced with the way material goods are produced.”

Of course, it would be wrong to derive the way ideas are produced—and especially their content—mechanically from the way material goods are produced. This does not mean rejecting Chattopadhyaya’s conclusion. But we do need to add the influence of earlier ideas and intellectual traditions, above all religious traditions, which have always had, and still have, an especially powerful influence on Indian culture.

We should also remember that mystical theories did not develop in a vacuum. They too were shaped by a whole range of political and intellectual traditions. Even Epicurus, despite his reputation for atheism, still spoke about the gods. In Indian philosophy, religious traditions were much stronger. Alongside changes in technology, these traditions were among the factors that helped change the form taken by atomism in the Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika school.

In explaining how the followers of this school understood divine intervention in the movement of atoms, the Indian philosopher Shastri writes:

“The atomic theory of the Nyāya system included the assumption that the will of almighty God awakens in the atoms the necessary effects of the actions and conduct of the souls, or jīvas, that reside in bodies. It also awakens in them different kinds of activity connected with the qualities inherent in the atoms. Under the influence of this activity, atoms join together in pairs, groups of three, groups of four, and so on. Creation (sṛṣṭi) takes place in this way. If the jīvas no longer require creation in this form, the almighty will of God produces other kinds of activity in the atoms. These cause them to split apart, destroying the forces that hold two atoms together in a pair, and the atomic combinations then dissolve, beginning with the pair.”

We have gone into this much detail about Greek and Indian atomic theories for a deliberate reason. These are the two main ancient sources of atomism, and we wanted to present them clearly enough, both historically and scientifically, to make a serious comparison possible between them and the atomic theories found in the Arab-Islamic intellectual tradition.

Only then can we make a sound judgment about the older sources from which Arab atomists may have borrowed, or drawn inspiration, when developing theories of their own.

We might even say that this detailed account of Greek and Indian atomism helps fill a gap in modern Arab knowledge of the subject.

After this extended overview of atomic theories in ancient philosophy, one further comparison may help complete the picture: the difference between ancient and modern ideas about the atom.

The first thing that stands out is one basic difference between the ancient view and the modern one. It may even be the decisive difference.

Ancient thinkers—Democritus above all—believed that division must eventually reach a final point, beyond which the atom could no longer be divided. Modern science, by contrast, has shown through experiment that the atom can continue to be divided without such a final limit.

There is another difference as well. Ancient theories did not solve the problem of what holds the parts of an atom together, or what holds atoms together when they form different combinations. Different answers were proposed, but none reached the heart of the problem. On this point, they all remained trapped within a rather simple way of thinking.

Modern science, by contrast, was able to solve the problem through the development of experimental methods and technology. It showed that when atoms meet, they bind together through chemical affinities that arise between them.

Yet despite the many deep differences between ancient and modern thought in this field, we still have to recognize that modern chemistry and physics rest, at a fundamental level, on Democritus’s theory and developed from the assumptions with which he began.

In the nineteenth century, Cournot wrote in his Study of the Sequence of Fundamental Ideas in the Sciences and in History (p. 245) that no idea inherited from antiquity had reached anything like the importance of Democritus’s idea of the atom.

Galileo almost certainly knew the teachings of Democritus. Pierre Gassendi, who helped bring atomic theory into modern science, began from his study of Epicurus, the great continuator of Democritus. Even Descartes, who rejected atomic theory, was so deeply influenced by Democritus in his mechanical explanation of nature that, in a letter to Mersenne dated 30 August 1640, he had to answer the accusation that he had done little more than patch up the worn-out clothes of Democritus.

We should also mention what Kedrov wrote about atomism in the Great Soviet Encyclopedia:

“The view that atoms never change, that they are incapable of development or qualitative transformation, that the relations between them are purely external and mechanical, and that they possess no motion except mechanical motion—this is the view characteristic of the metaphysical and mechanical conception of atoms, that is, of old atomism.

“The dialectical conception of atoms, confirmed by modern science, is characterized instead by the view that atoms are capable of change, that they form a successive series of stages of development that grow qualitatively more complex, that they continually enter into both organic and inorganic combinations governed by definite patterns, and that they are in permanent and uninterrupted motion.”

E — The Atomic Question in Arab-Islamic Thought

1 — Searching for the Source

We have now reached the point toward which this long discussion of the different ancient forms of atomism has been leading.

Our aim is to identify the source from which Arab-Islamic thought took the basic elements of atomism and then brought them into Islamic theological debate, reshaping them according to its own outlook and giving them a largely independent character.

There are two questions we need to examine.

The first is the source used by the earliest Arab-Islamic thinker to introduce the idea of the “indivisible part” into Islamic thought. As we have already seen, that thinker was Abū al-Hudhayl al-ʿAllāf.

We put the question this way because scientific research cannot reasonably assume that al-ʿAllāf began thinking about the “indivisible part,” or the “indivisible substance,” in complete isolation from the theories that had existed for more than a thousand years before him.

Those theories had developed among peoples whose cultures, especially their philosophical traditions, had by al-ʿAllāf’s time come into extensive contact with Arab-Islamic thought, though the depth of that contact differed from one culture to another.

We also know from al-ʿAllāf’s own life that he had encountered forms of foreign philosophical knowledge that had become available to Arab thinkers in his time. These ideas had entered the wider Arab intellectual movement and were already having a visible effect on its rapid development.

In short, no researcher taking a scientific approach can easily believe that al-ʿAllāf discovered atomic theory entirely on his own, independently of everything known by the ancient philosophers.

There must therefore have been some earlier model of the theory—drawn from one or another of the ancient traditions we have already discussed—on which he built his own thinking.

The second question is how the theory of the “indivisible part” entered Muʿtazilite thought, how the Muʿtazilites used it in arguing for the central principles of their school, and what kind of character the theory acquired in their hands.

As for the source from which al-ʿAllāf and the other Muʿtazilites—and later the Ashʿarites—took the basic theory, we cannot reach a final and certain conclusion.

But we can weigh the different possibilities in the light of the clear evidence provided by historical reality.

On this basis, the Greek source seems to us the most likely direct model from which these thinkers first began, especially the pioneer in this field, al-ʿAllāf.

We base this judgment on two considerations.

The first is that Indian philosophy in general—let alone the detailed teachings and theories of its different schools—was still only poorly known to Arabs in al-ʿAllāf’s lifetime, between the eighth and ninth centuries CE.

Fragments of Indian culture had reached them, usually through Persian intermediaries, but they had arrived in a scattered and unsystematic form.

Even the Muslim historian al-Qifṭī, who wrote well after the ninth century and whose historical works include The History of the Wise—a work closer to a history of philosophy than to general history—could still say:

“Because India is so far from our lands, few of their writings have reached us. Only fragments of their sciences have come to us, and we have heard of only a small number of their scholars.”308

Abū Rayḥān al-Bīrūnī did present examples of Indian religious philosophy in his famous book Verification of What India Says. But that book appeared much later than the time of al-ʿAllāf, in the eleventh century.

It is therefore difficult for a researcher to suppose that al-ʿAllāf knew the atomic theory of Indian philosophy, or at least that he knew it as clearly as he knew Greek atomic theory.

We have little doubt that he had access to enough material to gain a reasonably coherent understanding of Democritus’s theory, even if this came not through direct sources—which seems unlikely—but indirectly.

Al-ʿAllāf lived for about a hundred years, from 135 to 235 AH.309 Those hundred years covered both the first and second major periods in which Greek science and philosophy were translated into Arabic, or transmitted through summaries, explanations, and commentaries.

During this period, thinkers in Abbasid Arab society became familiar with the theories of many ancient Greek philosophers.

We know for certain that they knew Aristotle, at the very least.

As we saw earlier, Aristotle wrote about the views of Leucippus and Democritus on the full and the void, one of the most important foundations of their atomic theory.

We also know that Arabs of the period had access to an Arabic translation of Aristotle’s Metaphysics, which contains substantial discussion of Democritus’s atomism.

There is another point as well. Most historians of the Islamic schools, including al-Shahrastānī, report that al-ʿAllāf took his ideas about the divine attributes from Greek philosophers.

This means that his familiarity with Greek philosophy was taken for granted by these historians. They had no serious doubt about it.

His familiarity with Indian philosophy, by contrast, is much less certain.

None of the early historians of Arab philosophy said anything about a connection between the atomism of al-ʿAllāf and other Arab-Islamic thinkers and Indian atomism. Some Orientalist scholars later suggested such a connection, but without providing convincing historical or scientific evidence for it.

The French Orientalist Henry Corbin, for example, discussed the Ashʿarite idea of the creation of the world and the relationship it implies between the Creator and the universe. He wrote that the Ashʿarites found a “foundation and justification” for their view:

“in their theory of the indivisible substance, or the indivisible part, which is what is known as atomism. This theory was known in ancient times among Greek and Indian thinkers, but the Ashʿarites developed and explained it according to their own philosophical tendencies, so that the consequences of the theory would support their views about infinite divine power and creation.”310

But this is only a passing reference to the Greek and Indian sources together. Corbin makes no attempt to define the exact relationship between either source and Ashʿarite theory.

The Orientalist S. Pines did try to make that connection more precise. He argued that Indian atomism was the source used by al-ʿAllāf and the other Muslim thinkers who accepted the theory of the indivisible part.

But his argument did not produce convincing proof. It rested largely on interpretation and personal inference rather than on historical analysis.311

There is also a useful observation in Goldziher’s discussion of Indian influences on Muslims. He says that the influence of Indian Buddhism on them was only secondary.312

By Buddhism here, he cannot simply mean Buddhism as a religion in itself, nor only its purely theological side stripped of its philosophical ideas. As we saw earlier in our discussion of Indian atomism, the theory itself had roots in early Buddhist belief.

The second consideration is the character of Greek philosophical thought itself.

Its strongly rational and logical character was the dominant model among Arab theoretical thinkers, and among Muslim thinkers more generally, in al-ʿAllāf’s time. This same character is clearly visible in al-ʿAllāf’s own thought.

It also seems that these thinkers regarded Indian philosophy as lacking the kind of rational and logical character that fascinated them and gave their own theoretical work its distinctive shape.

In our view, this impression among Arab and other Muslim thinkers of the period had two main causes.

First, as we have already said, logical and rational thought had become dominant in their own intellectual work during the flourishing of the Abbasid scientific revival in the third and fourth Islamic centuries.

Second, while they were themselves working in this rational style, it seems that the part of Indian thought familiar to them came mainly through Persian Gnostics and consisted largely of its spiritual and contemplative side.

If our estimate is correct, this gives further support to the view that they did not yet know the atomic theory of Indian philosophy.

Strangely enough, Abū Rayḥān al-Bīrūnī came along in the fifth Islamic century—the eleventh century CE—and confirmed this impression of Indian thought in very broad terms.

He wrote his famous book on India after spending forty years there in scholarly study. Yet even he criticized the method of Indian scholars and philosophers as unscientific. He argued that their knowledge had not freed itself from superstition, and that what was found in their books was like:

“shells mixed with pottery, pearls mixed with dung, or fine steeds313 mixed with pebbles. To them the two things are alike, because they have no path by which to rise to the level of demonstration.”314

It is also striking that the same impression of ancient Indian thought passed from early Arab thinkers to modern Arab researchers.

We can see it clearly even in a scholar known for his care and precision, Aḥmad Amīn.

When discussing Indian culture, its influence on Arab culture, and the relationship between Greek and Indian metaphysical philosophy, he writes:

“Indian philosophy became completely mixed with religion and took on a poetic rather than a scientific character. It did not move step by step from what can be sensed to what can be understood by reason. In many cases it was content with poetic expression full of metaphors, images, and imaginative language, instead of following the scientific method, which requires explanation through facts rather than metaphors.”

He then identifies another difference between the two traditions. Indian philosophy, he says:

“defined the purpose of philosophy as serving the human being, whereas Greek philosophy sought knowledge for its own sake. The main motive of Indian philosophy was the human longing for release from the pains and hardships of this world. Among the Greeks, the first motive of philosophy was wonder: wonder at the appearances of the world, which led people to seek to understand them and thus to philosophize.”315

Our purpose here is not to debate Aḥmad Amīn’s judgment.

What matters to us is the persistence of this view among Arab researchers, both ancient and modern, and what we can draw from it for the question before us.

The persistence of this view is itself one useful sign supporting our conclusion that the Greek source, rather than the Indian one, was the direct model from which atomism first entered Arab-Islamic thought.

The situation is different when we turn to Persian Gnostic and Manichaean sources.

Here we cannot claim that Arab thinkers in the age of Abū al-Hudhayl al-ʿAllāf knew little about them. Intellectual and historical evidence strongly suggests the opposite: that these thinkers knew a great deal about such movements, and that some of them were even influenced by certain parts of their beliefs and ideas.

But the issue before us concerns Muʿtazilite and Ashʿarite thinkers.

Despite the major differences between these two schools, both stood very far from the basic ideas and assumptions of Gnosticism and Manichaeism.

The Gnostic and Manichaean theories of the basic elements of the universe rested on a dualistic view of its origin.

This was fundamentally incompatible with the Muʿtazilites in particular, because they insisted so strongly on divine transcendence: God had to be kept completely free of anything that might cast even the slightest shadow over the principle of divine unity as they understood it.

B — A Comparative Study

Since we consider Greek atomic theory the most likely source used by the Muʿtazilites, we can now move to our second task: comparing Greek atomism with the atomic theory of the Muʿtazilites.

This will help us see how they used the theory of Democritus in their own system, and how they made its early materialist and dialectical tendencies fit with their own idealist and metaphysical starting points.

We will naturally begin with al-ʿAllāf, since he was the first Muʿtazilite to adopt the theory of the indivisible part.

After that we will turn to the Ashʿarites, who made the theory one of the basic foundations of their argument for the existence and eternity of God the Creator, and for the claim that the world itself came into existence later.

Before beginning the comparison, however, we should stress a point already mentioned at the start of our discussion of atomism.

When Muʿtazilite thinkers, beginning with al-ʿAllāf, and later the Ashʿarites took up this question, their aim was not to study the natural world for its own sake, as the Greek philosophers had done in their philosophy of nature.

Al-ʿAllāf, the first Arab-Islamic thinker to take up the question, was not trying to build a theory of nature or of the material world.

His aim and motive remained entirely within the same metaphysical world that formed the general framework of Muʿtazilite thought, just as it had formed the general framework of other Muslim thinkers before Arab philosophy emerged as an independent discipline.

As we explained at the beginning of this discussion, the Muʿtazilites and Ashʿarites adopted the theory of the indivisible part mainly because of two theological questions: the eternity of the Creator and the created nature of the world, and the problem of how God’s knowledge and power could extend over everything that exists.

In other words, all of them began from the same Islamic intellectual ground.

We can now begin the comparison between al-ʿAllāf’s theory and its Greek source.

From what we have already seen, it is clear that al-ʿAllāf and the other Muʿtazilites influenced by him took only one main element from the atomism of Democritus: the element they could use to prove that the world had been created.

This was the idea that division eventually reaches a final point beyond which an atom can no longer be divided.

For al-ʿAllāf, this meant that matter was finite.

And if matter was finite, then it could not be eternal. It must have come into existence after previously not existing.

Its existence therefore required a cause outside itself.

That cause could not itself have come into existence later. It had to be eternal.

That cause was God.

1 — The Atomic Structure of the World According to al-ʿAllāf

Let us now look at how al-ʿAllāf understood the atomic structure of the world, and how he understood atoms themselves.

It is not easy to reconstruct his views with complete confidence, because historians of the Islamic schools have not preserved enough of his own words on this subject.

Al-Shahrastānī, for example, says nothing at all about al-ʿAllāf’s view of the matter. Yet when discussing al-Naẓẓām, he does mention that al-Naẓẓām agreed with the philosophers in rejecting the indivisible part.

Abū al-Ḥasan al-Ashʿarī, however, preserves a passage that gives us some idea of al-ʿAllāf’s position.

From al-Ashʿarī’s account, we understand that al-ʿAllāf believed the world to be made up of finite atoms, or indivisible parts.

He held that:

“The indivisible part has no length, no width, and no depth. It contains neither joining nor separation.”

He also believed that every existing object could be reduced to its final parts, and that the largest number of these smallest parts was eight.

Thus:

“A mustard seed may be divided into two, then four, then eight, until each of its parts becomes indivisible.”

He also maintained that:

“A single indivisible substance, when existing by itself, may undergo what bodies undergo in the form of motion and rest, and what results from them”—that is, from motion and rest—“such as joining and separation. But colours, tastes, smells, life, death, and things of this kind cannot exist in the substance. They can exist only in bodies.”

In other words, al-ʿAllāf allowed an individual substance to possess those states whose nature could be understood, but not those whose nature could not.316

By this last phrase, al-Ashʿarī means that al-ʿAllāf allowed motion and rest to belong to the individual substance—the indivisible part—because the nature of motion and rest was understood.

But he did not allow colour, taste, smell, life, death, and similar qualities to exist in the substance, or atom, because their nature was not understood. Their true character remained unknown.

Al-Ashʿarī’s statement that joining and separation are produced by motion and rest also suggests that indivisible parts, or atoms, sometimes come together and sometimes move apart.

From this we can conclude that, in Islamic atomism, the compound bodies found in the world are formed when atoms join one another, and dissolve back into their final indivisible parts when those atoms separate.

Bodies therefore come into being through the joining of atoms and pass away through their separation.

On the surface, this seems to fit a theory in which generation and decay take place within nature itself.

But neither the Muʿtazilites nor the Ashʿarites accept the conclusion that would normally follow from this.

All of them reject it, because it directly contradicts the doctrine of divine creation from which they begin.

As for time and space, the logic of motion and rest in al-ʿAllāf’s theory seems to require both.

Time, in fact, would be nothing more than the counting of the successive moments in the motion of atoms, or indivisible parts.

Space would be the field through which those atoms move over time.

Can we therefore conclude that al-ʿAllāf, the Muʿtazilites who followed him, and the other Muslim thinkers who accepted the theory of the indivisible substance—above all the Ashʿarites—also accepted Democritus’s idea of the void?

There is nothing in their surviving statements that clearly shows this.

The words “void” or “empty space” do not appear in the texts transmitted from them.

Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī, however, one of the major Ashʿarite philosophers, did accept the existence of empty space when discussing the “indivisible substance.” He treated it as the field through which the indivisible part moves.

2 — Comparing al-ʿAllāf’s Theory with the Theory of Democritus

We can now compare the atomism of al-ʿAllāf with that of Democritus and identify where they agree and where they differ.

This comparison will also help us understand the philosophical direction taken by the Muʿtazilites, beginning with al-ʿAllāf, on the structure of the world and on the relationship between this world and Islamic metaphysics as the Muʿtazilites understood it.

We can set out the main conclusions as follows.

A — Al-ʿAllāf, like Democritus, accepts that matter is in motion.

But al-ʿAllāf adds rest alongside motion.

Democritus did not do this, because for him motion belongs inseparably to the existence of atoms.

Al-ʿAllāf may have added rest because both he and the Muʿtazilites as a whole believed that the world had been created, in keeping with the doctrine of divine creation.

If matter—that is, the natural world—came into existence, then motion must also have come into existence.

This means that motion must have an end just as it had a beginning.

And if motion has both a beginning and an end, then it must be preceded by rest and must eventually return to rest.

This helps explain one of al-ʿAllāf’s best-known doctrines, which was unique to him and his followers among Muslim thinkers.

He held that the “movements of the inhabitants of the two eternal abodes” would eventually stop. In other words, even Paradise and Hell in the next world would come to an end as places of continuing motion.

Their inhabitants would:

“enter into everlasting stillness and inactivity. In that stillness, all pleasures would be gathered together for the people of Paradise, and all pains would be gathered together for the people of Hell.”317

Al-Shahrastānī reports al-ʿAllāf as saying:

“Just as I do not accept movements that extend infinitely backward, I do not accept movements that extend infinitely forward.”

Al-Shahrastānī then objects:

“It is as though he imagined that what applies to motion does not also apply to rest.”318

By this he means that if the doctrine that the world came into existence requires motion to have a beginning and an end, then the same problem should apply to rest as well.

B — Because al-ʿAllāf believed that motion came into existence together with matter, he also held that motion was neither eternal in the past nor everlasting in the future.

Here he differs from Democritus, who regarded motion as eternal and everlasting because of his materialist explanation of the existence of the world.

C — Democritus and al-ʿAllāf agree that bodies are formed when atoms join together and dissolve when atoms separate.

This is their explanation of what Aristotle called “generation and decay.”

But they part company over the final conclusion to be drawn from this theory.

For Democritus, the theory implies that the natural world exists in and through itself. In other words, it removes the need for creation from outside the world and therefore removes the need for a Creator.

Al-ʿAllāf rejects this conclusion because, as a Muslim thinker, he remains committed to divine creation.

So although he explains the formation and dissolution of bodies through atoms joining and separating as they move and come to rest, he explains the existence of the atoms themselves—and the existence of motion and rest within them—through a Creator outside them.

That Creator is God.

This is the basic point at which Muʿtazilite and Ashʿarite atomism separates from the atomism of Democritus.

At this point, the two views take fundamentally different directions.

The Muʿtazilite and Ashʿarite view is metaphysical in content and carries an objectively idealist tendency, even though it also contains an early form of dialectical and materialist thinking.

Democritus’s view, by contrast, contains an early materialist and dialectical tendency in both its content and its form.

D — At first sight, Democritus and al-ʿAllāf may appear to agree in the way they describe atoms.

Democritus says that in the void through which atoms move there is no above or below, no middle, no end, and no boundary.

Al-ʿAllāf says that:

“The indivisible part has no length, no width, and no depth, and contains neither joining nor separation.”

But in reality, the two statements do not agree and are not even talking about the same thing.

Democritus is saying that the void is infinite.

This puts him in direct opposition to al-ʿAllāf, because the infinity of the void is connected, in Democritus’s theory, with the infinity of atoms and the infinity of motion.

The result is an infinite material world.

As we have seen, al-ʿAllāf says the opposite.

His commitment to the created nature of the world means that the world is not eternal in the past and, as a consequence, is not everlasting in the future.

Infinity, by contrast, would imply that the world has no beginning and no end.

When al-ʿAllāf says that the indivisible part has no length, width, depth, joining, or separation, he is describing the nature of the atom itself as something of the greatest possible simplicity.

The two statements therefore do not meet, because they are speaking about different things.

E — Democritus identifies four differences between atoms: shape, size, position, and arrangement.

We find nothing in al-ʿAllāf about these differences or any others of the same kind.

F — The two theories do agree in denying that atoms possess any particular qualitative properties.

Democritus says this explicitly.

Al-ʿAllāf likewise denies that qualities such as colour, taste, smell, life, death, and similar things can exist in the individual substance.

He allows only motion and rest, together with the joining and separation that result from them.

G — Finally, there is the question of change in the natural world.

From everything we have already said about the two theories, it seems that for Democritus—as Aristotle interprets him—the principle of change lies in the changes atoms undergo because of differences in their shape, position, and arrangement, and because their motion brings them together and separates them.

This joining and separation produces combination and dissolution, or “generation and decay.”

These changes come to the atoms from outside their fixed basic nature, or follow from their eternal motion.

They provide the real explanation, and the only causes, for the different phenomena of nature.

Here we find a way to bring together Democritus’s idea that existence does not change at the most basic level with Heraclitus’s idea of generation and becoming.

Bringing these two ideas together also means bringing together the multiplicity of individual things and the unity of existence in a single relationship with a dialectical character: there is no multiplicity without unity.

So Democritus does not absolutely deny change in the natural world.

For al-ʿAllāf, his Muʿtazilite followers, and the Ashʿarites, however, the idea that the world changes is the very foundation on which they build their theory of the indivisible part.

It is also the religious reason they adopted the theory in the first place.

Instead of using Aristotelian syllogistic reasoning to prove that the world had come into existence, as some theologians did, they used atomism.

They found in the atomists’ theory of the “indivisible part” a basis for concluding that matter is finite.

That conclusion then became their inductive proof for the existence of an eternal divine power that encompasses this finite world, just as the world is encompassed by divine knowledge.

3 — Atomic Theory Among the Ashʿarites

From the time of al-ʿAllāf onward, the theory of the “indivisible part” spread widely through Arab-Islamic thought.

It eventually came to include many of the major Ashʿarite thinkers, beginning with the founder of the school, Abū al-Ḥasan al-Ashʿarī himself.

The Ashʿarites adopted the theory as a way of explaining the natural world, much as the Muʿtazilites had done.

Their purpose was to provide a rational proof that the world had come into existence.

At the same time, this would prove that nature had been created from outside itself, and that its Creator—God—existed eternally.

Here we see the common foundation underlying both Muʿtazilite and Ashʿarite thought.

Both begin from the same Islamic starting point.

The Ashʿarites believe that the natural world is made up of substances and accidents.

The substances themselves do not change. They are the things in which accidents occur.

The accidents are the source of the changes, or qualities, that appear in the substances.

The indivisible parts are the substances.

The accidents are the events or qualities that occur in them.

Different natural things come into existence when these accidents occur in substances, parts, or atoms.

One fixed feature of the atoms is that they have no size and that there is no connection or direct contact between them.

This follows from the Ashʿarite view that an accident can exist only in a single individual substance that is separate from all others and exists independently.

Indeed, even one accident that occurs in a particular substance cannot itself exist in another accident of the same kind.

This belief—that substances are separate from one another, that there is no direct connection or contact between them, and that the same accident is never literally repeated—leads the Ashʿarites to deny that universals exist outside the mind.

For them, universals exist only in thought. Outside the mind, only individual things exist.

The reason is this: if an accident exists only in an independent substance completely separate from every other substance, with no relation of action and reaction between them, and if one accident cannot exist through another accident, then nothing universal can exist outside the mind and be shared by more than one substance.

Nor, of course, can universals exist inside individual things as universals once those things have become particular individuals.

So there are only two basic categories through which we can think about things that actually exist outside the mind: substance and accident, or quality.

The other familiar categories—such as quantity, position, action, and being acted upon—have no objective existence in the external world.

They exist only in the mind as assumptions.

In other words, the relations we add to things and call categories are only mental relations. They do not exist outside the mind.

Put differently, they are purely mental operations with nothing corresponding to them in the objective world outside us.

For al-Ashʿarī and his followers, atoms also have no lasting existence in either space or time, because they are “events with no extension and no dimensions,” much as al-ʿAllāf had imagined them earlier.

Space, then, is simply a collection of separate atoms.

Time likewise consists of separate moments, with an interval between each pair.

The same is true of motion.

Like time and space, motion is divided into parts that have no extension, and each individual movement is separated from the next by a period of rest.

If the period of rest is short, the movement appears fast.

If the period of rest is long, the movement appears slow.

So in itself there is no difference between slow motion and fast motion. The difference lies only in whether the periods of rest are long or short.

The Ashʿarites also adopted the theory of the “leap” to explain motion.

They said that motion consists of a leap from one point to another.

They therefore also held that time moves by a kind of leap from one moment to another through the empty space in which substances, or atoms, move.

According to many historians of the Islamic schools, Ibrāhīm al-Naẓẓām was the first Muʿtazilite or Ashʿarite thinker to adopt this theory of the leap.

We will return later to al-Naẓẓām’s theory of the leap and to his position on atomism.

Because atoms are entirely distinct and separate from one another, and because they have no lasting existence in time any more than they have lasting existence in space, al-Ashʿarī held that an accident:

“does not remain for two times or two moments.”

In other words, an accident lasts for only one indivisible part of time: the present moment.

There is therefore no single unit that continues and repeats itself through time.

The accident that belongs to a substance at one moment is not literally the same accident that belongs to it at another moment, or that belongs to another substance.

For this reason, an accident can exist only within a single moment of time.319

The logical conclusion al-Ashʿarī draws from this account of the natural world is that atoms, or substances, are the places in which changing accidents occur.

They therefore change because they are the bearers of change, both within themselves and outside themselves.

And anything that changes cannot be eternal, because what is eternal does not change.

It must therefore have come into existence.

If this world came into existence, then it must have been brought into existence by a Creator who acts by choice and has power over everything.

But al-Ashʿarī believes that reaching this conclusion requires another step.

First, he rejects the idea that a “natural cause” created the world.

If creation were attributed to a “natural cause,” then the Creator would be stripped of knowledge, power, will, life, and the other divine attributes that Sunni Muslims agree belong to God.

Second, he rejects Aristotle’s idea of the “unmoved first mover.”

This idea too, in his view, strips the Creator of divine attributes.

The Creator must therefore be understood as a God who chooses and has power over everything—not as a natural cause and not as an “unmoved first mover.”

Only in this way can the whole world be embraced by God’s power and by His infinite knowledge and will.

At first sight, this conclusion about divine creation may seem to be shared by both the Muʿtazilites and the Ashʿarites.

But Ashʿarite thought goes beyond this common ground in one important respect.

Al-Ashʿarī holds that God continually recreates the individual parts that make up the material world—that is, substances and accidents.

God first creates these parts, then they cease to exist, and He creates them again, and so on without interruption.

The real meaning of this view is that the existence of a thing at one moment does not necessarily require its existence either in the immediately preceding moment or in the immediately following one.

So even if we observe a succession of things appearing one after another, this does not prove that they form a single continuous world, even though that is how things appear to us.320

What looks to us like a chain of cause and effect between things and events has another explanation.

God has chosen to create things in this sequence as a matter of custom, according to a will whose hidden reason we cannot know.

Because this sequence occurs regularly, we imagine that one thing causes another.

But according to this view, that is not what actually happens.

It is simply the custom according to which God has chosen to create things, for a wisdom hidden from us.

Al-Ashʿarī therefore believes that everything whose existence is merely possible depends directly on God for its existence, with no chain of causes standing between created things.

He denies that events are causally connected.

What looks like a connection between them comes only from God’s custom of creating one thing after another.

We are used, for example, to seeing burning occur after something touches fire.

So it appears to us that the fire causes the burning.

But on this view, the burning is created directly by God, independently of His creation of the fire.

God has simply established the custom that one follows the other.

From this position, al-Ashʿarī concludes that God, because He has power over everything, can cause contact with fire without burning, and can cause burning without contact with fire.

If this happens, it does not violate the law of divine creation.

It merely breaks the usual pattern to which we have become accustomed.321

This position clearly leads its supporters to deny the law of causality in the universe.

Yet causality is the objective law that defines the real relationship between necessity and chance in nature and society.

The same position also leads to the denial of the order of the universe as a whole, since that order rests on objective laws governing the phenomena of nature and society.

This view therefore moves very far, both in its direction and in its content, toward metaphysical thinking on the one hand and idealist thinking on the other.

In the theory of knowledge, it ultimately makes human knowledge impossible.

If the world contains no stable laws, and if there are no necessary connections or relationships between things and events, then the human mind loses the path by which knowledge can be reached.

There is no longer any basis for rational knowledge, nor for experimental knowledge in which the senses and reason work together.

Even sensory knowledge by itself is reduced to a fragmented and mechanical awareness of isolated particulars, each observed separately from any relationship with anything else.

To deny all these relationships is therefore to disable completely the powers through which human beings sense and understand the world.

Taken to its conclusion, this would mean abolishing science and scientific laws altogether.
