Al-Ashʿarī and those who followed him in the doctrine of continuous divine recreation—which denies the law of causality in the universe—do not seem to have been frightened by this serious consequence.

They accept it.

They then reinterpret the problem of knowledge in a way that still keeps them within an idealist and metaphysical framework.

Al-Ashʿarī himself, for example, when he tries to correct his position on science or knowledge, says that knowledge comes after reasoning as a matter of custom—that is, because God customarily creates beings and events one after another in a regular sequence. At the same time, however, al-Ashʿarī holds that reasoning does not itself necessarily produce knowledge. In his view, knowledge is something God creates after the act of reasoning.322

The theologians who followed this doctrine put it this way:

God knows all things before they happen. He creates them, and He creates whatever seems to us to result from them. He even creates our knowledge of them within the human mind. What God creates in us by way of knowledge is enough for us. We have no need to know more than He does, for He is the best of those who know.323

When al-Ghazālī came later, he adopted this view and accepted its consequences. He used it to answer the philosophers who believed that things and events in the universe are linked by cause and effect.

He writes:

The connection between what is normally regarded as a cause and what is normally regarded as its effect is not, in our view, a necessary connection. Whenever two things are not identical, and neither one is contained in the other, the existence of one does not necessarily imply the existence of the other, nor does the absence of one necessarily imply the absence of the other.

This applies, for example, to drinking and the quenching of thirst; eating and becoming full; contact with fire and burning; sunrise and light; cutting off the head and death; taking medicine and recovery; taking a laxative and the emptying of the bowels; and so on through all the connections we observe in medicine, astronomy, crafts, and trades.

These things occur together because God has already decreed that He will create them in this sequence—that is, one after another—not because the connection itself is necessary and could not occur otherwise. It lies within God’s power to create fullness without eating, death without cutting off the head, or continued life after the head has been cut off, and the same applies to all such connected events.

Al-Ghazālī then presents the philosophers’ position. According to them:

Fire alone is the agent that produces burning. It acts by its nature, not by choice, and therefore cannot refrain from doing what belongs to its nature once it comes into contact with something capable of being burned.

Al-Ghazālī replies:

This is precisely what we deny. We say instead that God is the agent that produces the burning. It is God who creates the blackening of the cotton, separates its parts, and turns it into burned material or ash, either through the mediation of angels or without any intermediary. Fire itself is an inanimate thing and performs no action.324

On the question of knowledge, al-Ghazālī adopts the same basic position as al-Ashʿarī. In his reply to the philosophers, he writes:

There is therefore nothing to prevent something from being possible within God’s power while God has already known that He will not do it at a particular time, despite its being possible. He may then create in us the knowledge that He will not do it at that time.325

The result is no different from the one we reached earlier. There we saw this position do away with the laws of the universe and the laws of science. Here it goes further and does away with the active role of human consciousness itself. If every piece of knowledge a human being gains about events in the universe is simply created by God, then human consciousness itself has no part in producing that knowledge.

But this Ashʿarite position did not go unanswered. Other intellectual currents of the same period challenged it from within the same historical setting.

4 — Al-Naẓẓām Rejects the Theory of the Indivisible Particle

Any discussion of atomism in Arab-Islamic thought would remain incomplete without considering the position of Ibrāhīm ibn Sayyār al-Naẓẓām. This major Muʿtazilite thinker, together with the intellectual current that influenced him, represents an important stage in the development of philosophical thought before Arab-Islamic philosophy emerged in a form independent of the school of kalām.

Al-Naẓẓām lived during the most flourishing period of Muʿtazilite thought and took an active part in its intellectual and theoretical work. He also helped organize the questions studied by kalām in a way that developed both their intellectual content and the methods used to investigate them. Over time, these inquiries acquired a coherent set of principles and rules, allowing kalām to take shape as a distinct field of knowledge with principles of its own.

One reason al-Naẓẓām was able to occupy such an important position in the intellectual life of his age seems to have been his close engagement with earlier cultures, both Eastern and Greek. He was widely acquainted with the Greek philosophy that had reached Arab-Islamic thought during the eighth and ninth centuries.

The early historians of Islamic sects give us plenty of evidence for the depth of this connection, especially his connection with Greek philosophy. Even the titles of the books they attribute to him make this clear.

Al-Ashʿarī,326 for example, mentions two of his books. One is The Book of the Particle, which, as we understand al-Ashʿarī, presented the views of Muslim thinkers on the question of the “indivisible particle.” The other is Motion, or The Motion of Bodies.

Al-Ashʿarī quotes al-Naẓẓām as saying in this work:

All bodies are in motion. Motion is of two kinds: motion of impulse and motion from one place to another. All bodies are therefore truly in motion, even though ordinary language may describe them as being at rest. Motions are nothing other than being itself.327

Al-Baghdādī also attributes to him a Book of Generation (al-Farq bayna al-Firaq, p. 117). Al-Khayyāṭ mentions a book by him on divine unity (al-Intiṣār, p. 172). Ibn al-Murtaḍā, in al-Munya wa-l-Amal, mentions a work entitled Refutation of Aristotle. And there were others.

As for al-Naẓẓām’s theory of atoms, the historians of the Islamic sects agree that his position set him apart from the other Muʿtazilites. He rejected the idea of an “indivisible particle.”

Al-Shahrastānī says that this position brought al-Naẓẓām closer to the philosophers.328 Al-Ashʿarī reports him as saying that every part has another part, every portion has another portion, and every half has another half. A part can therefore always be divided again, with no final end to the process of division.329

Al-Khayyāṭ, however, interprets al-Naẓẓām’s infinite division as something that happens only in the mind, rather than as an actual physical division. He bases this interpretation on al-Naẓẓām himself:

What Ibrāhīm denied was that bodies are made up of parts that cannot themselves be divided. He held that there is no body that the mind cannot imagine dividing into two halves.330

But the objection raised against al-Naẓẓām by his contemporaries suggests that they understood him differently. They seem to have taken his theory of infinite division to mean actual division, not merely division in the imagination.

Al-Naẓẓām’s own reply to their objection supports this reading, as we will now see.

5 — Al-Naẓẓām’s Theory of the Leap

Al-Naẓẓām’s theory of infinite division immediately raised a problem.

If the parts of a body can be divided without end, what happens when an ant walks across a rock from one side to the other?

The ant is finite. But according to al-Naẓẓām’s theory, the parts of the rock are infinitely divisible. That would seem to mean that something finite—the ant—has crossed something infinite. And that appears impossible.

Al-Naẓẓām answered this objection by introducing another idea that completed, or at least explained, his theory of infinite division. This became known as the theory of the leap.

Al-Shahrastānī describes it as follows.

The ant crosses some of the rock’s parts by walking and crosses others by leaping over them.

Al-Naẓẓām compared this to a rope stretched over a horizontal beam in the middle of a well. The rope is fifty cubits long and carries a bucket. Another rope, also fifty cubits long, has a hook attached to it and is used to pull the first rope. In this way, the bucket reaches the top of the well after covering a distance of one hundred cubits, even though the rope itself is only fifty cubits long and the movement takes place in the same period of time.

Al-Naẓẓām’s explanation was that part of the distance had been covered by a leap.331

[Diagram in the original]

Al-Shahrastānī objects:

Al-Naẓẓām failed to realize that a leap also crosses a distance corresponding to another distance. The difficulty therefore remains. The only difference between walking and leaping lies in how quickly or slowly the movement takes place.332

Al-Ashʿarī gives a somewhat different account of al-Naẓẓām’s theory:

Al-Naẓẓām claimed that a body may be in one place and then move to a third place without passing through the second. This happens by way of a leap. He used several examples to support the idea, including a spinning top. Its upper part moves more than its lower part and covers more distance. Al-Naẓẓām said that this happens because its upper part moves alongside things that the part below it had not previously faced.333

By the last sentence, al-Naẓẓām seems to mean that the upper part of the spinning top moves more freely than the lower part and meets less resistance. The upper part reaches things first, before pressure and obstruction have accumulated enough to slow its movement.

Al-Ashʿarī himself simply reports the theory in this form. He does not state his own view of it. Instead, he records the replies made by other theologians.

Among them were Abū al-Hudhayl al-ʿAllāf and others, who argued that:

It is impossible for a body to arrive at a place without passing through what comes before it. This cannot happen. A body may, however, have one part at rest while most of it is moving. A horse, even while walking or running hard, has tiny moments of rest as it places and lifts its feet. This is why one horse may be slower than another. A stone rolling downward likewise has tiny moments of rest, and this is why it may move more slowly than another, heavier stone released beside it.334

Al-Ashʿarī also reports that many speculative thinkers believed that, if two stones are released together, the heavier one will move faster. Their explanation was that the lighter stone meets more obstacles. It is pushed to the right and left, forward and backward, while the heavier stone continues downward during the moments when the lighter one is being deflected. The heavier stone therefore reaches the bottom sooner.335

Al-Baghdādī336 and Ibn al-Murtaḍā337 describe al-Naẓẓām’s theory of the leap in much the same way as al-Shahrastānī.

Taken together, these different accounts of the theory, and the objections made against it, suggest that al-Naẓẓām believed in an actual infinite division of matter, not merely a possible or imaginary division in the mind.

Consider the form of the original objection. The ant crosses the parts of the rock from one side to the other. If those parts can be divided without end, then something finite—the ant—has crossed something infinite.

Then consider al-Naẓẓām’s reply: his example of a fifty-cubit rope somehow covering one hundred cubits, followed by his further example of the spinning top.

All of this shows that the debate between al-Naẓẓām and his opponents was based on the idea of an actual, physical, infinite division. It was not about an infinite division that existed only in thought.

If al-Naẓẓām had meant only an imaginary division—one existing in the mind rather than in reality, or existing only as a possibility rather than in actuality—there would have been no need for these concrete physical examples.

Indeed, if imaginary division had been all he meant, he would have had no need for the theory of the leap at all.

The whole idea of the leap rests on a theory of motion understood as something real and actual, not imaginary.

So what was al-Naẓẓām’s theory of motion?

6 — Al-Naẓẓām’s Theory of Motion

Al-Shahrastānī and al-Ashʿarī give us our two best sources for this theory.

Among the views that al-Shahrastānī says distinguished al-Naẓẓām from the other Muʿtazilites was this:

All human actions are nothing but motions. Rest is a motion of impulse. Acts of knowledge and acts of will are motions of the soul. By “motion” he did not mean only motion from one place to another. He understood motion as the beginning of some kind of change, as the philosophers did when they spoke of motion in quality, quantity, position, place, time, and the other categories.338

This passage makes it clear that al-Naẓẓām regarded motion as the form taken by every human action, including acts of consciousness such as knowing and willing, which he called “motions of the soul.”

He also seems to have treated rest as a form of motion. He called it a “motion of impulse,” apparently meaning a hidden internal motion within the act itself. He may have had in mind a kind of inner self-propelling force that also resists whatever obstructs outward movement.339

Al-Shahrastānī says that al-Naẓẓām “did not mean motion from one place to another” and that, for him, “motion is the beginning of some kind of change.”

This seems to suggest that, when al-Naẓẓām speaks of the motion involved in human actions, he is referring specifically to what Aristotle placed under the category of quality. Movement from one place to another, by contrast, belongs to the category of place.

Al-Shahrastānī’s text appears to rule out this second meaning from what al-Naẓẓām intended.

This may agree in some respects with Aristotle. Aristotle often uses the word “change” specifically for qualitative change, even though his wider concept of motion includes the different forms of becoming covered by all ten Aristotelian categories. In its broad sense, change itself includes all these different kinds of motion, which in Aristotle are really general forms of being.

If this reading of al-Shahrastānī is correct, and if al-Naẓẓām really did restrict human action to qualitative motion, then al-Shahrastānī has contradicted himself.

On the one hand, he tells us that al-Naẓẓām did not mean movement from one place to another, which belongs to the category of place. But on the other hand, he also says that al-Naẓẓām followed the philosophers in recognizing motion in “quality, quantity, position, place, time, and so on.”

In any case, al-Shahrastānī’s passage alone does not give us al-Naẓẓām’s complete theory of motion. It deals only with human actions. We still need to know what al-Naẓẓām thought about motion in bodies and in the other material forms found in the world.

Al-Ashʿarī fills this gap in several passages of his Maqālāt al-Islāmiyyīn.

He first reports al-Naẓẓām as saying:

All bodies are in motion. Motion is of two kinds: motion of impulse and motion from one place to another. All bodies are therefore truly moving, though in ordinary language they may be called still.340 Motions are nothing other than being.

I also read in a book attributed to al-Naẓẓām that he said: “I do not know what rest is, unless it means that a thing remained in the same place for two moments—in other words, that it moved there for two moments.”

He also held that when God creates bodies, they are already moving with a motion of impulse.341

This passage gives us several important parts of al-Naẓẓām’s theory.

First, it shows how broad and unified the theory was. Motion appears here as something absolute, while rest appears as something relative.

In his treatment of motion and rest, al-Naẓẓām therefore begins from a position that contains a materialist and dialectical tendency, even though it remains inside a metaphysical framework.

In fact, the philosophical importance of his view becomes especially clear within that very framework.

To say that bodies are already moving with an internal motion when God creates them means that al-Naẓẓām has managed to push through the metaphysical barrier at precisely the point where it is strongest: the idea of divine creation itself.

Even while retaining that idea, he is moving toward the recognition of an objective motion within matter itself.

In other words, al-Naẓẓām comes close here to treating matter as a philosophical category in its own right.

Now add this view—that matter has an objective motion even at the moment when it is created from outside—to the position we discussed earlier: that bodies are made up of atoms, substances, or particles that can be divided endlessly in reality, not merely in the imagination, as al-Khayyāṭ claimed in al-Intiṣār.

Taken together, these ideas allow us to see an early form of philosophical thinking about matter and its objective motion. Within a wider framework that remains idealist and metaphysical, a materialist and dialectical position begins to shine through.

We should now return to al-Shahrastānī’s earlier statement and look more closely at his report that, for al-Naẓẓām, all human actions are motions; that acts of knowledge and will are also motions, even if he calls them “motions of the soul”; and that motion is the beginning of change.

If we combine these statements with al-Ashʿarī’s account—that all bodies are moving and that motions are nothing other than being—we can draw out a remarkably unified view, especially for its time.

Al-Naẓẓām seems to be trying to discover that motion is the form in which matter exists and continues to exist, and that motion is therefore a property inseparable from matter. Matter does not exist without motion.

He also seems to be moving toward an understanding of the relationship between thought and matter, since he treats acts of knowledge and will themselves as motions.

The fact that this attempt appeared within a religious form of thought does not reduce its importance. On the contrary, that historical setting is part of what gives the attempt both its intellectual and historical value.

We can see the point more clearly if we remember that al-Naẓẓām’s theory included every kind of continual change in the things and phenomena of the universe, from the simplest forms of change to the most complex of all: thought itself.

We should also remember that modern experimental science, through its great achievements, has confirmed the objective reality of this truth.

Al-Naẓẓām also moved far away from the metaphysical understanding of rest when he rejected the idea that rest means the absence of motion.

As we saw, al-Ashʿarī reports him as saying:

I do not know what rest is, unless it means that a thing remained in the same place for two moments—in other words, that it moved there for two moments.

Al-Naẓẓām is therefore insisting that matter can never be separated from motion. Rest exists only in an apparent and conventional sense.

In this way, he comes close to the scientific dialectical view, which does not accept the complete absence of motion and recognizes rest only as something relative. A body may be described as being at rest in relation to another body at a particular moment, while in reality it is still moving.

This also sets al-Naẓẓām apart in an important way from his fellow major Muʿtazilite thinker Abū al-Hudhayl al-ʿAllāf.

Their disagreement was not limited to the question of the indivisible particle. It also concerned motion and rest.

Abū al-Hudhayl held that bodies can truly move and truly be at rest, and that motion and rest are different from being itself. At the moment when God creates a body, he said, it is neither at rest nor in motion.342

7 — Looking at Al-Naẓẓām’s Thought as a Whole

Scientific method requires us not to look at al-Naẓẓām’s views on motion and the infinite division of matter in isolation from his views on other questions.

If we did that, we would make a serious mistake both in our method and in the conclusions we draw.

We therefore need to follow the strong materialist tendency we have seen in al-Naẓẓām across his other ideas as well. We need to ask how far the same logic runs through his thought as a whole.

Did this distinctive thinker really have a coherent and connected intellectual system?

Or was the materialist tendency we have seen so far no more than a passing idea, unrelated to other scattered philosophical thoughts that were themselves equally temporary and disconnected?

To answer this, we need to examine several of al-Naẓẓām’s positions on questions that were widely discussed and disputed among the theologians of his time.

A — Al-Naẓẓām held that it is impossible for something in motion to move “in nothing” or “toward nothing.”343

What does this mean?

What moves here is the body—in other words, matter.

His statement therefore means that matter cannot exist outside space, since it cannot move “in nothing,” and cannot exist outside time, since it cannot move “toward nothing.”

The second point follows from the fact that changes in material phenomena unfold through time, moving from the past to the present and then into the future.

Within the historical setting of his own period, al-Naẓẓām therefore arrives at a view containing the beginnings of a materialist and dialectical tendency.

First, matter cannot be separated from space and time.

Second, space and time cannot be separated from each other.

This early view fits closely with his materialist position on the endless division of material particles.

B — Al-Naẓẓām also held:

Every thing can interpenetrate with its opposite and with what differs from it. An opposite is something that resists and counteracts another thing, as sweetness opposes bitterness and heat opposes cold. Things that differ without being direct opposites include sweetness and coldness, or sourness and coldness.

He also held that something light may interpenetrate with something heavy. A light thing may have less volume than a heavy thing yet possess greater force. When it enters the heavy thing, it may occupy it.

In other words, something small in volume but great in force may occupy something large in volume but weak in force.

By “interpenetration” he meant that the space occupied by one body is also occupied by the other, so that one thing is inside the other.344

What do we see here?

We see a philosophical consistency with al-Naẓẓām’s two earlier ideas: his theory of motion and his theory of the endless division of material particles.

The connection becomes clearer once we place his remarks in their wider historical setting.

In speaking about the interpenetration of opposites, al-Naẓẓām brings us back to an old problem in the history of philosophy, one that goes back to the sixth and fifth centuries BCE.

This was the period in which a materialist tendency appeared among the Greek philosophers of Miletus and later in Heraclitus of Ephesus. At the same time, an idealist tendency began to emerge among the Pythagoreans and later among the Eleatics, especially Zeno of Elea.

As the materialist tendency developed and entered into conflict with idealist thought from the time of Pythagoras and the Pythagoreans onward, Heraclitus proposed that things are continually transformed into one another according to necessity.

He linked this to another idea: that opposites possess an inner unity and at the same time struggle against one another. This unity and struggle, in his view, are what drive the continual transformation of things.

Then, in the late fifth century BCE, Zeno of Elea denied the possibility of motion. His denial followed from his idealist and metaphysical outlook.

Zeno argued that both the existence of motion and even the attempt to think motion logically require contradiction. But he denied that contradiction can exist in nature.

His famous example of the flying arrow was meant to show why motion was impossible.

If an arrow is moving, Zeno argued, then at the same moment it must both be in a particular place and not be in that place. That is a contradiction. Since contradiction is impossible, motion itself must also be impossible.

To complete this background, we should note what the development of modern thought and science has shown.

Motion is not only an objective and universal reality in the world. It is also inseparable from contradiction understood as a real relationship between interpenetrating opposites.

Indeed, motion itself—which we accept as a real fact—cannot be understood without this contradiction.

In practice, contradiction means a relationship between two opposites that appears in the movement of things in three forms.

First, the two opposites possess an inner unity.

Second, they struggle against one another within that unity.

Third, the struggle is resolved through each side negating the other.

This negation is the real meaning of the transformation Heraclitus had already pointed toward in the sixth century BCE.

According to the dialectical law of their unity, struggle, and transformation, opposites therefore depend on one another and negate one another within a single connected process.

Throughout the history of philosophy, this question—the conflict of opposites—became one of the dividing lines between metaphysical and idealist thinkers on one side, and thinkers with materialist and dialectical tendencies on the other.

The first group denied that opposites and contradictions exist in nature at all, let alone that opposites can interpenetrate or form a unity. They reached this conclusion partly by treating nature in the same way they treated human statements, especially the statements of scholars and philosophers, where contradiction was something to be avoided.

The second group, by contrast, recognized all three features in the motion of matter: the inner unity of opposites, their struggle within that unity, and the eventual resolution of this struggle through their mutual negation.

With that background in mind, we can return to al-Naẓẓām’s statement that:

Every thing can interpenetrate with its opposite and with what differs from it,

and that:

Interpenetration means that the space occupied by one body is also occupied by the other, and that one of the two things is inside the other.

This fits closely with what he says elsewhere about motion as something universally present.

He affirms motion, and at the same time he says that one opposite can exist within another. He defines an opposite as something that “resists and counteracts” the other opposite or differing thing. He then defines interpenetration by saying that the two occupy the same space and that one is “inside” the other.

All of this strongly suggests that, in thinking through this problem, al-Naẓẓām again came close to the dialectical idea of both the inner unity and the conflict of opposites.

What else could it mean for two opposites to occupy the same space and for one to be inside the other, if not some form of inner unity?

And once this is accepted, what else could al-Naẓẓām mean by saying that each opposite “resists and counteracts” the other, if not a contradiction between them—a struggle taking place within their unity?

There may even be significance in al-Naẓẓām’s choice of the Arabic words translated here as “resists” and “counteracts.” Both are formed in a grammatical pattern that normally suggests reciprocal action between two sides.

That choice does not seem accidental or merely stylistic.

The reciprocal form implies motion, and it implies that the motion takes place within a single process involving two sides. Here that process is one of mutual resistance and counteraction—in other words, a struggle and contradiction between two sides occupying the same “space” and taking part in the same movement.

This is what we meant when we spoke of al-Naẓẓām’s consistency across two questions that, in the logic of reality and in dialectical thought, belong closely together: the question of motion and the question of the unity and contradiction of opposites.

A scientific researcher examining al-Naẓẓām’s treatment of these questions could hardly place him in the same camp as metaphysical and idealist thinkers.

This conclusion holds even if, for the moment, we limit ourselves to the three questions we have examined so far:

the division of material particles, motion in nature, and the interpenetration and struggle of opposites.

In our view, a thinker’s position on these three questions can tell us a great deal about the general character of his thought. They are central questions in determining where a thinker stands within the long philosophical conflict between materialism and idealism—a conflict that, directly or indirectly, is rooted in differences of ideological position.

But we must add an important scientific qualification.

Especially in an age such as al-Naẓẓām’s, it is extremely difficult to classify a thinker’s position on one question, or even several questions, in a final and absolute way.

Materialist and idealist elements, and metaphysical and dialectical elements, were often mixed together within the thought of the same person.

But this historical reality does not free the researcher from the task of identifying these different tendencies, showing the form each one takes in a particular thinker, and examining what it contains, while always keeping its historical setting in view.

Let us therefore continue examining al-Naẓẓām’s positions on some of the theoretical and intellectual questions disputed in his time. We may find further evidence confirming the intellectual and ideological character we have identified so far—or evidence that challenges it.

C — Al-Ashʿarī writes:

Al-Naẓẓām was reported to have said that length is the long thing itself and width is the wide thing itself.

He held that colors, tastes, smells, sounds, pains, heat, cold, moisture, and dryness are subtle bodies.

He held that the space occupied by a color may also be occupied by a taste and a smell, and that subtle bodies345 may exist together in a single space.

He recognized no “accident” except motion.346

Several different ideas appear in this passage, but they all seem to come from the same starting point. We will return to that common starting point after looking at each idea separately.

First, al-Naẓẓām’s statement that “length is the long thing itself and width is the wide thing itself” resembles, in some respects, Aristotle’s view of essence.

For Aristotle, the essence of a thing arises from the thing’s own external existence. Essence therefore has no existence apart from the thing itself. In the external world, what actually exists is the thing, not a separate essence alongside it.

“Humanity,” for example, understood as a universal meaning or universal reality, does not possess an independent existence in the outside world. What actually exists is the individual human being.

This seems to be what al-Naẓẓām means when he says that length is the long thing and width is the wide thing.

Length and width do not exist independently in the external world as separate essences. What exists is the actual individual thing that is long or wide—the concrete example in which each quality appears.

The theoretical starting point of this view is opposition to the logic of Plato’s Forms.

In Platonism, the essence has an existence independent of the external thing. More than that, the external thing depends for its existence on the essence, or “Form,” so that the thing we encounter in the world is only an imperfect or shadow-like reflection of the true reality of the Form.

The Aristotelian starting point here clearly contains a materialist tendency. Its most important feature is that it recognizes the independent, objective existence of the external thing.

Al-Naẓẓām appears to accept the same starting point, in line with the tendency we have already seen in several of his other theories.

Second, al-Ashʿarī’s account tells us that al-Naẓẓām regarded smell, color, taste, sound, pain, heat, cold, moisture, and dryness not as purely abstract or immaterial things, but as material things.

In his view, they are “subtle bodies.” In other words, although they lack the visible density of ordinary bodies, they still possess the characteristics of things that exist materially in the objective world.

Modern science, of course, distinguishes between many of these phenomena and would not accept al-Naẓẓām’s single explanation for all of them.

But that is a separate issue.

We cannot expect a thinker who lived at such an early stage in the history of knowledge to have possessed the discoveries of our own age of extraordinary scientific development.

The important question here is the materialist starting point from which al-Naẓẓām tries to explain things.

For our present purpose, it matters less whether his explanation of one particular phenomenon was right or wrong. What matters is how he begins thinking about it, and where he begins from.

From this point of view, the account attributed to him by al-Ashʿarī again reveals a materialist tendency. Al-Naẓẓām assigns bodily characteristics even to something like pain, which in reality is a sensory response to something perceived through the senses.

Third, al-Naẓẓām’s claim that subtle bodies can exist together in the same space contains a dialectical element that is not very far removed from discoveries made by modern chemistry and physics about combinations in which natural properties and phenomena interpenetrate.

Fourth, the same passage gives us another confirmation of al-Naẓẓām’s view of motion as an absolute reality in the existence of matter.

D — Al-Ashʿarī also attributes the following view to al-Naẓẓām:

The spirit is a body, and it is the soul. The spirit is alive in itself.

He denied that life and power are meanings separate from the living and powerful being.

He held that the spirit exists in the body in such a way that the body is an affliction upon it and a cause that leads it to choose. If the spirit were freed from the body, its actions would take place by generation and necessity.347

Elsewhere, al-Ashʿarī reports him as saying:

The human being is the spirit, but the spirit interpenetrates the body and is interwoven with it. All of this is in all of that, and all of that is in all of this. The body is an affliction upon it.348

Al-Shahrastānī presents al-Naẓẓām’s view of the spirit, body, and human being somewhat differently:

He also followed the philosophers in saying that the human being, in the true sense, is the “soul” or “spirit,” while the body is its instrument and its mold.

But he did not fully grasp their doctrine and instead adopted the view of the natural philosophers among them. He said that the spirit is a subtle body interwoven with the physical body and penetrating every part of it, just as water is present in a rose, oil in sesame seeds, and butterfat in milk.

He said that the spirit is what possesses power, ability, life, and will; that it has ability in itself; and that ability exists before the act.349

There is an important difference between al-Ashʿarī and al-Shahrastānī here.

Al-Shahrastānī says that the body is the spirit’s instrument and mold. Nothing like this appears in the two passages from al-Ashʿarī.

Instead, al-Ashʿarī emphasizes the interpenetration and interweaving of spirit and body: “all of this is in all of that.”

Al-Shahrastānī himself also emphasizes the same interpenetration when he compares the relation to water in a rose, oil in sesame, and butterfat in milk.

But if spirit and body interpenetrate one another in this way, the idea that the body is merely an instrument or mold becomes difficult to maintain. The two ideas almost contradict each other.

We can therefore say that al-Shahrastānī introduces a tension into his own account by first speaking of the body as an instrument and mold and then describing spirit and body as interpenetrating one another like water in a rose, oil in sesame, or butterfat in milk.

Apart from this, al-Ashʿarī and al-Shahrastānī agree that al-Naẓẓām treated the spirit as a body.

Al-Ashʿarī alone, however, records several other important details about al-Naẓẓām’s doctrine.

Because al-Ashʿarī lived earlier than al-Shahrastānī and was much closer in time to al-Naẓẓām himself, we will rely mainly on his account when trying to reconstruct al-Naẓẓām’s position.

What can we draw from the two passages preserved by al-Ashʿarī?

First, al-Naẓẓām treats the spirit or soul as material. Both al-Ashʿarī and al-Shahrastānī agree that he called the spirit a body.

Second, he presents the relation between body and spirit as one of interpenetration and interweaving, to the point that “all of this is in all of that,” as al-Ashʿarī puts it, or that the spirit is in the body “as water is in a rose,” as al-Shahrastānī says.

The two images express essentially the same idea.

But how should we understand this relationship between spirit and body?

Is it a relationship between two separate things, so that al-Naẓẓām is ultimately defending a dualism of spirit and body—a position whose basic character belongs to idealist thought?

Or is it a single unified relationship that rules out dualism altogether?

The explanatory images used by both historians point more strongly toward a unified whole than toward a strict dualism.

Unfortunately, we have no surviving text by al-Naẓẓām himself that would allow us to settle the matter directly. Nothing from his theories has reached us except through historians of Arab philosophy and historians of Islamic sects.

Whatever al-Naẓẓām’s exact understanding of the relationship between spirit and body may have been, his statement that the spirit is a body still points toward philosophical starting points marked by a materialist tendency.

That tendency takes forms particular to his own historical setting, a setting still deeply shaped by metaphysical and idealist ideas.

Third, al-Ashʿarī tells us that al-Naẓẓām denied that “life and power are meanings separate from the living and powerful being.”

This confirms the same Aristotelian idea we saw in his statement that “length is the long thing and width is the wide thing”: essence does not exist independently in its own right. What actually exists are the concrete things in which that essence appears.

Fourth, we come to al-Naẓẓām’s statement that:

The spirit exists in the body in such a way that the body is an affliction upon it and a cause that leads it to choose. If the spirit were freed from the body, its actions would take place by generation and necessity.

According to al-Ashʿarī’s account, this means that the spirit’s presence in the body creates a kind of interpenetration between opposites—the body being an “affliction” upon the spirit.350

The presence of the spirit in the body is what makes bodily actions voluntary. In other words, it gives rise to the consciousness through which a human being can choose.

If the spirit were to leave the body, the actions produced by the body would instead become necessary. They would arise naturally, mechanically, and automatically, like the actions of non-human or non-living things.

A stone, for example, produces a sound when it falls or strikes another hard object.

What do we find in this view?

In reality, idealist and materialist tendencies are mixed together here so closely that it becomes difficult to separate one from the other.

The idea that the body is an affliction upon the spirit has a familiar mystical tone. To some extent, it recalls the Neoplatonic idea of an upward and downward pull between body and spirit.

From this side, the view belongs quite clearly to idealist thought.

But from another side, the same statement contains an idea of the unity of opposites in the joining of the spirit with what is described as its affliction, the body.

From a third side, al-Naẓẓām gives consciousness a central role in distinguishing human beings from other forms of existence. He gives the spirit the character of consciousness, and through that consciousness the human being possesses will and choice.

Yet from a fourth side, the same view still suggests a dualism between spirit and body, and as we have said, dualism is fundamentally an idealist idea.

But this brings us back to the point we made earlier.

Among thinkers and philosophers who lived in an age such as al-Naẓẓām’s and developed their ideas within a religious framework, it is extremely difficult to find a materialist tendency completely free of idealist elements.

E — Al-Jāḥiẓ reports that al-Naẓẓām said:

The soul perceives sensible things through these openings: the ear, the mouth, the nose, and the eye. It is not that the human being possesses a hearing faculty separate from himself or a sight faculty separate from himself. The human being hears by himself, though he may become deaf because of some injury that affects him. In the same way, he sees by himself, though he may become blind because of an injury.351

To us today, this statement may seem almost too obvious to be worth making.

But al-Naẓẓām was not simply stating something everyone in his time already accepted. We cannot take the statement out of its historical setting.

In his age, different schools, sects, and thinkers disagreed sharply over the nature of the senses. Many even denied the senses in one form or another.

Al-Ashʿarī says that among these were thinkers who denied the existence of accidents.

He also reports that the Marcionites held that the body contains a spirit and five senses, with the spirit being something different from both the senses and the body.

The Manichaeans, he says, held that the human being is the five senses, that these senses are bodies, and that nothing exists beyond them. For them, reality consisted of two things: light and darkness.

Light had five senses, and darkness had five senses: hearing, sight, taste, smell, and touch.

The Dayṣānites, by contrast, said that darkness is dead and ignorant and has no sensation, while light is alive in itself and capable of sensation.

They held that light’s hearing is the same thing as its sight, taste, and smell. Only the direction of perception differs, so that it perceives through one direction what it does not perceive through another.352

And there were many other strange views of the same kind.

Once we picture this mixture of doctrines about the senses, their perceptions, their relationship to spirit and body, and their connection with theories of knowledge, we can better understand the progressive significance of al-Naẓẓām’s position.

Within this confused field of competing views, he returned the senses to their organic basis in the human being and recognized both their bodily function and their role in knowledge.

Seen in this historical setting, the question was not nearly as obvious as it seems to us today.

But we still need to look carefully at al-Naẓẓām’s statement that “the soul perceives sensible things through these openings.”

Does this mean that he denies the senses any role in knowledge because he assigns sensory perception to the soul, acting through the “openings” of the ear, mouth, nose, and eye?

The issue seems largely one of wording.

As we saw earlier, for al-Naẓẓām the soul or spirit is the human being.

So it is the human being who perceives sensible things through these five senses.

And that is indeed the case.

Even if al-Naẓẓām believed that the senses had no existence independent of the human being, would that mean that he denied their role in knowledge?

Or could they still remain the means through which sensory knowledge is acquired, whether or not they exist independently?

F — In the debates over accidents, al-Naẓẓām also disagreed with his teacher Abū al-Hudhayl al-ʿAllāf.

Al-ʿAllāf held that an accident could exist without being in a body and that an event could occur without being in a place.

Al-Naẓẓām denied both possibilities. He rejected the idea that an accident could exist outside a place or come into being outside a body.

Al-Ashʿarī tells us that many speculative thinkers agreed with him.353

It should be clear that here too al-Naẓẓām remains consistent with the materialist tendency we have tried to draw out from his different views.

This position follows naturally from his theory of motion.

For al-Naẓẓām, motion is the only real accident belonging to bodies, and all other accidents arise from it.

He also holds that something moving cannot move “in nothing” or “toward nothing”—in other words, that it cannot move outside space and time.

Given these premises, he is entirely consistent when he rejects the possibility that an accident could exist without a place or occur without a body.

8 — Final Conclusions

At the end of this examination of al-Naẓẓām, and after trying to identify the intellectual basis from which his various positions develop, we can now draw a more general conclusion about him.

His thinking shows enough consistency for us to say that the materialist tendency visible across his philosophical views was not merely an isolated tendency that appeared in one question and disappeared in another.

When we follow his ideas from one subject to the next, he seems to have built a reasonably coherent system of ideas, positions, and concepts around several of the major questions debated and investigated in his time.354

But we are certainly not claiming that al-Naẓẓām consciously understood this tendency as leading him toward a definite position in the continuing objective conflict between materialism and idealism.

Finally, we should explain why we have spent so much time on al-Naẓẓām.

To study him at length is really to study an entire philosophical current within Muʿtazilite thought, a current associated with his name and one that had a deep influence during the third and fourth centuries of the Islamic calendar.

The Social Basis of the Muʿtazilite Idea of Divine Unity

Up to this point, in our discussion of the Muʿtazilite principle of divine unity, we have examined the main areas of Muʿtazilite thought connected with that principle, whether directly or indirectly.

One question still remains.

What was the relationship between this intellectual doctrine of divine unity, in all its different theoretical forms, and its social basis?

In other words, what was its relationship to the ideological side of Islam?

After traveling through such a wide area of Muʿtazilite thought in this chapter, it may seem that we have moved very far away from that social and ideological foundation.

That impression may become even stronger because our discussion has taken us deep into questions that can look like purely metaphysical mazes, almost completely cut off from the world of human social activity.

This raises an obvious question.

When Muʿtazilite thinkers debated the divine “attributes” and all the purely metaphysical problems surrounding them, were they thinking about these questions in complete isolation from the social world in which they lived?

At the beginning of the next chapter, which we will turn to shortly, we will answer this question.

The answer will show that these thinkers never truly left their human and social world behind.

Their engagement with metaphysical questions was not a withdrawal of thought from that world.

On the contrary, it was one particular way of taking part in it.

How so?

Their engagement was an intellectual struggle to develop a rational form for the basic principles on which the ideology of Islam rested.

If we look closely at the direction taken by Muʿtazilite discussions of the divine “attributes”—the group of questions centered on the principle of divine unity—the picture becomes clearer.

All this intense intellectual effort was directed toward establishing divine unity on an extremely firm foundation: the absolute transcendence of God, placing the divine being completely beyond comparison with the created world and completely above it.

This absolute transcendence stood at the center of the ideology of Islam—that is, of the social and political order of the Islamic state.

The social, or more precisely social-political, meaning of this transcendent concept of divine unity, as the Muʿtazilites developed it, pointed toward an image of an enormous distance between the person at the head of the Islamic state—the caliph—and the institutions of the state on one side, and the human members of Arab-Islamic society on the other.

That distance mirrored the vast separation between the transcendent and unique divine being and our material world.

This was the basic foundation of the ideological structure of the caliphal state.

Does this mean, then, that when the Muʿtazilites struggled intellectually to establish divine unity on the basis of absolute transcendence, they were also helping to create an ideology of absolute separation between the head of the caliphal system and the society ruled by that system—between an absolute ruler and those he ruled?

Broadly speaking, there is no doubt that they moved within the limits of this ideology, whether they intended to or not, and whether they were conscious of it or not.

The social and intellectual conditions of their time, and the objective historical relationships within those conditions, placed them in a position to produce the ideology of the caliphal system in a rational form.

But because thought has its own internal movement and a degree of relative independence, producing the ideology of the system in this rational form also meant producing contradictions within that ideology at the same time.

We have already seen several examples of this contradiction in the present chapter on divine unity.

The most important was the breakthrough made in what we might call the Islamic theory of knowledge.

The Muʿtazilites opened more and more space for reason to enter fields of inquiry, investigation, and discovery that had previously been closed to it.

As reason pushed into these new areas, further contradictions within the ideology of the established order began to appear.

We saw this in al-Naẓẓām’s system of thought.

And we will see it again in the chapter on justice, to which we now turn.

Chapter Five

PreviousMuʿtazilite Divine UnityNextMuʿtazilite Justice

Muʿtazilite Justice

1 — “The People of Justice”

“...The title most closely associated with the Muʿtazilites, even in their later period when their thinking turned to questions in which philosophy and kalām overlapped, was ‘the People of Justice.’ They held that no evil comes from God, and that He rewards or punishes people according to what they themselves have done.”355

It was no accident that the followers of the Muʿtazilite school as a whole came to be known as the “People of Justice.” After all, belief in divine justice lies at the heart of Islam for all Muslim groups and schools. In the previous chapter, we saw that it was equally significant that the Muʿtazilites were called the “People of Divine Unity,” even though belief in God’s oneness is also a basic principle shared by all Muslims.

The reason is that the Muʿtazilites did not understand divine justice in the simple sense accepted by the earliest Muslims, or in the later traditionalist sense, which was defined like this:

“God is just in His actions because He has full authority over what belongs to Him. He does whatever He wishes and judges however He wishes. Justice means putting a thing in its proper place, and this means dealing with what belongs to Him according to His will and knowledge. Injustice is the opposite. It is therefore impossible for Him”—that is, for God—“to judge unjustly or act wrongly in what is His.”356

What this definition seems to mean is that justice rests on faith in the idea that God’s absolute will never puts anything in the wrong place. The traditionalist idea of justice therefore comes down to “putting a thing in its proper place.”

But this remains extremely general and open-ended. The standard used to decide what the “proper place” of something is remains absolute as well, because in the end everything goes back to God’s will: “He does whatever He wishes and judges however He wishes.”

We are therefore dealing with a vague idea of justice grounded entirely in faith in the religious texts themselves, without reason playing any independent part in defining it.

The Muʿtazilites tried to do something different. They subjected the idea of divine justice to rational interpretation and gave it a theoretical treatment drawing on both kalām and philosophy. In doing so, they tried to define the relationship between God’s actions and human actions—and, as we will see, even the actions of nature.

De Boer summed up this theoretical development in the statement quoted at the beginning of this discussion. In the Muʿtazilite view, divine justice could only make sense within Islamic belief if the relationship between God and human beings was understood in a way that allowed people to choose their own actions. Only then could a person be responsible for what they did, and only then could God’s reward or punishment follow from that responsibility.

If human beings had no choice in what they did, the Muʿtazilites argued, they could not be held responsible for their actions, whether good or bad. If they were not responsible, then reward would be pointless and arbitrary, while punishment would be unjust.

Both absurdity and injustice are forms of evil. And no evil comes from God.

For the Muʿtazilites, then, divine justice had a very specific meaning. It rested on a logically ordered argument built on two principles: first, evil does not come from God; second, rewarding or punishing someone for an act they did not freely choose would itself be evil.

But beneath these two principles lay the larger and more basic issue that had given rise to this whole way of thinking: human freedom of will and action.

The Qadarites, who were the intellectual predecessors of the Muʿtazilites, had rejected predestination and defended human freedom from a directly political starting point. Its content was almost class-based, even though its outward form was religious, as we explained earlier.

By the time the Muʿtazilites entered the period of systematic kalām and philosophical thought, however, the question had become somewhat independent of that original political setting. It had developed into a theoretical intellectual problem in its own right. The Muʿtazilites built a logical system around it, and then developed further theories based on concepts organized in much the same way.

2 — The Social Basis of the Idea of Justice

None of this means that the original social and political roots of the issue disappeared from Muʿtazilite thought.

Throughout the period when their kalām was developing, the social basis of their thinking remained present, even if it is not always easy to see at first glance.

It is striking that most of the leading Muʿtazilite thinkers—and especially those who were most committed to reason, human freedom, and the rejection of predestination—came from the social group known as the mawālī.

The mawālī occupied a lower social position in Arab society than people who were not mawālī. Some had been slaves. Some had been enslaved after capture in war. Others had become dependants of particular tribes through alliances in which the weaker party became so closely attached to the stronger that the relationship could extend even to genealogy.

Almost every major Muʿtazilite thinker carried some version of the description “mawlā of so-and-so” or “mawlā of such-and-such tribe or clan,” even at the height of his intellectual reputation.

It is difficult to imagine that this did not make such men aware, at some level, of the limits placed on their social standing. And it is quite possible that this experience influenced parts of their intellectual outlook even if they were not consciously aware of it.

Abū al-Hudhayl al-ʿAllāf, for example, was followed by this label throughout the historical tradition and is still described by modern researchers as “a mawlā of ʿAbd al-Qays.”357

The same is true of al-Naẓẓām. Despite his enormous intellectual stature, even modern writers continue to mention that “he was one of the mawālī.”358

The same applies to al-Jāḥiẓ, who was said to have been a mawlā of the Kināna tribe.359

So al-Baghdādī’s statement that creative excellence in every field came from the children of slaves was not without some basis in the actual history of Arab intellectual life.360

At this point, the logic of our investigation allows us to ask a question:

Could this historical and social reality have played some part in the development of the Muʿtazilite idea of justice?

There is good reason to ask.

Human freedom is one of the two main foundations of the Muʿtazilite idea of justice. We are not claiming that the social influence we are describing was something the Muʿtazilites consciously recognized. Nor are we claiming that it acted directly.

What we are suggesting is that their social position may have worked quietly beneath the surface and helped shape their strong attachment to human freedom and their rejection of a mysterious destiny imposed from above.

We have already seen that this rejection had an ideological side. Historical evidence shows that belief in divine decree and predestination often expressed the ideology of a particular ruling class. The Umayyad rulers defended the idea strongly and used it against their opponents, especially the early Qadarites such as Maʿbad al-Juhanī and Ghaylān al-Dimashqī.

We may be able to see another trace of this social reality in some of the Muʿtazilites’ known political positions, whether toward events in their own time or toward earlier conflicts from the first period of Islam.

For example, they agreed that Muʿāwiya was wrong to fight ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib.361

Some of them also criticized the third Rightly Guided Caliph, ʿUthmān, saying:

“He placed the Umayyads over the necks of the people, appointed them to governorships, and granted them landed estates. Armenia was conquered during his reign, and he took the entire fifth of the spoils and gave it to Marwān. He reserved the grazing lands around Medina from the livestock of the Muslims, except for those of the Umayyads. And on the same day that he ordered one hundred thousand from the public treasury to be given to Marwān ibn al-Ḥakam, he gave Abū Sufyān ibn Ḥarb”—Muʿāwiya’s father—“two hundred thousand from the Muslims’ treasury...”362

An even clearer example of the social basis of Muʿtazilite thought can be found in the political position taken by some of them on the question of leadership.

Some accepted the Khārijite view that the imam did not have to come from Quraysh. Others went even further. One Muʿtazilite argued that if a Qurashī Arab and a non-Arab were equally qualified, the non-Arab should be made imam.

This was the opinion of Ḍirār ibn ʿAmr. He explained his reasoning by saying that the non-Arab would have fewer powerful relatives around him.363

The political and social meaning of this argument is clear.

It points directly to a criticism often made of many caliphs, including the criticism of ʿUthmān quoted above: rulers used the benefits of political power for their own relatives and clans, giving them preference over the rest of the population.

The following passage from al-Ashʿarī may give us a useful way into the relationship between Muʿtazilite political thought and Muʿtazilite intellectual thought. Abū al-Ḥasan al-Ashʿarī writes:

“They disagreed about how numerous and powerful they would need to be before they were required to rise against the ruler and fight the Muslims. The Muʿtazilites said: If we form a group and believe that we are strong enough to overcome our opponents, we appoint an imam, rise up, kill the ruler and remove him, and compel the people to accept our teaching. If they accept our view of divine unity and our view of divine decree, then so be it. If not, we fight them. The Muʿtazilites therefore made rebellion against the ruler obligatory whenever they had the opportunity and the power to do so.”364

This passage gives us a clear picture of the Muʿtazilite position on political authority.

They were prepared to seek power so that they could put their ideas into practice, even by violent means, if they believed they had enough strength to succeed.

Another passage from al-Ashʿarī tells us something equally important. When the Muʿtazilites developed their particular idea of divine justice, they were also thinking about its relationship to another kind of justice: justice as something embodied in actual human relations, and therefore in real political and religious authority.

Al-Ashʿarī tells us that Muslims disagreed over whether a political uprising could take place without an imam, and whether punishments such as cutting off the hand of a thief, carrying out retaliatory punishment, and enforcing legal judgments could take place without one.

According to him, most Muʿtazilites said:

“There can be no uprising except under a just imam. And no one may enforce judgments, cut off the hand of a thief, or carry out retaliation except the just imam or someone acting on his orders. Nothing else is permitted.”365

So the Muʿtazilites believed that political and religious authority had to be led by an imam, and that this imam had to be just.

But what did justice mean here?

From the earlier passage, where they speak of rising against a ruler and removing him by force, we can see that the justice they demanded from an imam included acceptance of their own views on divine unity and divine decree.

And since their view of divine decree was inseparable from their belief in human freedom—that is, from their rejection of a predetermined fate that removes human choice—we can conclude that their worldly idea of justice was also closely tied to human freedom.

This allows us to see a connection within Muʿtazilite thought between their metaphysical idea of justice, meaning divine justice, and their practical, earthly idea of justice embodied in the just imam—that is, in a political and religious authority that was socially just.

Seen in this way, Muʿtazilite “rationalism” was not simply an abstract and purely metaphysical rationalism. It also had a practical side rooted in real human life, even when that side does not appear directly in their theoretical discussions.

3 — The Main Questions Raised by Muʿtazilite Justice

The Muʿtazilites’ particular understanding of divine justice led to a number of further questions. These occupied the thinkers of their own age and later became major subjects in both old and modern studies of Muʿtazilite thought.

The most important of these questions concerned the limits of God’s power and the limits of human power over human actions.

A — The Limits of Divine Power

The Muʿtazilites had established that both good and evil human actions come from the human being, in keeping with their understanding of divine justice, which makes people responsible for everything they do.

This means that human freedom places a limit on God’s power over human action.

But does this mean that God is unable to commit evil or sinful acts? Or does it mean that He is able to do them but chooses not to because doing so would violate justice as the Muʿtazilites understood it?

Muʿtazilite thinkers did not agree on the answer.

Most of them said that God has the power to commit evil and sinful acts, but does not do so because such acts are wrong.366

ʿAbbād ibn Sulaymān and his followers expressed the matter differently. They said that God has the power over injustice and wrongdoing, but they would not say that He has the power to act unjustly or to do wrong.367

This wording shows the intellectual difficulty they were facing.

They were trying to reconcile two ideas: that God’s power—indeed, God’s very being—embraces everything, and that human beings freely choose their own actions.

ʿAbbād’s solution seems to avoid the problem by playing with the wording rather than truly resolving it.

Al-Naẓẓām rejected both positions.

He argued that God cannot be described as having the power to commit evil or sinful acts at all. Such acts are simply not within His power.

His argument was that if wrongness belongs to the evil act itself, and this is what prevents us from attributing the act to God, then:

“To allow that an evil act could come from Him would itself be evil.”368

In other words, it is wrong even to say that God could possibly do wrong.

Al-Naẓẓām therefore concluded that God cannot have the power to do evil, because saying that He has such power means admitting that evil could possibly come from Him.

At this point, however, al-Naẓẓām partly moved the discussion away from the specifically Muʿtazilite idea of justice and toward another idea: divine grace and care for human beings.

He said that God can do only what He knows will benefit people in their worldly lives.

As for the next life, God cannot be described as having the power to increase the punishment of the people of Hell or to reduce it. Nor can He reduce the happiness of the people of Paradise or remove anyone from Paradise. None of these things lies within His power.369

Muʿtazilite writings sometimes used this kind of language—that God acts for what benefits human beings—to explain the idea of divine grace.

By this they meant that God knows from eternity what each person will choose to do, but may, through His grace, help those who choose the good.

Bishr ibn al-Muʿtamir explained the idea by saying that if God knows that a particular person would become a believer if allowed to remain alive, then keeping that person alive is better for them than allowing them to die as an unbeliever.370

This is essentially what al-Naẓẓām was pointing toward in the argument above.

But in another statement he returns directly to the distinctively Muʿtazilite idea of justice.

He says that if a child were standing at the edge of Hell, God would not have the power to throw the child in, although the child would have the power to throw himself in.371

Here the issue is no longer divine grace. It is Muʿtazilite justice itself, where the limits of divine power are set by the human being’s freedom to choose.

Another group of Muʿtazilites objected to al-Naẓẓām.

They argued that if God has no power to do evil or commit sin, then He would be naturally compelled to do what He does rather than freely choosing it. A being truly described as powerful, they argued, must be able either to act or not to act. Al-Naẓẓām’s position removes that choice from divine power.

Al-Naẓẓām replied:

What you say about power applies equally to what you yourselves say about action. You say that it is impossible for God to do evil even though He has the power to do it. So what is the difference between our two positions?372

His point was simple.

If it is impossible for God actually to do evil, whether or not He theoretically has the power to do so, then in either case God does not have a real choice between doing evil and not doing it.

The problem therefore remains.

The Muʿtazilites tried to solve it by turning to another idea: divine wisdom.

God, they said, is unquestionably wise, and a wise being does nothing without wisdom.

God’s wisdom in commanding human beings to obey and avoid wrongdoing lies in choosing what is best for them. And what is best for human beings requires that they have the power to perform their own actions.

God therefore gave them reason, through which they can understand good and evil and choose between different actions.

Human power and human choice thus fall within a permanent and consistent law of divine wisdom.373

The Baghdad Muʿtazilites took this argument further than the Basra Muʿtazilites.

According to the Baghdad school, divine wisdom requires that everything that happens to a person in this life—misfortune, pain, or their opposites—and everything that happens in the next life—happiness or punishment—must be what is good, or best, for that person.

Poverty may therefore be better for one person than wealth, while the opposite may be true for another. Illness may be better than health, or health better than illness. Even remaining forever in Hell might be better for someone than remaining forever in Paradise.374

This way of handling the problem seems to involve a partial return to the traditionalist outlook that the Muʿtazilites had opposed.

It also seems to move away from the rationalist approach they defended so firmly in many of the great intellectual battles of their history.

The Basra Muʿtazilites came less close to traditionalism and moved less far from their rationalism.

They agreed that divine wisdom led God, out of generosity, to create human beings and place them under the obligations of religious law. But they also held that this same wisdom required God to remove the obstacles that prevent human beings from achieving what is best for them.

And what is “best” can be defined here quite clearly: human beings must be able to understand through reason and must have the power to act.

Because they have this capacity, they must then receive reward for obedience and punishment for wrongdoing.375

Abū al-Hudhayl al-ʿAllāf, one of the leading figures of the Basra school, explained this idea of “what is best” by saying that God has the power to do something less than the best, but does not do so. Instead, He does what is better.

He explained:

“To do something less good when something better could be done would be corruption. If God did what was less good and withheld what was better, both things would be corrupt. Nor can it be said that God could have done something better than what He actually did. If He could have done something better, then doing the better thing would have been more fitting. God does not leave aside what is best, because what is best is what is most fitting for Him.”376

In another passage, also preserved by al-Ashʿarī, Abū al-Hudhayl says that God has the power to commit injustice and wrongdoing, and to act unjustly and wrongly, but does not do so. It is impossible for Him to do so in practice because such acts could come only from deficiency, and deficiency cannot be attributed to God.

God did not create human beings because He needed them. He created them because creating them was wise. He intended their benefit and is not miserly. It is therefore impossible for Him to leave aside what is best and do something inferior instead.377

Yet although al-ʿAllāf clearly affirms in theory that God has the power to do less than what is best, and even has the power to act unjustly, he ends up denying this power in practice.

The issue becomes especially clear when the following question is raised: if God has given a human being the power to perform a certain act—an act of injustice, sin, or evil, for example—does God still retain the power to perform that same act?

On this question, al-ʿAllāf gives an explicit answer.

He denies that God retains such power, relying on an old philosophical principle:

“It is impossible for one and the same act to lie within the power of two agents.”378

In general, then, the Basra and Baghdad Muʿtazilites differed in how they tried to escape the difficulty their theory of justice and power had created for them. But they agreed on the essential point: human freedom of action is the central content of justice.

They therefore agreed that God does not commit evil or sinful acts, whether He theoretically has the power to do so, as most Muʿtazilites held, or does not have that power at all, as al-Naẓẓām’s school argued.

Their determination to defend freedom of the human will went very far.

Bishr ibn al-Muʿtamir expressed the point by saying that God is not the ally of an obedient person at the moment that person is performing the act of obedience, and is not the enemy of an unbeliever at the moment that person is committing unbelief.

God becomes the ally of the obedient person only after the act of obedience has taken place, and becomes the enemy of the unbeliever only after the act of unbelief has taken place.379

What Bishr means is that God’s will does not enter into the person’s act of obedience or unbelief while the act itself is happening.

God judges the obedient person only after the act of obedience has occurred, and judges the unbeliever only after the act of unbelief has occurred.

In other words, whether an action is good or bad, it happens only because the human being freely chooses and wills it.

Reward for obedience and punishment for wrongdoing are therefore nothing more than God’s judgment about what a person deserves for something they themselves freely chose to do.

B — The Opposition to Limiting Divine Power

As we have said, the Muʿtazilites placed themselves in a difficult position before the wider Sunni public when they developed their distinctive theory of justice.

They faced fierce opposition. Many traditionalists went so far as to accuse them of abandoning Islam itself.

The central idea behind this opposition was that God’s power is absolute and unlimited, while His will includes everything and is itself contained by nothing.

God creates every action and every event.

Human beings do not create any of their own actions, because to say that they do would be to place human power alongside God’s power. This, the critics argued, would mean introducing a second creator.

For this reason, the Muʿtazilites were compared in their own age to the Zoroastrians, who were accused of believing in two creators.380

This comparison went back to the first appearance of the Qadarites.

Opponents of the view that human actions are free from divine predestination deliberately called the earliest supporters of human freedom “Qadarites” so that they could apply to them the reported saying of the Prophet:

“The Qadarites are the Zoroastrians of this community.”

We discussed this earlier when examining the origins of the issue.

The Ashʿarites found in the Muʿtazilite idea of justice—and especially in the claim that human power limits divine power—fertile ground for attacking Muʿtazilite beliefs.

Sometimes they went so far that they interpreted Muʿtazilite statements in ways the Muʿtazilites themselves did not intend.

One of the clearest examples appears in al-Isfarāyīnī’s al-Tabṣīr fī al-Dīn (p. 48). Al-Isfarāyīnī, one of the major Ashʿarite writers, pushes the Muʿtazilite position much further than it actually goes.

He says that the Muʿtazilite belief that human beings create their own acts leads to the conclusion:

“That every one of them—like a gnat, mosquito, bee, ant, worm, or fish—is a creator who creates his own acts; that God does not create their acts and has no power over any of what they do; and that He has no power over anything done by all the animals. They”—the Muʿtazilites—“thus established countless creators beyond number. They removed the actions of animals from God’s power while placing no corresponding restriction on describing Him as powerful. In this way they prepared the road to dualism.”

We do not know where al-Isfarāyīnī got the idea that the Muʿtazilite teaching about human beings creating their own acts could be extended to animals.

Even the Arabic term ʿibād—“God’s human servants”—is not normally used in Arabic terminology or texts to refer to animals.

Nor is there anything in the statements of Muʿtazilite thinkers on this issue that suggests their discussion of human actions also included animal actions or that the creation of actions extended beyond human beings.

It is especially strange to accuse the Muʿtazilites of dualism, or even of preparing the way for belief in two creators.

These were the very thinkers who defended belief in God’s absolute oneness so intensely that the history of Arab-Islamic thought came to call them the People of Divine Unity.

Their concern for the purity of this belief led them to investigate the divine attributes in a new theoretical way that had not existed before them.

It also led them into some of their fiercest intellectual battles, especially against those they regarded as dualists and against those who described God in human or bodily terms.

This commitment was so obvious that many of their fiercest historical opponents admitted it, and modern opponents have done the same.

One contemporary Ashʿarite researcher, for example, admits that the Muʿtazilites’ special theory of justice was:

“A branch of their theory of divine unity. They denied attributes of God in order to keep Him free from resemblance to created beings, and in the same way they keep Him free from injustice so that He does not resemble created beings in committing injustice.”381

Yet after making this admission, the same researcher gives another criticism that also seems unfair.

He argues:

“By affirming justice alone, they truly tore divine unity apart. In the question of justice, God is not alone in His action. Human beings share with Him in cosmic action.”382

But the Muʿtazilites did not treat justice differently from the other divine attributes.

Their denial of separate divine attributes, understood in the special way they explained it, applied to every quality Muslims attributed to God.

That is the first point.

The second is that the Muʿtazilite texts we quoted earlier do not strip God of power over everything.

They make God the one who gives human beings the power to act.

Human power over human actions therefore remains contained within God’s power. It does not stand beside it as a partner “in cosmic action,” as this researcher claims.

If we also take into account what the Muʿtazilites said about divine grace, divine wisdom, and God doing what is best for human beings, it becomes clear that they were extremely careful in their arguments not to undermine the foundations of Islamic metaphysics as a whole.

The truth is that the Muʿtazilites never left the Islamic metaphysical framework.

What they tried to do, from within that framework, was something else.

With great courage, persistence, intellectual honesty, and openness, they tried to raise the human being above the level of a mere thing, or a purely mechanical object.

They tried to give human reason the highest place that their philosophical and social awareness could reach under the historical conditions of their society and their age.

Their problem was that this effort remained tied to an equally firm commitment to the Islamic metaphysical framework as a whole. They were unwilling to disturb the basic articles of faith on which that framework rested.

As a result, they often struggled to create a fully consistent connection between their metaphysical commitments and their rational and, at times, realistic approach.

This produced tensions in the inner logic of some of their most important ideas.

But under the conditions in which their movement developed, this was natural and probably unavoidable. We will return to this when we later examine the Muʿtazilite movement as a whole.

C — The Argument for Human Freedom of Choice

Since freedom of human will and action formed the basis of the Muʿtazilite idea of justice, the Muʿtazilites tried to support this freedom with rational arguments.
