These arguments grew out of the same rationalist outlook that connected the different parts of their doctrine.

Let us look at the main ways they tried to prove that human beings freely choose their actions.

First — The argument from immediate experience

We call it this because the Muʿtazilites based it on something a person directly experiences within themselves.

They observed that:

“A person feels within himself that his actions follow his motives and restraints. If he wants to move, he moves; if he wants to remain still, he remains still. Whoever denies this denies something obvious and necessary. If the power that arises in the human being were not capable of bringing about what he intended, he would not experience this within himself.”383

This argument begins from an ordinary fact of everyday human life.

When a person performs an action, they experience themselves as acting because certain inner and outer reasons lead them to act. When they decide not to do something, they experience themselves as holding back because certain inner and outer reasons lead them not to do it.

In both cases, they experience themselves as choosing.

The Muʿtazilites then draw a second conclusion from this.

A person could not experience themselves in this way unless they actually had the power to perform the action they perform, or to refrain from the action they leave undone.

This basic human awareness of acting or not acting is therefore one sign that human power really exists.

And if that power exists, then human freedom of will exists as well.

When al-Shahrastānī presents this argument, he also refers to a distinction we discussed earlier: the Muʿtazilite distinction between necessary movement and voluntary movement.

Necessary movement is completely governed by an objective law independent of human will and power.

Voluntary movement, by contrast, is connected to human will and human power. It depends on the motives that lead a person toward an act and the restraints that hold them back from it.

The presence of these motives and restraints is what allows the person to choose and then decide either to act or not to act.384

Second — The argument from divine commands

This argument is based on rational reflection about the nature of religious obligation.

God addresses human beings through commands such as “Do this” and prohibitions such as “Do not do this.”

According to the Muʿtazilites, reason immediately shows that there are only two possible ways to understand such commands. If one proves impossible, the other must be correct.

The first possibility is that the human being is not capable of doing or avoiding what God commands.

But if that were true, the command itself would be foolish.

It would also be self-contradictory, because God would effectively be saying:

“Do this, you who cannot do it.”

Foolishness and contradiction cannot be attributed to God.

There is another problem with this first possibility.

A command is a request for something to be done. A request only makes sense if the person receiving it is actually capable of carrying it out.

If a person has no freedom to choose and therefore no power to fulfill the command, then the request itself becomes meaningless.

And this too cannot be attributed to God.

There is a third problem.

God’s commands are accompanied by promise and threat: the promise of reward for obedience and the threat of punishment for disobedience.

But if human beings do not possess the power and freedom to choose between obedience and disobedience, then both promise and threat become meaningless.

Reward and punishment would become meaningless as well.

Again, this cannot be attributed to God.

And there is a fourth problem.

If human beings have no choice, there would be no meaningful difference between God addressing a rational person and God addressing an inanimate object.

There would also be no difference between a command that demands something from a responsible person and a command that merely subjects something to force or demands the impossible.385

The second possibility follows from the failure of the first.

If it is impossible to say that human beings cannot carry out God’s commands because they lack freedom, then we must recognize that human beings do possess freedom of choice in the actions God commands or forbids.

That is the second possibility.

We can see that this Muʿtazilite argument from divine commands is essentially the same reasoning that lies at the foundation of their whole idea of justice.

Third — The argument from ordinary social understanding

Like the first argument, this one also begins from real human life.

It begins from the fact that people naturally understand, through ordinary practical reason, that when we give one another commands, prohibitions, praise, blame, or warnings, we assume that the person we are addressing has the freedom to choose.

Al-Shahrastānī presents the Muʿtazilite argument like this:

“Leave religious obligation aside—that is, imagine for a moment that there were no religious law. Is it not normal and familiar among us for people to address one another with commands and prohibitions, to attribute good and evil to someone who chooses freely, to ask them to perform good actions and warn them against bad ones, and then to reward or punish them accordingly?

“Anyone who denies this has stubbornly stepped outside the bounds of reason. There is no point arguing with such a person except in the way one argues with a sophist: insult him and treat him unjustly. If he becomes angry at the insult, feels pain at the injustice, and tries to defend himself or respond, then he has admitted that the person who dealt with him did something. Otherwise, why did he become angry and hurt? And why did he attribute the act to that person?

“If he tries to respond in kind, he has also admitted that the other person committed an act that deserves a corresponding response.”386

Beyond the general argument we have already described, this passage tries to force the opponent to accept the principle through his own practical behavior.

Suppose someone is debating the issue and is then harmed by an action that makes him angry or causes him pain.

If he becomes angry or feels hurt, then in practice he has already admitted that the act which caused his anger or pain was freely performed by the person who did it.

And if he then believes that person deserves some response or punishment, he has also admitted that the person was responsible for what he did.

Otherwise, why should he deserve any response at all?

We can now see how deeply the Muʿtazilites were concerned with human freedom of action, with the human capacity to use that freedom, and with the relationship between freedom and moral, social, and religious responsibility.

These questions occupied some of the deepest and widest areas of Muʿtazilite intellectual activity.

Seen in this light, we can also understand how these same concerns drew them toward their distinctive idea of justice—an idea that set them apart from the other Muslims of their time and exposed them to some of the fiercest opposition and hardship.

We can also see how the question of the human being, in all its different aspects, sometimes drew the Muʿtazilites toward starting points rooted in reality, and at times even toward positions that were materialist in the philosophical sense.

Through the force of their own logic and rationalism, the issue pulled them away from a purely metaphysical world and toward the actual natural and social world.

It also brought them close to a scientific way of thinking, despite the abstract and highly conceptual form their thought still took and despite the fact that they lacked the practical tools of experimentation that such thinking would eventually require.

There is nothing surprising about the fact that the question of the human being drew them in this direction.

The question itself had real roots. As we suggested at the beginning of this chapter, its hidden origins lay in actual social conditions.

D — Actions Generated by Human Actions

One striking feature of Muʿtazilite thought is the way its thinkers keep following a single idea or problem as far as it can go.

They constantly open up new sides of every question they examine.

Sometimes they do this in a completely abstract way. At other times their reasoning remains indirectly connected to concrete life.

A good example of the second kind is their discussion of what Muʿtazilite writings call actions generated by human actions.

Once the Muʿtazilites had established that a person is responsible for an act because it comes from that person’s own free will, their method pushed them toward a further question.

What about the actions or effects that normally follow from an act a person performs directly?

Are these later effects also created by the person because they arise from an act the person freely chose?

And if so, is the person responsible for them just as they are responsible for the original act?

At first, this may sound like a purely theoretical question, or even an exercise in abstract reasoning.

But the examples the Muʿtazilites use show that the question has an inner logic closely connected to real life.

Suppose someone strikes another person and the person who is struck feels pain.

There are now two events: the act of striking and the pain that follows.

The first clearly comes from the person who struck the blow. That person is responsible for it because they freely chose to do it.

But what about the second event—the pain produced by the blow?

Should the pain also be attributed to the person who struck, because it was generated by that person’s act?

If so, the person is responsible for the pain as well.

Or should the pain not be considered that person’s act because it was not something they did directly, in which case they would not be responsible for it?

So the real issue is not merely the abstract question of whether the second event was “created” by the person who performed the first act.

The discussion ultimately concerns real responsibility.

And in this case responsibility includes moral and social responsibility just as much as responsibility within a metaphysical framework.

The Muʿtazilite debate over generated actions therefore did not remain purely theoretical. It also had practical, legal, and social implications.

We should first ask how the Muʿtazilites defined a “generated” act, and then how they understood the responsibility that followed from it.

Different Muʿtazilite thinkers gave different definitions.

Al-Iskāfī, for example, defined it like this:

“Any act that can happen by mistake, without being deliberately intended or willed, is a generated act. Any act that can occur only through deliberate intention, and whose every part requires a renewed decision, intention, and will, falls outside the category of generated acts.”387

Other Muʿtazilites defined a generated act in other ways:

“An act that happens because of something I do, but occurs in someone or something other than myself.”

Or:

“An act whose cause I brought about, after which I can no longer prevent it.”

Or:

“An act produced by an agent indirectly, as opposed to an act performed directly.”388389

The difference between al-Iskāfī’s definition and the others is clear.

Al-Iskāfī makes it part of the definition that the generated act happens “by mistake, without being deliberately intended or willed.”

The other definitions only require that the generated act be caused by the original or direct act, whether intentionally or accidentally.

This difference matters because it affects the question of responsibility.

If an act is defined from the start as something that happens accidentally and without intention, this tends to suggest that the person who performed the original act did not “create” the later effect.

The other definitions point in the opposite direction.

They describe the later act as something that happens “because of” the first actor, whose action “brought about its cause,” or as something that “proceeds from” that actor.

This suggests that the later act should also be attributed to the person who performed the first act.

And if so, that person is responsible for it.

The Muʿtazilites also disagreed directly over responsibility itself.

The first thinker to mention here is Abū al-Hudhayl al-ʿAllāf, one of the earliest thinkers to discuss generated actions.

He distinguished between two kinds.

The first kind is generated by an action whose manner the person understands.

The second also follows from the person’s action, but the person does not understand how it occurs—for example, color, taste, smell, and similar qualities.390

Acts of the first kind count as human acts.

Acts of the second kind do not.

We find a clearer explanation of this distinction in al-Ashʿarī’s account of the Muʿtazilite position on human power.

According to this account, God gives human beings power over things whose manner they understand—such as movement, stillness, sounds, pain, and pleasure—because these are things human beings are capable of bringing about.

But God cannot give them power over things whose manner they do not understand—such as colors, tastes, life, death, and incapacity—because a human being cannot bring these things about.391

Here the phrase “cannot bring about” appears to mean simply “is unable to bring about.”

The basic distinction seems to be between things that happen through human will and things that happen without human will playing a part in their occurrence.

From a moral or legal point of view, this distinction has a clear logic.

From a philosophical point of view, however, we will shortly see that there is more to say.

Bishr ibn al-Muʿtamir, the leading Baghdad Muʿtazilite whom al-Shahrastānī describes as “one of the finest Muʿtazilite scholars” and as the thinker who introduced the doctrine of generated acts and “took it to an extreme,” held a different view.

Bishr argued:

“Color, taste, smell, and all forms of perception—including hearing and sight—can be generated by a human act if their causes come from that person’s action.”392

The meaning is clear.

If someone causes themselves or someone else to experience a sensation—such as seeing a color, tasting something, smelling something, feeling touch, or hearing a sound—then that experience can be regarded as an act produced by the person who caused it.

Everything generated by a person’s action is therefore attributed to that person because they caused it to happen.

Bishr makes no distinction here between effects in which the actor’s will directly plays a part and effects that follow without any further act of will.

So where does the difference between Abū al-Hudhayl and Bishr come from?

Al-Ashʿarī reports that Abū al-Hudhayl believed God could keep a heavy stone suspended in the air for a long time without allowing it to fall, and that the stone could remain still.

He also believed that fire and cotton could come together without the cotton burning.

Al-Ashʿarī therefore says that al-ʿAllāf “disagreed with the people of rational inquiry on this question.”393

If we take this report about al-ʿAllāf at face value, the difference between his theory of generated action and Bishr’s would seem to come from Abū al-Hudhayl’s tendency to deny the principle of causality in nature and to deny the law of motion.

But denying causality would contradict one of the two principles on which the Muʿtazilite idea of generated action—and the responsibility connected with it—was built.

One of those principles was causality.

The other was human freedom of choice.

We will see, however, that there is a mistake in understanding al-ʿAllāf’s position in this way.

Bishr ibn al-Muʿtamir, by contrast, clearly bases his view on the principle of causality.

In this respect, his position fits directly with the wider Muʿtazilite idea.

We find the same consistency in another leading Muʿtazilite thinker, al-Khayyāṭ.

Al-Khayyāṭ connects generated action directly to both the necessary causal order of nature and the law of motion.

He explains his position with two examples.

In the first, a person sends a stone rolling from the top of a mountain. The stone falls toward the ground. Suppose the person dies before the stone reaches the bottom.

The stone’s continued fall after the person’s death is still generated by the act of releasing it.

Its movement must therefore still be attributed to the person who set it in motion, and to no one else.

In the second example, a man shoots an arrow at a target and dies after the arrow has left the bow but before it reaches the target.

The arrow’s continued movement after the archer’s death is generated by his shot.

It therefore remains attributable to him and to no one else.394

In both examples, an act begun by a person continues to produce effects after that person has died.

This gives the question two sides.

One concerns purely natural causality and, as we will see, the law of motion.

The other concerns legal and moral responsibility.

For the Muʿtazilites, however, the two cannot really be separated.

If a generated act remains attributable to the person who began the original action even after that person has died, this is because that person remains the first cause of everything that follows from the original act.

This is why Abū al-Hudhayl al-ʿAllāf could say, quite literally rather than figuratively, that the dead can kill the living, healthy, and strong.395

The meaning is clear.

The Muʿtazilites base their judgment here on two principles.

The first is that events follow fixed laws of nature—in this case, the law of causality.

The second is that human beings are responsible for their own actions because they freely choose them.

That responsibility applies not only to acts they perform directly, but also to acts and effects generated by those direct acts.

And it is precisely the principle of causality that allows responsibility to extend from the first act to everything that follows from it.

There are also signs in some Muʿtazilite texts that they took the law of motion into account in this question. We see this especially in al-Khayyāṭ’s philosophical explanation of why the movement of an arrow should be attributed to the person who shot it.

Al-Khayyāṭ says that when someone shoots an arrow, its movement must be one of four things: an act of God, an act of the arrow itself, an act with no agent behind it, or an act of the person who shot it. He then argues against the first three possibilities and accepts only the fourth.

We can clearly see that his whole argument rests on the principle of necessary causation in nature, alongside the established Muʿtazilite principle that human beings freely choose their actions.

Al-Khayyāṭ rejects the idea that God causes the arrow to move on the following grounds. Human beings have the power to act and freely choose their actions. God does not enter into human actions or force people to perform them. If God were the one who caused the arrow to move, then a person could shoot an arrow and God could simply choose not to make it move. The arrow would then remain where it was. For al-Khayyāṭ, this is impossible.

We can see why he considers it impossible. An arrow failing to move after being shot would violate the law of motion, which necessarily requires it to move once it has been launched.

Al-Khayyāṭ says that if we accepted this impossibility, we would also have to accept many others. If God could choose not to make an arrow move after it had been shot, then we would also have to allow, for example, that an extremely strong person could press a sword against the back of someone’s neck, yet God might not cause the sword to cut it. Or fire could be brought into contact with esparto grass,396 yet God might not cause it to burn.

In other words, al-Khayyāṭ considers it impossible for a neck not to be cut when a sword is pressed against it with great force, or for esparto grass not to burn when it comes into contact with fire. And it is clear that these things are impossible for him because they would violate fixed laws of nature—above all the law of causation, together here with the law of motion.

Al-Khayyāṭ also rejects the second possibility: that the movement of the arrow is an act performed by the arrow itself. His reason is that an arrow is an inanimate object. It is neither alive nor capable of acting. It cannot perform an action because it has no choice, will, or knowledge.

This follows the Muʿtazilite understanding of human action, according to which an agent must possess all three: choice, will, and knowledge.

As for the third possibility—that the arrow’s movement is an act with no agent behind it—al-Khayyāṭ rejects this by saying that, if such a thing were possible, a book could exist without anyone having written it. That, he says, is impossible.397

Why is it impossible? Surely the point is that a natural event cannot occur without a cause.

E — Objective Laws in Nature

From everything we have seen so far, it appears that the Muʿtazilites came close to recognizing that nature has objective laws of its own and that natural events take place according to those laws.

We do not find a direct statement from them explicitly setting out this idea. But we do find statements on other subjects that come very close to expressing it.

We can return, for example, to our earlier discussion of the “indivisible part,” and to the different Muʿtazilite views on substance and accident. There we find attempts to understand the laws of nature in whatever way the knowledge available in their own time allowed.

Consider, too, a statement by al-Naẓẓām reported by al-Baghdādī. Al-Naẓẓām says that one kind of thing cannot produce two opposite kinds of action, just as fire cannot both heat and cool.398 In other words, each kind of body produces a particular kind of effect.

Al-Shahrastānī reports another statement by al-Naẓẓām that gives an example of how every natural body is subject to fixed laws. If a stone is pushed, it moves. Once the force of the push has run its course, the stone naturally returns to its place—that is, it does so because of its own nature.399

Taken together, these two statements show al-Naẓẓām making a serious attempt to recognize that the laws of nature exist objectively.

We find similar attempts among other thinkers as well.

Muʿammar ibn ʿAbbād al-Sulamī, for example, argues that whatever occurs in bodies—motion and rest, color and taste, smell, heat and cold, moisture and dryness—is produced by the body itself according to its nature.400

He expresses the same idea in another way when he says that an inanimate body produces the accidents that occur in it according to its own nature. Life is the action of what is alive; power is the action of what has power; and death is the action of what is dead.401

Elsewhere Muʿammar states the idea even more explicitly. He says that the movements of the heavenly bodies, along with everything in the world that moves or remains still, joins or separates, touches or moves apart, are the acts of something other than God.402

In other words, whatever happens to the heavenly bodies results from natural laws present within those bodies themselves. It does not come to them from an outside divine action.

We find similar language in al-Jāḥiẓ, who was himself a Muʿtazilite. He says, for example, that bodies have their own natures and actions specific to them.403

At first sight, a statement attributed to Abū al-Hudhayl, al-Iskāfī, and al-Jubbāʾī might seem to deny the existence of such objective laws in nature. But this impression comes from misunderstanding what they mean.

Al-Ashʿarī reports that these three thinkers said it was possible for a heavy stone to remain together with the air for some time without God creating its descent or fall, so that it remained still. They also said that fire and cotton could be brought together without burning taking place.404

Does this mean that they denied the natural law that makes a heavy stone fall through the air, or the law that makes combustible material such as cotton burn when it comes into contact with fire?

We do not think so.

Their point is that these natural laws do not necessarily produce their effects immediately. Another natural factor may temporarily prevent the expected result.

This is how we understand the phrase “for some time” in the passage reported by al-Ashʿarī. The statement does not say without qualification that a heavy stone can remain in the air without falling, or that fire can touch cotton without burning it. It places a limit on this possibility: it can happen only for a period of time.

And in scientific terms, such a situation can indeed last for a certain period. In the case of the stone, this is the interval between its upward movement and its fall. In the case of fire, it is the period during which some natural cause delays the fire’s effect.

So here we have examples from major Muʿtazilite thinkers that show very early attempts within Arab-Islamic thought to recognize objective laws of nature. These attempts came before the age of practical scientific discoveries, when the existence of such laws could be demonstrated directly through experiment.

These examples also reveal early expressions of materialism within Arab-Islamic metaphysical thought during its great flowering in the Muʿtazilite period.

We might even say that these expressions represent a particular historical form of materialism—one shaped by the conditions of medieval Arab-Islamic society.

F — Causality: Between Determinism and Freedom

We said earlier that, for the Muʿtazilites, there was no separation between necessary causation in nature and the responsibility that follows from causation in human social life.

We should also remember that, in their view, human responsibility rests on freedom of the will. Their refusal to separate objective necessity from human freedom therefore shows a striking rational insight. In an early and undeveloped form, it points toward an awareness of the dialectical relationship between “necessity and freedom.”

But we should not take this too far.

The Muʿtazilites made a basic and important distinction between causes in nature and causes in human society. Natural processes operate through mechanical necessity, while human actions include an additional element: the will.

This follows from one of the most basic principles of Muʿtazilite thought: human beings freely choose their actions.

They believed that human beings alone possess reason in the special sense that matters here. Reason gives us the ability to compare different possibilities, choose the one we think is best, will that choice, and then act on it. This is why the Muʿtazilites hold human beings responsible for their actions in both morality and metaphysics.

Because they distinguish so sharply between natural causes and human causes, they also understand the relationship between cause and effect differently depending on the kind of action involved.

When an action comes directly from a person’s will and freedom of choice, the connection between cause and effect is immediate. A voluntary act has only one direct cause: the first cause in which will is joined to the practical ability to act, which the Muʿtazilites call istiṭāʿa, or capacity.

But once other actions are generated by that first act, the relationship changes. The same is true of all involuntary actions, including the processes of nature.

In such cases, the connection between the first voluntary cause and the later involuntary effects remains in place, no matter how many intermediate causes and effects appear between them. The first cause, which began in the human will, continues to stand behind a series of later effects even though the intermediate causes themselves contain no element of will.

The example of the arrow makes this clearer.

Here we find both kinds of action. First there is the voluntary act: the action that comes directly from the will of the person shooting the arrow. This is the act of shooting.

Then there are the actions generated by that first act—for example, the arrow striking one target or another even though the archer did not intend to hit it.

The act of shooting itself is voluntary because it follows directly from a voluntary cause. What comes after it does not follow directly from the will and is therefore not voluntary.

Voluntary causation is limited to the act produced directly by the will. It does not extend in the same way to all the later events produced by that act.

Yet those later events do not lose their connection with the first cause—the original act of shooting. The connection simply changes in character. From that point on, the events follow the necessary principle of causation that governs nature, rather than the kind of causation that governs voluntary human action.

In short, a cause in nature can produce a whole chain of successive effects. Its connection with the final effect remains in place no matter how many other natural causes and effects come between them.

A voluntary human cause, by contrast, has only one direct effect: the act produced immediately by the will.

Once that act produces further effects, those effects belong to the other category. They become natural events governed by necessary causation rather than by the will.

Abū al-Hudhayl al-ʿAllāf expressed this Muʿtazilite position by saying that a person’s “acts of the heart cannot exist when capacity is absent. Capacity accompanies them at the moment of the act.”405

By “acts of the heart,” he means voluntary acts.

His point, then, is that voluntary action can exist only where the person has the power to carry it out. And that power exists at the moment the action is performed—when the will is actually being put into effect.

Anything that happens after that original act and is generated by it has moved beyond the agent’s direct power, because it has moved beyond the agent’s will. From that point on, it is governed only by the natural laws of motion.

Abū al-Hudhayl calls these generated or involuntary actions “acts of the limbs,” as opposed to “acts of the heart.”

Al-Shahrastānī says that Abū al-Hudhayl allowed “acts of the limbs” to proceed from a human being even when direct capacity was no longer present—that is, even when the will was no longer controlling those acts. He also says that Abū al-Hudhayl regarded the capacity as coming before them.406

What this means is that, for acts of the limbs, it is enough that will or capacity existed earlier, together with the first act that generated the later ones.

This is the basis on which the Muʿtazilites hold people responsible not only for their first voluntary act but also for the actions generated by it, as we saw earlier in our discussion of actions generated by human action.

Al-Iskāfī gives an even clearer distinction between voluntary and generated acts.

He describes a voluntary act as “every act that can take place only through intention, and whose every part requires renewed resolve, intention toward it, and will for it. Such an act lies outside the category of generation and within the category of direct action.”

A generated act, by contrast, is “every act that may occur by mistake, without intention toward it or will for it.”407

On the same question, Muʿammar says that “the human being has no act except the will, whether directly or by generation.”408

So Muʿammar includes generated actions within voluntary action, unlike al-ʿAllāf and al-Iskāfī.

Thumāma ibn Ashras al-Numayrī, a Baghdad Muʿtazilite who died in 213 AH/828 CE, also distinguishes between voluntary acts and generated acts. But he argues that “generated acts have no agent.”

Al-Shahrastānī explains why. Thumāma could not attribute a generated act to the person who caused it, because that would sometimes force him to attribute an action to someone who was already dead. A person might perform the original act, die, and only afterward would the generated effect occur.

Nor could Thumāma attribute the generated act to God, because that could mean attributing an evil act to God, which he considered impossible.

So, al-Shahrastānī says, Thumāma was left without an answer and concluded: “Generated acts are acts with no agent.”409

Al-Jāḥiẓ, by contrast, followed the Muʿtazilite position associated with al-ʿAllāf. He distinguished voluntary action from necessary natural action by saying that a human being has no act other than the will, while all other accidents are actions that bodies produce according to their own nature.410

In other words, these are actions governed by necessary, objective laws of nature.

Al-Aswārī, one of al-Naẓẓām’s followers, held a view that was not fundamentally different from that of al-ʿAllāf and others who followed the same path. But al-Aswārī used a different way of defining voluntary action—that is, human action.

While discussing the limits of God’s power, he says that God cannot be described as having the power to do something He knows He will not do, or something He has said He will not do. A human being, however, can have such power, because “the servant’s power extends to both opposites.”411

What he means is that a person’s knowledge does not remove freedom of choice.

Before choosing between two opposite actions, a person is capable of doing either one. This remains true whether the person knows that he will do something or knows that he will not do it.

For the followers of al-Naẓẓām, this is another expression of human freedom in action.

When it comes to nature, however, they accept the Muʿtazilite idea that natural events are governed by objective and necessary laws, even though al-Naẓẓām ultimately traces those laws back to a divine source.

Al-Shahrastānī reports a statement transmitted by al-Kaʿbī—Abū al-Qāsim ibn Muḥammad al-Balkhī, a Baghdad Muʿtazilite who died in 319 AH/931 CE—in which al-Naẓẓām says:

“Every act that goes beyond the limit of human capacity”—meaning human power and will—“is an act of God through the necessity built into creation. God gave the stone a nature and created it in such a way that, when someone pushes it and the force of the push has run its course, it naturally returns to its place.”412

This clearly shows al-Naẓẓām recognizing that natural events take place according to general and necessary laws, such as the law of causation and the law of motion.

PreviousChapter FiveNextThe Muʿtazilite Theory of Knowledge

The Muʿtazilite Theory of Knowledge

Muʿtazilite Justice and Knowledge

The Muʿtazilites believed that human beings are unique among living beings because they can freely choose their actions. They also believed that reason is what gives human beings this freedom.

It was therefore natural for them to ask how people acquire knowledge, what part reason plays in the process, how far reason can reach, what different kinds of knowledge exist, what means we have for acquiring each kind, how each kind is acquired, and how much value we should place on knowledge gained in one way rather than another.

These questions form part of the foundations of the Muʿtazilite doctrine of justice.

The wider and deeper the powers of human reason are, and the more knowledge reason can attain, the stronger the Muʿtazilite case for their doctrine of justice becomes.

So how did they approach the problem?

To give the question reasonably full treatment, we can follow the traditional division of knowledge into two main kinds: sensory knowledge and rational knowledge.

This division remains logically useful, and it also matches the way the Muʿtazilites themselves approached the subject.

1 — Sensory Knowledge

The Muʿtazilite discussion of sensory knowledge is closely connected to their extensive debates about the human soul or spirit: its relationship with the body, its relationship with the five sense organs, the relationship of those senses to one another, and the part each sense plays in knowledge.

Their accounts of the soul or spirit differed greatly. As a result, they also disagreed about the part it plays in sensation and perception—that is, in knowledge.

Al-Naẓẓām’s Theory

The first name that stands out here is Ibrāhīm al-Naẓẓām, because he discussed the subject at great length.

We have already seen that al-Naẓẓām identifies the human being with the soul or spirit. He says that the soul penetrates the body and is interwoven with it so completely that, as he puts it, “every part of this is with every part of that.” In other words, every part of the soul is present with every part of the body.

But he also regards the body as an impediment to the soul.

Al-Ashʿarī reports a statement that Zurqān attributed to al-Naẓẓām: “The soul is what senses and perceives. It is one single thing, and it is neither light nor darkness.”413

If this statement really belongs to al-Naẓẓām, we can draw an important conclusion from it. The soul would then be the source of every power of sensation and perception, including the power to perceive the outside world through the senses.

But the surviving reports about al-Naẓẓām’s view of the relationship between soul and body are themselves inconsistent.

In one place, al-Ashʿarī reports him as saying that “the spirit is the body and is the soul.”414

Al-Shahrastānī, however, reports him as saying:

“The human being in the true sense is the soul and the spirit, while the body is its instrument and its mould.”

Al-Shahrastānī adds that al-Naẓẓām leaned toward the view of the natural philosophers, according to which the soul is a subtle body interwoven with the physical body. It enters into the body in every part, “as water enters the rose, oil enters sesame, and fat enters milk.”415

Looking across the different statements attributed to al-Naẓẓām in our sources, it seems that his basic position is still a dualism between soul and body, despite the extremely close interpenetration he describes between them.

What matters for us here, however, is his view of where sensory perception comes from.

From what we have already seen, we can conclude that al-Naẓẓām describes the soul as “what senses and perceives.” If the soul is different from the body, and if the soul is what senses and perceives, then it follows that he does not recognize the bodily senses as independent powers of perception.

On this view, it is the soul—not the body—that perceives sensible things through the openings we call the ear, mouth, nose, and eye.

A person does not possess a faculty of hearing separate from himself, or a faculty of sight separate from himself. Rather, the person hears through the self and may become deaf because of some defect affecting him. Likewise, he sees through the self and may become blind because of some defect affecting him.416

So according to this account, a person does not have a separate faculty of hearing apart from the soul, which for al-Naẓẓām is the person himself. The same is true of sight.

A human being hears and sees through the soul alone. If he becomes deaf or blind, the deafness or blindness affects the soul itself because of some defect that has affected the human being—that is, the soul.

The physical organs that we normally call the five sense organs are therefore only openings or channels. The soul uses them as routes through which it reaches the things it perceives.

The soul “leaps” through the opening of the eye toward the object being seen, enters into contact with it, and comes alongside it. In the same way, it leaps through the opening of the ear, meets the sound and joins with it, and thus hears it. The same applies to smell and taste.417

Sensory knowledge, then, is for al-Naẓẓām an internal function of the soul. It is not produced by the external bodily organs that we normally call the five senses.

This also helps explain his view that the senses are not different powers in themselves. They all operate through a single power.

Al-Jāḥiẓ describes the view in these words: the senses “belong to one kind. The sense of sight is of the same kind as the sense of hearing and all the other senses. The difference lies only in the kind of thing perceived and in the locations of the senses. There is no other difference between them.”418

If the soul itself is the source of all sensory knowledge, then it follows naturally that the senses belong to one kind, because the soul itself is one.

But how can this explain the obvious differences between our senses? Hearing is clearly different from sight, and both are different from smell, taste, and touch.

The statement from al-Jāḥiẓ points toward an answer.

What differs, on this view, is not the senses themselves. The difference comes from two things.

The first is the kind of object being perceived.

The second is the location through which the soul perceives things in the outside world.

Al-Naẓẓām himself explains what he means by the obstacles involved. He says:

“What prevents hearing from perceiving color is something mixed with it, an obstruction of the same kind as darkness, which prevents the perception of color but not the perception of sound. What prevents sight from perceiving sounds is something mixed with it of the same kind as glass, which prevents the perception of sound but not the perception of color.”

Al-Naẓẓām used this same idea to explain the different obstacles and obstructions affecting the various senses and the openings through which they operate.419

So hearing, sight, and the other senses all come from one power: the power of the soul or spirit.

By its own nature, this power would be capable of hearing color or seeing sound. What prevents it from doing so are obstacles that do not belong to the soul’s own nature.

The sensory faculty as a whole is surrounded by different kinds of obstacles. Each sense is affected by a different kind of obstacle.

Things in the outside world also have many different qualities, and these qualities affect the senses in different ways. A sense therefore responds only to those qualities that are not blocked by the particular obstacles affecting it.

What, then, can we conclude from al-Naẓẓām’s explanation of how we sense the external world—in other words, of sensory knowledge?

It seems to us that his account ultimately turns what we call sensory knowledge into a kind of rational perception. The main difference is simply that sensory knowledge deals with the qualities of things in the outside world.

The bodily senses themselves are little more than channels through which those qualities pass. Through them, the sensible object affects the perceiver, who is the soul—that is, the human being.

All of this leads us to accept the view that al-Naẓẓām and al-Jāḥiẓ were influenced here by Aristotle’s account of sensory knowledge.420

Aristotle says that the soul perceives through these openings and channels. They become different senses—one hearing, another sight, another smell—because of the different obstacles mixed with them. But the underlying faculty that senses does not itself differ. If it did, the different senses would obstruct and destroy one another, just as different and opposing things do.421

Al-Naẓẓām’s overall position clearly rests on his belief that the human being is the soul or spirit, while the body is only a temporary dwelling or mould for it. This is why he assigns all the functions of sensation and perception directly to the soul.

Yet al-Naẓẓām also made another attempt to explain sensory knowledge, this time by looking at the interaction between the thing perceived and the faculty that perceives it.

He says:

“Sight perceives colors because color is transmitted from the perceived object. If there were more of it, its effect would be stronger; and if it became excessive, we would no longer perceive any color at all.”422

This does not overturn his earlier position about the source of sensation in the perceiver.

We can say instead that his earlier account explained sensory knowledge from one side of the process: the perceiver, meaning the soul.

This later statement approaches the same process from the other side: the object being perceived.

His earlier treatment had a clearly metaphysical character. Here, however, we see a more physical approach with a significant materialist content.

Al-Naẓẓām is now trying to identify what determines whether sensible things affect our senses and how strongly they do so. To explain this, he turns to physical features of the things themselves.

He believes that the amount of color present in visible things—whether there is little or much of it—determines the strength of its effect on the senses. The same principle applies to sound, smell, taste, and the other things perceived by the different senses.

We should connect this view of the “amount” of color, sound, smell, and taste with al-Naẓẓām’s theory of accidents.

He is known for denying the existence of accidents in general. In his view, the only true accident is motion.

What other thinkers call accidents are, for al-Naẓẓām, actually very fine bodies emitted by natural things. He regards “colors, tastes, smells, sounds, pains, heat, cold, moisture, and dryness as subtle bodies.”423

This is why al-Ashʿarī says that, according to al-Naẓẓām, “nothing is seen except a body, and nothing is heard except a body, because sounds are bodies for him. Likewise, nothing is tasted, smelled, or touched except a body.”424

Al-Shahrastānī gives a useful example of this part of al-Naẓẓām’s theory:

“Al-Naẓẓām held that speech is a subtle body emitted by the speaker. It strikes the particles of air, causing the air to move in waves and take on its form. It then strikes the nerve spread through the ear, which takes on the same form. From there it reaches the imagination and is presented to rational thought, which understands it.”425

We can apply the same reasoning to color, taste, and smell.

It is clear that al-Naẓẓām’s conclusions here are not very far from some of the results reached by modern experimental science in the physical sciences.

But the same example also reveals another side of his theory of knowledge.

It gives us a clear picture of how he imagines the stages of knowledge unfolding one after another: beginning with the direct effect of sensible things on the nerves of the senses and ending with the final stage, where those effects enter the realm of rational knowledge.

From this we can conclude that the direct object of sensory knowledge is the external world: a world made up of natural bodies with a real, objective existence.

That same external world also becomes, in the end, the indirect object of rational knowledge.

But does al-Naẓẓām believe that the external world is the only object of rational knowledge?

We will answer that question when we turn to Muʿtazilite views on rational knowledge.

For now, what we can conclude is that sensory knowledge can give us knowledge that the thinking mind can then use.

Our final conclusion from al-Naẓẓām’s views on sensory knowledge is that, taken as a whole, they contain two almost opposing sides.

One is purely metaphysical. This appears in his view of the powers of sensory perception. He locates these powers entirely in the soul or spirit, while separating soul from body and treating their relationship in dualistic terms.

The other side is materialist. We see it in his account of the nature of sensible things and the way they affect the senses.

If we use the language of Marxist philosophical writing, we can say that al-Naẓẓām’s theory of sensory knowledge as a whole represents one historical form of “objective idealism.”

The same description may also apply to many other Muʿtazilite ideas and theories.

This becomes clearer when we remember that the great majority of Muʿtazilite thinkers begin from the view that the body is an objective natural reality. They also accept that bodies physically affect the sources of sensation and the centers of perception in human beings, even though their understanding of those sources and centers is usually metaphysical.

The Theory of al-ʿAllāf and Muʿammar

Abū al-Hudhayl al-ʿAllāf and Muʿammar ibn ʿAbbād al-Sulamī, two leading figures among the Basra Muʿtazilites, believed that the five human senses are accidents distinct from the body.426

This view makes the connection between soul and body an accidental one.

Al-Naẓẓām’s position, by contrast, makes the connection essential, since he describes soul and body as penetrating and interweaving with one another “as water enters the rose, oil enters sesame, and fat enters milk,” or as he says elsewhere, “every part of this is with every part of that.”

The essential character of this relationship becomes clearer when we remember that al-Naẓẓām traces the senses themselves back to the soul. As we saw earlier, this follows from his denial of all accidents except motion.

There is another difference between al-ʿAllāf and al-Naẓẓām.

Al-ʿAllāf says that the senses belong to different kinds. Al-Naẓẓām, by contrast, treats them as belonging to one kind.

Al-ʿAllāf explains his position by saying:

“Each sense is different from the others, but we do not say that it is opposed to them, because opposition is difference through a contrary quality.”427

His point is that the senses differ from one another, but they are not in conflict. They are simply distinct and multiple.

Al-Ashʿarī describes the same idea and attributes it to the Muʿtazilites in general:

“The senses belong to different kinds, but they are not opposed. Hearing belongs to a different kind from sight, and the same applies to every sense: its kind is different from the kinds of all the other senses. Despite these differences, the senses are accidents distinct from the one who senses.”428

But what exactly does this difference mean?

It means that each sense differs according to the kind of effect that sensible things have on it. Each sense responds to the qualities that suit it.

Sight, for example, responds to color because color is the quality suited to sight. Hearing responds to sound because sound is suited to hearing, and so on.

Here we can see the basic difference between this view and al-Naẓẓām’s.

For al-Naẓẓām, sight would by its own nature be capable of hearing sound were it not for outside obstructions that prevent it from doing so. Likewise, hearing would be capable of seeing color were it not for a different set of obstructions.

The statements of al-ʿAllāf, Muʿammar, and the Muʿtazilites who agreed with them clearly show that they accepted the possibility of knowledge through the senses.

But because they distinguish between substance and accident, and accept the existence of accidents, they argue that only accidents can be objects of sensory knowledge.

Sensory knowledge cannot reach substances themselves. Substances lie beyond what the senses can perceive.

Muʿammar also tries to explain how the senses perceive sensible things—that is, sensible accidents—and how the effect of those things becomes sensation.

His explanation leads him to treat sensory knowledge as an event that is generated necessarily when sensible things affect us.

He says:

“The perception of sensible things does not occur by choice. It is an act of nature.”429

In other words, perception does not happen because the senses choose it. It follows necessarily from their own nature.

When the human senses are exposed to the effects of sensible accidents in bodies, they respond involuntarily. They have no choice in the matter. Their own nature requires this response, and the response becomes sensation.

Sensation—or sensory knowledge—is therefore generated in human beings by a necessary natural law in which the will plays no part.

This is also what Muʿammar means when he says:

“Generated acts, and whatever occurs in bodies—motion and rest, color and taste, smell, heat and cold, moisture and dryness—are acts of the body in which they occur, according to its own nature.”430

There is therefore no basic difference between sensation generated in a human being through contact with sensible things and any other natural event governed by necessary laws of nature rather than by the will.

This view seems to rest on Muʿammar’s rejection of the idea that God directly causes sensation.

As we saw earlier, Muʿammar regards the senses as accidents, and he holds that God does not produce accidents.

He therefore says:

“God does not produce an accident and is not described as having power over an accident, or over life, death, hearing, or sight. Hearing is the act of the one who hears, sight is the act of the one who sees, and sensation is the act of the one who senses.”431

For Muʿammar, life itself is an accident,432 as are death and the other things listed in this passage.

He tries to prove that accidents—and for him all the natural actions of bodies are accidents—are not acts of God and are not things over which God can be described as exercising direct power.

To do this, he uses a logical argument based on color, which is one of the accidents of a natural body.

He says:

“Either it belongs to the nature of a body to become colored, or it does not. If it belongs to its nature to become colored, then color must follow from the body’s own nature and is therefore the body’s own act. Something that follows from a thing’s own nature cannot at the same time depend on something else, just as what a thing acquires for itself cannot be the creation of another.

“But if it does not belong to the body’s nature to become colored, then God could color it and yet it might not become colored.”433

In this final sentence, Muʿammar means that if color did not arise naturally from the body itself, it would have to come from God.

But that creates, in his view, an unacceptable possibility. God might will the body to become colored, while the body—because of a natural law—failed to become colored. What actually happened would then differ from what God had willed.

For Muʿammar, that is impossible.

So according to his logical argument, color must arise from the natural activity of the body itself.

The same idea of generated action also appears in Muʿtazilite discussions of sensory perception among the Baghdad school.

One of its most important supporters was Bishr ibn al-Muʿtamir, the founder of the Baghdad Muʿtazilite school, who died in 226 AH/841 CE.

He says:

“A human being can produce perceptions through generation when he produces their causes.”434

By “produces their causes,” we think he means that a person deliberately exposes his senses to sensible things. Sensation, or sensory perception, is then generated.

Sensation is therefore a generated act: a natural and involuntary event preceded by a voluntary cause, namely the person’s deliberate decision to expose the senses to something capable of producing sensation.

To sum up, this group of Muʿtazilites understands sensory knowledge as arising through two successive and connected stages.

First, the accidents of a body affect the senses.

Second, sensation—or sensory perception—is generated by that effect.

Both stages take place through necessary natural processes. But they may be preceded by a voluntary cause: the person deliberately exposing the senses to the qualities of natural bodies that can affect them.

Abū al-Hudhayl al-ʿAllāf agrees with Muʿammar ibn ʿAbbād in distinguishing substance from accident, in accepting the existence of accidents, and in holding that accidents alone can be objects of sensory knowledge. Substances themselves, for both thinkers, can be known only through reason.

But al-ʿAllāf disagrees with Muʿammar’s explanation of sensory knowledge as a generated act ultimately attributable to the person who senses.

Here al-ʿAllāf takes a purely metaphysical position. He explains the transformation of sensible accidents into sensation, or sensory knowledge, as an act of God.

This is what we understand from the report of al-Ashʿarī, which is our only source for al-ʿAllāf’s position.

Al-Ashʿarī says:

“Abū al-Hudhayl held that pleasure, color, tastes, smells, heat, cold, cowardice, courage, perception, and knowledge that arises in another person as a result of his action—all of these, according to Abū al-Hudhayl, are acts of God.”435

Returning to al-Naẓẓām

At this point we need to return to al-Naẓẓām.

In al-Ashʿarī’s Maqālāt, we find a statement attributed to him that differs from the view of sensory knowledge we discussed earlier. In this statement, he combines Muʿammar’s idea that sensation is generated through a necessary natural process with al-ʿAllāf’s idea that sensation—the transformation of an external effect into sensory perception—comes about through divine action.

Al-Naẓẓām says here that both the movement of a stone as it falls or rises and the occurrence of perception are acts of God operating through a natural law.

A stone “moves when someone pushes it, falls when someone throws it downward, and rises when someone throws it upward. Perception is the same. All of this is an act of God through the necessity built into creation. This means that God gave the stone a nature such that, when someone pushes it, it moves. The same applies to all other generated things.”436

This view agrees completely with the statement of al-Jāḥiẓ, al-Naẓẓām’s student, that all forms of knowledge arise necessarily through nature and that none of them are acts performed by human beings.437

But if we accept this later statement from al-Naẓẓām, can we really say that it reconciles Muʿammar’s explanation of sensory knowledge with al-ʿAllāf’s?

It seems to us that al-Naẓẓām does not succeed in reconciling the two opposing views.

In fact, his solution conflicts with both.

On one side, it conflicts with Muʿammar, who completely rejects divine intervention in the production of perception.

On the other, it conflicts with al-ʿAllāf, who rejects the idea that any natural law stands between the effect of a sensible object and the sensation or perception that arises in a human being. Al-ʿAllāf makes that transformation an act of God alone.

The Limits of Sensory Knowledge

We have seen where sensory knowledge begins in Muʿtazilite theory.

We now need to ask where it ends. In other words, how far can sensory knowledge take us in discovering the truths of the universe, the truth about God, and the nature of existence?

Our earlier discussion showed that the Muʿtazilites agree that sensory knowledge deals only with things that can be sensed—that is, with the material world.

This means that the senses reach their limit as soon as we confront realities whose objects are not material.

This is the starting point for the Muʿtazilite rejection of the idea that God can be seen with the eyes in the afterlife.

Their rejection follows from the first of their five principles: divine unity.

At its core, this principle rejects anything that would make God resemble material things.438

Since sight perceives only colors and shapes, and colors and shapes are material, the Muʿtazilites unanimously deny that God can be seen with the eyes in the next world.

Abū al-Hudhayl and most Muʿtazilites nevertheless said: “We see God with our hearts, meaning that we know Him with our hearts.”439

Here “knowledge” could mean rational knowledge or intuitive knowledge. Either way, it is not sensory knowledge.

But how can we know God through reason?

We will come to that question shortly.

For now, the conclusion is that sensory knowledge cannot, for the Muʿtazilites, provide a path to knowledge of God.

But why can it not provide a path to all other philosophical and cosmic truths—for example, the truth of existence, substances, and essences?

We can find the answer by returning to some of their arguments against seeing God with the eyes.

One of those arguments says that God is a pure substance, stripped of every accident—a simple and immaterial being.

Since substance itself cannot be seen with the eyes, they argue, God cannot be seen with the eyes either. To say otherwise would amount to attributing accidents to God, which they regard as impossible because it directly contradicts their claim that He is pure substance.

From this argument we can conclude that the senses, including sight, are also incapable of perceiving substances.

Their reason is that sight, for example, can be affected only by colors and shapes. But colors and shapes are accidents, not substances.

The same applies to the other senses.

Essences—what things are in themselves—are likewise simple, universal, and abstract. How, then, could the senses perceive them?

The same is true of “existence” when we mean existence in the universal and all-encompassing sense.

It follows that, for the Muʿtazilites, sensory knowledge cannot take us beyond the external world insofar as that world is made up of material things that can be sensed.

Yet although sensory knowledge cannot perceive what lies beyond the material and sensible, the Muʿtazilites still accept what the senses tell us within the material world. They treat sensory knowledge as a valid way of knowing that world.

At the same time, they also speak about the errors that often occur in sensation—what modern scientific language calls the deception of the senses.

Al-Naẓẓām, for example, says that bodies do not remain permanently the same but are renewed from moment to moment, even though the senses tell us otherwise.

He says of this: “The observer imagines that there is one single thing continuing unchanged.”440

This is an acknowledgment that what actually happens in the material world—the constant renewal of bodies one after another—can differ from what the senses tell us, namely that bodies remain continuously the same.

Does this mean that al-Naẓẓām rejects the idea that sensory knowledge is a valid way of knowing the external world?

We have no direct statement from him that clearly answers this question.

Dr Albert Nasri Nader attributes to al-Naẓẓām the view that the error lies in the imagination rather than in sensation itself, because sensation cannot be wrong.441

Dr Nader does not give a source for this claim. He may have inferred it from al-Naẓẓām’s statement that “the observer imagines…”—in particular, from the word “imagines.”

We doubt that al-Naẓẓām intended this meaning.

But even if we accept that the word can bear the meaning Dr Nader gives it, the first part of al-Naẓẓām’s statement says that “the senses judge otherwise.” Here al-Naẓẓām himself attributes the mistaken judgment to the senses, not to the imagination.

As for Dr Nader’s interpretation of this passage—that al-Naẓẓām means “the error of the senses here is an error in the whole, that is, in all judgments about particular things”—this reading likewise has no basis in al-Naẓẓām himself.

In any case, everything we have seen about sensory knowledge among the Muʿtazilites leads us back to the conclusion we reached earlier: in general, the Muʿtazilites accepted sensory knowledge as a valid way of knowing the external world.

B — Rational Knowledge

By now it should be clear that the Muʿtazilites gave reason the highest place in the foundations of their system, and in the principles from which Muʿtazilite thought as a whole developed.

Their belief in human freedom of will is, at its core, one creative application of their basic view of reason. The same is true of the issue known in Muʿtazilite writings as “the question of rational good and evil,” which we will examine later in this study.

In fact, almost every question raised by the changing life of Arab-Islamic society in the Muʿtazilite period—whether it concerned doctrine, religious law, or human life—was approached by the Muʿtazilites through reason. They relied on reason to judge these questions, both in theory and in practice.

By now, this should be familiar enough that we do not need to spend much more time establishing it. What we need instead is to define, as far as the surviving Muʿtazilite sources allow us, what they meant by reason and by rational knowledge.

The first questions we face are these:

What is reason in Muʿtazilite theory? What does it do? And what are the limits of its ability to know?

1 — Reason and Its Function

The sources give us only a small number of passages in which the Muʿtazilites directly define reason. Even so, we can build up a broader picture from the many ways they apply reason when dealing with different problems.

The few direct definitions that have survived are concise and remarkably precise. They are enough to tell us a great deal. We also find many practical examples among Muʿtazilite thinkers, especially when they discuss things that cannot be known directly through the senses. These examples make it quite clear what they mean by reason, particularly when they speak about its role in knowledge.

We have two main definitions of reason before us. One comes from Abū al-Hudhayl al-ʿAllāf, and the other from Abū ʿAlī Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Wahhāb al-Jubbāʾī, a Basran Muʿtazilite who died in 303 AH/915 CE.

Al-Ashʿarī preserves al-ʿAllāf’s definition in three statements that complete one another and together form a single picture.

According to this definition, reason is “the power to acquire knowledge.” It is also “the power by which a person distinguishes himself from all other things.” And, he says, “we distinguish one thing from another through reason. We call sensory knowledge ‘reason’ only in the sense that it is something understood by reason.”442

As we can see, this definition covers several things at once: what reason is capable of doing, how it works, what its role in knowledge actually is, what kinds of things it can know, and what kind of knowledge it produces.

First, reason is described as “the power to acquire knowledge.”

In Muʿtazilite terms, this means that reason can draw a universal idea from particular cases. As we have already seen, this is what the Muʿtazilites mean by knowledge.

If knowledge means discovering what a number of particular things of the same kind have in common, and then turning that shared feature into a general abstract concept, then reason is the power that allows a human being to make this discovery and carry out this transformation.

So this first part of the definition begins to tell us what reason does.

The second part takes us further. It says that reason is “the power by which a person distinguishes himself from all other things.”

This means, first, that a person becomes aware of himself. He then discovers what separates him from other things, and therefore what kind of relationship exists between the human self and the rest of existence.

From there, he can also discover the relationships between things themselves. As the third part of the definition says, we distinguish one thing from another “through reason.”

This gives us the second aspect of the definition: the function of reason.

The third aspect concerns the things that rational knowledge deals with.

From the definition, we can see that rational knowledge deals with abstract universals, with the self, with the relationship between the self and other things, and with the relationships between things themselves.

It also deals with “sensory knowledge,” which, as the definition says, we call reason only in the sense that it has been understood by reason.

This adds another function: reason turns sensory perception into abstract rational understanding.

The fourth aspect concerns the nature of rational knowledge itself.

The phrase “acquire knowledge” tells us that, for the Muʿtazilites, human knowledge is acquired through a person’s own activity and choice. It is not recollection, as Plato claimed. Nor is it instinctive or something that simply appears by necessity.

Its only instrument is reason.

So in the end, Abū al-Hudhayl’s definition is less a definition of the essence of reason than a description of these four aspects of it.

Now let us look at al-Jubbāʾī’s definition:

“Reason is knowledge. It is called reason because through it a person restrains himself from things that a madman does not restrain himself from. The word is taken from the hobble used on a camel, which is called an ʿiqāl because it restrains the camel.”443

This differs from the earlier definition in two ways.

First, al-Jubbāʾī says that “reason is knowledge” itself. Al-ʿAllāf, by contrast, says that reason is “the power to acquire knowledge.”

The difference is clear and important.

If reason is the power by which knowledge is acquired, then knowledge is the result produced by that power. But if reason is knowledge itself, then reason is no longer the tool that leads us to rational knowledge. It becomes the knowledge produced by the process.

There is one possible exception. Al-Jubbāʾī might be using the word “knowledge” to mean the act of knowing—the process by which knowledge is acquired—rather than knowledge as the final result.

But this seems unlikely, because if that were what he meant, the definition would no longer really define anything.

The second difference is that al-Jubbāʾī points to a practical function of reason. Reason guides a person’s conduct.

Al-ʿAllāf’s definition does not mention this.

Alongside these two definitions, al-Ashʿarī gives us a third, which he attributes to the Muʿtazilites in general rather than to any particular thinker.

It is almost identical to the first part of Abū al-Hudhayl’s definition:

Reason is “the power within a human being that enables him to acquire knowledge.”444

We can therefore say that Abū al-Hudhayl’s definition expressed the general Muʿtazilite view of reason and rational knowledge in much the way we have just described.

2 — “Knowledge” of God

Does everything we have said mean that knowledge of God falls outside rational knowledge and outside the work of reason, since none of the three definitions openly mentions it?

The answer lies in the kind of reason these definitions are describing.

They are concerned with theoretical reason—reason as “the power to acquire knowledge” through reflection and argument.

But in Muʿtazilite theory, theoretical reason belongs to the final stage of rational knowledge. The Muʿtazilites first divide rational knowledge into two kinds, and then place these within different stages.

Abū al-Hudhayl al-ʿAllāf, for example, says:

“Knowledge is of two kinds. One is necessary knowledge: knowledge of God and knowledge of the evidence that leads to knowledge of Him. Everything beyond these, whether it comes from the senses or from reasoning by analogy, is knowledge acquired by choice.”445

This second kind is what we mean by theoretical knowledge, and it is the kind discussed in the definitions above.

Knowledge of God, by contrast, is classed by the Muʿtazilites as necessary knowledge. It is not produced through deliberate choice and acquisition, but through what they regard as the immediate self-evidence of reason.

In other words, it does not arise by turning sensory perceptions into rational concepts, nor through a process of abstraction based on logical argument and purely theoretical reflection.

The “evidence that leads to knowledge” of God rests on necessary or self-evident rational evidence, rather than on theoretical reasoning.

The Muʿtazilites also place knowledge of basic moral principles—such as good and evil and the virtues—among these forms of necessary knowledge.

From this we can see that, whatever kind of knowledge is involved—necessary or acquired, self-evident or theoretical—the final authority is reason alone.

They say, for example, that knowing God is required by reason.

Even the judgment that a person is obliged to know God therefore comes from reason itself. In this matter, reason is the authority they follow, not consensus and not scriptural verses.446

Al-Shahrastānī confirms this conclusion when he says that the Muʿtazilites

“agreed that the foundations of knowledge and gratitude toward the Benefactor [God] are obligatory before revelation is heard.”447

In other words, they are obligatory even before divine commands and prohibitions are revealed.

The difference between necessary knowledge and theoretical knowledge is therefore only a difference in the level at which reason operates, or in the kind of rational understanding involved.

This follows from the way the Muʿtazilites arrange the stages of rational knowledge.

Abū al-Hudhayl al-ʿAllāf describes these stages through the example of a child.

At the earliest stage, the child knows himself through the senses. He notices that he has a body and a self, and that he experiences sensations through his body.

At the second stage, the child is not yet required to possess, all at once, complete knowledge of every aspect of divine unity and justice. But once he knows God’s unity and justice, he must also know everything God has required him to do.

Abū al-Hudhayl goes so far as to say that if a person fails to acquire all this knowledge at the second stage, and then dies in the third stage, he dies as an unbeliever and an enemy of God, deserving eternal punishment in Hell.

Al-Baghdādī reports him as saying that in this second stage, once the child has reached maturity, he must also “know through transmitted reports what can be known only through hearing.”448

Al-Ashʿarī, however, reports Abū al-Hudhayl as saying that “maturity does not occur until reason is complete,” and that complete reason includes both “necessary knowledge” and “the ability to acquire knowledge.”449

This means that rational knowledge begins only after a person has passed through the stage of purely sensory knowledge, when the senses alone are developing.

Once that stage has been passed, the person enters maturity—that is, the stage in which reason has become complete.

At this point, the two kinds of rational knowledge begin: necessary knowledge and acquired, theoretical knowledge.

From Abū al-Hudhayl’s statements as a whole, we can conclude that theoretical rational knowledge belongs to the third and final stage in the development of reason.

At this stage, a person reaches a new understanding of divine unity and justice, as the Muʿtazilites understood them. This understanding is now based on argument, evidence, and demonstration rather than simply on the first self-evident judgments of reason.

3 — The Idea of the “Two Inner Promptings” in Rational Knowledge

The Muʿtazilite view of rational knowledge also rests on an idea that explains how rational choice takes place. They called this the idea of the “two inner promptings.”

They say:

“Before revelation is heard, a thinking person finds within himself two promptings. One urges him to know the Creator, to thank the Benefactor, and to follow the paths of goodness and virtue. The other urges him toward the opposite. He then chooses what leads to salvation and avoids what leads to destruction. These two newly arising promptings that call him in opposite directions are expressions of the speech and inner conversation of the self.”450

This shows that even the kind of necessary rational knowledge which Abū al-Hudhayl described as something “grasped by reason through reflection alone” still involves a process of human choice.

The Muʿtazilites were determined to preserve this principle of choice, not only in human actions but in the acquisition of knowledge as well.

This may explain al-Aswārī’s statement that a human being has a power that is equally capable of either of two opposites.451

The principle of choice itself requires a person to stand in relation to both possibilities before choosing one of them.

At first there is hesitation between two inner promptings: one calls the person toward one course, while the other calls him toward its opposite. The person then ends this hesitation by choosing one of them.

The Muʿtazilites call the human ability to do either a thing or its opposite, before the final choice is made, capacity (istiṭāʿa).

Al-Naẓẓām explains the idea of the two promptings on this basis when he says:

“There must be two promptings: one commanding a person to act, and the other telling him to hold back, so that choice can genuinely take place.”452

Again and again, whenever the Muʿtazilites discuss one of their basic principles or a question that follows from it, they make a point of defending human choice through the different theoretical principles on which their system rests.

This shows how strongly Muʿtazilite thought is marked by internal unity and coherence.

In our view, this is one of the features of a way of thinking deeply shaped by philosophical reflection and philosophical system-building.

4 — The Idea of Inner Speech

In the passage from al-Shahrastānī quoted above about the “two promptings,” there was a brief reference to what the Muʿtazilites called “the speech of the self and its inner conversation.”

We cannot simply pass over this without asking what they meant by it.

Al-Shahrastānī himself explains the Muʿtazilite view of this inner speech:

“As a person moves through the stages of reflection and reasoning, he proposes one statement and rejects another. He divides a general proposition into alternatives, rejects one of them, and thereby identifies the other. The act of dividing is itself the inner conversation of the self, while identifying one of the alternatives is itself the judgment of reason. A person may even take up a pen and write an entire volume from the conversation of his thought, filling a book with the conversation of his self, while his tongue remains silent and says nothing.”453

What can we learn from this account of the Muʿtazilite position?

We agree with Dr Albert Nasri Nader that in this discussion the Muʿtazilites “reached into the essence of the process of thought and regarded it as arising directly from the power of reason and being guided by its natural light.”454

The reason is that this passage gives an analytical description of the thinking process that comes close to a scientific account.

For the Muʿtazilites, the speech or inner conversation of the self is not some mysterious act of intuition outside reason or rational thought.

It is the first of two stages in the activity of theoretical consciousness. Together, these two stages make up the complete process of thinking and carry it forward toward reflection and reasoning.

As we understand al-Shahrastānī’s account, the speech of the self or its inner conversation is the internal process of reasoning by which the mind distinguishes one meaning from another.

It considers one general idea or another. It then looks at what that general idea contains, and at the different ways it can be divided. Finally, it selects one of these alternatives rather than the other.

So there are two movements within the overall process of thought.

The first is a movement of distinguishing, dividing, and comparing.

The second is a movement of deciding.

The first prepares the ground for the second.

The first is the “inner conversation of the self.”

The second is the “judgment of reason.”

This, then, is how the Muʿtazilites describe the process of rational reflection that produces rational knowledge, or science.

5 — Reason as the Most Distinctive Feature of Human Beings

The Muʿtazilites held that this inner speech forms the basis of rational thought.

They also held that it is completely internal and does not depend on spoken language. As al-Shahrastānī said in the passage above, a person may “take up a pen and write an entire volume from the conversation of his thought, filling a book with the conversation of his self, while his tongue remains silent and says nothing.”
